## Volume check now fails the suite

- **Stage 3.6**: a solid volume differing from the reference by >1% relative is a hard `--compare` error (was a warning).
- **Stage 4.1**: same for the output volume, and a written STEP that can't be re-read for round-trip validation is now an error too. This makes `-o /dev/null` incompatible with `--compare` — which exposed that `run_test_table.sh` had been using exactly that, silently skipping every 4.1 round-trip and volume check. The script now writes a real temp file, so the results table exercises the full pipeline including the round-trip.
- The whole zoo passes under the hard gates (worst volume error is cone_15x20's 2.0e-3, well under 1%), so the gate costs nothing today and would have caught the 46% regression that slipped through last time.

## Pre-NURBS work: what I did and what I recommend skipping

While assessing, I found and fixed one more robustness gap worth doing now: when both IntSS and the tangent-analytic constructions fail for an edge, stage 3.3 previously left no curve and 3.4 used fallback geometry with a warning. Now the **mesh boundary chain serves as the last-resort constructor** (vertex-to-vertex line, upgraded to the chain's circle when curved, accepted within surface tolerance). That recovered the two intersecting-fillet-cylinder junctions on stepped_block_toroidal_fine — 159/159 edge curves compute, and the "fallback geometry" warning class is gone from the zoo. This matters for NURBS specifically because IntSS gets *less* reliable with B-spline surfaces; the chain rescue is surface-type-agnostic. ## 🤖 Assistant
<!-- msg_011Ccrm2GViFYw7dmjDnoR3s -->

It's the one known unsatisfiable case in the seam-planning scheme, guarded by a hard error at [stage3.rs:4642](src/stage3.rs:4642). Here's the full picture:

## The invariant that creates the problem

A face whose boundary wraps a periodic direction (a full-revolution cylinder band, a torus fillet ring, an apex cap) needs a **seam edge** — an isoline at some azimuth — to close its UV boundary. For the wire to be topologically valid, the seam's endpoints must be **vertices of the winding boundary loops**; a vertex can't sit in the interior of another edge. So every winding loop of a wrapped face needs a vertex exactly where the seam crosses it. That vertex is the loop's *anchor*.

Since a face has exactly one seam, and the seam is an isoline at a single azimuth, a face with two winding loops (band between two circles) needs **both loops' anchors at the same wrap coordinate** in its chart.

## Why anchors can conflict

Anchors come in two kinds with very different freedom:

- A **vertex-free closed edge** (a plain junction circle) is a gauge: we rebuild it to start anywhere and put the anchor vertex there. Free choice — but only once, because the anchor becomes part of the *shared* edge, and both adjacent faces see it.
- A **real BRepVertex** already on the loop (a corner where 3+ surfaces meet) is a geometric fact. It cannot move.

Because anchors live on shared edges, the choice propagates: planning face A's seam pins the anchor on circle E; face B, which also wraps and shares E, must put *its* seam through that same point, which pins the anchor on B's other loop, and so on down the chain. `plan_seam_anchors` does this in waves — faces with an already-determined anchor plan first — and for coaxial stacks (plane–cylinder–torus–…, which is every model in the zoo) the constraints are always mutually satisfiable, because "same azimuth" means the same thing on every face in the chain.

The failure is when a face's two winding loops **both arrive pre-determined** — real vertices, or shared edges already anchored by earlier-planned neighbors — at azimuths that differ by more than the 0.01 rad congruence tolerance. No single isoline passes through both anchors, so no valid seam placement exists, and the code errors with "winding loops have incompatible seam anchors … edge splitting not implemented" rather than producing broken topology.

Two concrete geometries would trigger it:

1. **Vertex-split boundary circles at misaligned azimuths.** A cylinder band whose top circle is split by real vertices at 0° and 180° (some feature touches there) while the bottom circle is split at 90° and 270°. All anchors immovable, none aligned.
2. **Cycles of wrapped faces with holonomy.** A closed circuit of surfaces of revolution around *non-coaxial* axes — think a closed picture-frame pipe of straight cylinders and elbow tori. Each face rigidly maps "azimuth on one junction circle" to "azimuth on the next"; around a cycle the composition can return rotated, so no globally consistent assignment exists. (There's also a subtler third path: a closed-but-non-periodic curve, e.g. a closed IntSS BSpline, can't be re-ranged to a new start — the code keeps its existing start with a warning, and if that start later conflicts, same error.)

## What edge splitting would do

The recorded fix: when a face needs its seam at azimuth θ and a winding loop has no movable vertex there, **split the shared edge at the point with wrap-coordinate θ** — insert a new vertex, turning one edge into two arcs. Because the split happens on the shared `TopoDS_Edge`/`ReconEdge` before any face is assembled, both adjacent faces see the same two sub-edges: sharing is preserved, the neighbor's wire just contains two arcs instead of one, and pcurves are computed per sub-edge like any other. A loop could then carry anchors at as many azimuths as its neighbors demand.

## Why I deferred it

Three reasons, in decreasing importance: no current model reaches the case, so the implementation would be dead code with zero test coverage — exactly the kind of speculative machinery the rework removed; the NURBS pass won't reach it either, since `PointsToBSplineSurface` patches are non-periodic, so NURBS faces never wrap and never need seams; and it's the one extension that mutates the ReconEdge-level topology mid-assembly (edge lists, loop walks, and vertex adjacency all need updating), so it deserves a motivating model to develop against. The hard error message names the mechanism, so whoever first hits it inherits the plan rather than a mystery.

## 🤖 Assistant
<!-- msg_011CcrmCg1qyWKh5mX3ZrM2W -->

Three concrete classes of parts would hit it, in roughly increasing order of geometric depth. The common precondition for all of them: a face must *genuinely wrap* a periodic direction (needs a seam), and both of its winding boundary loops must arrive with anchors that are already pinned — by real vertices, or by seams of neighboring wrapped faces that share those loops' edges.

**1. A pipe crossed by two branch pipes (double-T manifold).** When two equal-ish cylinders intersect non-tangentially, the junction is a closed saddle curve — IntSS returns it as a closed but *non-periodic* B-spline, which the planner can't re-range to an arbitrary start (evaluating a non-periodic curve outside its stored range is invalid), so its anchor is stuck at the curve's existing start point. A single T-joint survives: the branch face has one stuck loop plus one free end circle, and the free one aligns to the stuck one. But the run-pipe segment *between* two branches is a wrapped cylinder whose two winding loops are both stuck saddle curves, each anchored wherever IntSS happened to start its parameterization — generically at different azimuths. This is the most likely first tripper in practice, and notably it's partly an implementation limitation rather than deep geometry: it could also be fixed by rebuilding closed IntSS B-splines as periodic curves (making them re-rangeable), which is cheaper than full edge splitting.

**2. A bore with mis-clocked features at its two ends.** Real vertices appear on a junction circle wherever a third surface touches it. Picture a through-hole whose top rim is nicked by a slot running north-south and whose bottom rim is nicked by a slot running east-west — with the slots touching only the rims, so the bore's cylindrical face still wraps. The top circle is now a chain of arcs with vertices at 0°/180°, the bottom at 90°/270°. All four anchors are immovable geometric facts, and no single generator line of the cylinder passes through a top vertex and a bottom vertex. Any "clocked" part — cross-drilled holes, keyway notches, lugs — where the angular features at the two ends of a full cylinder or cone don't line up is in this class.

**3. A closed pipe circuit routed in 3D (holonomy).** Chains of wrapped faces transport the anchor azimuth from one junction circle to the next: along a cylinder, the anchor's azimuth is preserved; around an elbow torus, it's carried by rotation about the elbow axis. In an *open* chain, or a *closed planar* circuit (a picture-frame duct), these transports compose to the identity, so propagation always finds a consistent assignment — that's why every current model works. But a closed circuit that leaves the plane — a duct run shaped like a skew polygon, three elbows bending in different planes before closing — composes rotations about non-parallel axes, and the net rotation around the loop is generically nonzero. This is genuine parallel-transport holonomy (the same reason a ribbon's frame doesn't close around a non-planar curve). The last face planned in the cycle inherits two anchors that disagree by exactly the holonomy angle, and no seam-anchoring scheme without splitting can fix that: it's a topological obstruction, not a bookkeeping one.

What *doesn't* trigger it — and why the zoo never has: coaxial stacks (every fillet/boss/hole model — all azimuth constraints agree by symmetry), planar closed circuits, single T-joints, and any part where features interrupt the wrap itself (a keyway cut through the full side wall makes the face partial-revolution, so no seam and no anchors are needed at all). And the NURBS pass stays clear of it entirely, since B-spline patches are non-periodic and never wrap.

If you ever want to pull the fix forward, a good forcing test model would be class 1 or 2 — both are easy to build in `gen-test-models` with OCCT booleans, whereas the holonomy circuit is the one that also stresses the propagation order.

```markdown
*Reconstruction note: the stage-3 shared-edge assembly rework (§3.x) is implemented and is the intended foundation for this stage. To reconstruct NURBS faces, extend `SurfaceChart` with a B-spline chart (point→UV via `ShapeAnalysis_Surface::ValueOfUV`, point_at via `Geom_Surface::Value`) and add the B-spline arm to `create_occt_surface`; the sampling/loop/winding/pcurve/wire machinery in stage 3.4 is surface-type-agnostic and needs no changes for non-periodic B-spline patches.*

**Implementation notes for the NURBS pass** (knowledge from the stage-3 rework, 2026-07-08 — read before starting):

- *The chart contract.* A chart provides `point_uv(p) → (u, v, pole_radius)` and `point_at(u, v)`, plus `u_periodic()`/`v_periodic()`. For a B-spline chart: `pole_radius` is ∞ (like the plane chart — fitted height-field patches have no UV degeneracies), and **both periodic flags must be false**. Every mod-2π unwrap/branch-lift in stage 3.4 is gated on those flags; reducing non-periodic parameter coordinates mod 2π silently corrupts them (this was a real bug on plane charts, masked for months by adaptive densification — see LEARNINGS). With both flags false, the whole seam/winding/degenerate-pole machinery self-disables and B-spline faces take the plain-loop path end to end.
- *The chart must wrap the exact `Handle(Geom_BSplineSurface)` stored in `FaceDescriptor.surface`* — never a reconstruction. (Analytic charts get away with rebuilding the gp_Ax3 only because that construction is deterministic.) Use one `ShapeAnalysis_Surface` per face: `new_handlegeomsurface` + `value_of_uv(&mut self, pnt, precision)` — note `&mut` (it caches internally). For sampling along an edge curve, prefer `next_value_of_uv(prev_uv, pnt, preci, maxpreci)` — it seeds the search from the previous sample, the B-spline analog of the analytic charts' branch-continuity unwrap. Validate each solution with `gap()` (ValueOfUV can return a poor projection rather than failing) and fall back to a fresh `value_of_uv` when the gap exceeds tolerance.
- *Every `match` on `SelectedSurface` needs a `BSpline` arm.* From crawling all of them: `create_occt_surface` and `surface_faces` (3.1), `surface_normal_at_point` (3.2 tangency detection and the 3.4 orientation compare — use D1 cross product on the handle), `project_point_to_selected` (corner-vertex refinement), `build_face_chart`, the concave-flag matches in `assemble_face`/`create_occt_faces_all`, the tangent-edge dispatch in 3.3, and the cosmetic `stype` labels + viz overlays.
- *Fix the fitted patch's normal orientation at fit time.* The shell orientation of a face comes from a single `concave` flag (natural surface normal vs. material). `GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface` follows the orientation of the input point grid, so build the grid such that d1u×d1v matches the mesh's outward normals — then B-spline faces are always `concave = false`/FORWARD and tangency-detection normals need no sign logic. Choosing the convention at fit time is one line; recovering it later is a per-face heuristic.
- *Edge curves will lean on the boundary chain.* Expect `GeomAPI_IntSS` to be flakier against B-spline surfaces than between quadrics, and expect tangent-classified junctions (a fitted patch usually meets its neighbors near-tangentially) to have no analytic construction — both routes end at the mesh-boundary-chain machinery (`repair_edge_curve_from_boundary`, `edge_curve_from_boundary_chain`), which is surface-pair-agnostic. The one known extension needed: the chain repair currently fits only a line or a circle through the chain; genuinely freeform junctions need a third arm that fits a B-spline curve through the chain vertices (`GeomAPI_PointsToBSpline`, binding verified) with the same accept-if-it-fits-the-chain-better rule. The repair already degrades gracefully (keeps the better curve), so this can be added when the first freeform-junction model demands it.
- *What NURBS will not stress — don't build for it:* seams, winding loops, degenerate pole edges, seam-anchor planning, and edge splitting all apply only to periodic/wrapped faces; non-periodic B-spline patches never take those paths.
- *Bindings verified present (2026-07-08):* `geom_api::PointsToBSplineSurface` (grid constructor `new_array2ofpnt_int2_shape_real`), `geom_api::PointsToBSpline` (curve fit), `shape_analysis::Surface::{new_handlegeomsurface, value_of_uv, next_value_of_uv, gap}`, `geom::BSplineSurface`; the generic `geom::Surface::{u_iso, v_iso, bounds, d0, d1}` all work on B-splines.
- *Test models first.* ccad cannot emit freeform surfaces (and the installed ccad segfaults on `ccad build` anyway); extend `gen-test-models` (src/bin/gen_test_models.rs) to write height-field STLs alongside reference STEPs built with `PointsToBSplineSurface` from the same grid. The `--compare` gates are now hard errors (volume >1%, round-trip re-read, surface distance), so NURBS reconstruction gets real pass/fail coverage from the first model — a green run means the geometry is actually right, not merely that nothing crashed.
```

```
400	
401	**Algorithm (\`refine_boundary_assignments\`, as implemented):**
402	1. Build the face → selected-surface map; walk every face that has a neighbor in a *different* selected surface (region-boundary faces — the original plan keyed on multi-hypothesis membership, but pruning/absorption destroy that; adjacency is the modern equivalent).
403	2. Compute the face's max vertex distance to its own surface and to each adjacent selected surface.
404	3. Move the face when an adjacent surface fits at least **2× better**. The margin prevents oscillation for true junction faces, whose vertices lie on both surfaces equally.
405	4. Iterate to a fixpoint (≤ 10 rounds; boundaries only move locally), then rebuild the affected hypotheses' vertex lists and drop emptied surfaces. Hypothesis *geometry* is not re-fitted: the fits were validated during BFS; only the region map changes.
406	
407	**Corner vertex refinement** (stage 3, \`refine_corner_vertices\`, runs after tangency detection): SHARP corner vertices are refined by cyclic projection onto their adjacent fitted surfaces — the raw mesh vertex at a corner is only as accurate as the tessellation puts it (where a fillet terminates, the mesh may have no vertex exactly at the CAD corner). Corners adjacent to any TANGENT edge are excluded: tangent surface pairs intersect along a curve rather than an isolated point, and cyclic projection slides along the tangent direction (observed drifting 0.57 mm). A safety guard keeps the original vertex if the refinement moves more than 2× surface tolerance.
408	
409	#### 2.7 NURBS fallback
410	
411	For groups of adjacent faces that remain as single-face planar hypotheses after stages 2.1–2.5 (i.e., they don't fit any analytic surface), try to fit a NURBS or B-spline surface.
412	
413	**Algorithm:**
414	1. Identify connected components of single-face planar hypothesis faces that are adjacent to each other in the mesh.
415	2. For each component with ≥ 4 faces:
416	   a. Compute UV parameterization of the face vertices (using discrete harmonic mapping or Floater's mean value coordinates).
417	   b. Use OCCT's \`GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface\` to fit a B-spline through the parameterized points.
418	   c. Validate: max vertex-to-surface distance < \`--surface-tolerance\`.
419	   d. If valid, create a NURBS hypothesis; if not, leave as single-face planar.
420	3. Add valid NURBS hypotheses to the surface selection.
421	
422	*Comment: NURBS fitting is complex: parameterization quality strongly affects fit quality, degree/knot selection matters, and thin features may need special handling. Start with OCCT’s built-in B-spline fitter which handles degree selection and parameterization internally. For “freeform” regions that are nearly planar, a plane with small tolerance is preferable to a NURBS that overfits noise.*
423	
424	*Reconstruction note: the stage-3 shared-edge assembly rework (§3.x) is implemented and is the intended foundation for this stage. To reconstruct NURBS faces, extend \`SurfaceChart\` with a B-spline chart (point→UV via \`ShapeAnalysis_Surface::ValueOfUV\`, point_at via \`Geom_Surface::Value\`) and add the B-spline arm to \`create_occt_surface\`; the sampling/loop/winding/pcurve/wire machinery in stage 3.4 is surface-type-agnostic and needs no changes for non-periodic B-spline patches.*
425	
426	**Implementation notes for the NURBS pass** (knowledge from the stage-3 rework, 2026-07-08 — read before starting):
427	
428	- *The chart contract.* A chart provides \`point_uv(p) → (u, v, pole_radius)\` and \`point_at(u, v)\`, plus \`u_periodic()\`/\`v_periodic()\`. For a B-spline chart: \`pole_radius\` is ∞ (like the plane chart — fitted height-field patches have no UV degeneracies), and **both periodic flags must be false**. Every mod-2π unwrap/branch-lift in stage 3.4 is gated on those flags; reducing non-periodic parameter coordinates mod 2π silently corrupts them (this was a real bug on plane charts, masked for months by adaptive densification — see LEARNINGS). With both flags false, the whole seam/winding/degenerate-pole machinery self-disables and B-spline faces take the plain-loop path end to end.
429	- *The chart must wrap the exact \`Handle(Geom_BSplineSurface)\` stored in \`FaceDescriptor.surface\`* — never a reconstruction. (Analytic charts get away with rebuilding the gp_Ax3 only because that construction is deterministic.) Use one \`ShapeAnalysis_Surface\` per face: \`new_handlegeomsurface\` + \`value_of_uv(&mut self, pnt, precision)\` — note \`&mut\` (it caches internally). For sampling along an edge curve, prefer \`next_value_of_uv(prev_uv, pnt, preci, maxpreci)\` — it seeds the search from the previous sample, the B-spline analog of the analytic charts' branch-continuity unwrap. Validate each solution with \`gap()\` (ValueOfUV can return a poor projection rather than failing) and fall back to a fresh \`value_of_uv\` when the gap exceeds tolerance.
430	- *Every \`match\` on \`SelectedSurface\` needs a \`BSpline\` arm.* From crawling all of them: \`create_occt_surface\` and \`surface_faces\` (3.1), \`surface_normal_at_point\` (3.2 tangency detection and the 3.4 orientation compare — use D1 cross product on the handle), \`project_point_to_selected\` (corner-vertex refinement), \`build_face_chart\`, the concave-flag matches in \`assemble_face\`/\`create_occt_faces_all\`, the tangent-edge dispatch in 3.3, and the cosmetic \`stype\` labels + viz overlays.
431	- *Fix the fitted patch's normal orientation at fit time.* The shell orientation of a face comes from a single \`concave\` flag (natural surface normal vs. material). \`GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface\` follows the orientation of the input point grid, so build the grid such that d1u×d1v matches the mesh's outward normals — then B-spline faces are always \`concave = false\`/FORWARD and tangency-detection normals need no sign logic. Choosing the convention at fit time is one line; recovering it later is a per-face heuristic.
432	- *Edge curves will lean on the boundary chain.* Expect \`GeomAPI_IntSS\` to be flakier against B-spline surfaces than between quadrics, and expect tangent-classified junctions (a fitted patch usually meets its neighbors near-tangentially) to have no analytic construction — both routes end at the mesh-boundary-chain machinery (\`repair_edge_curve_from_boundary\`, \`edge_curve_from_boundary_chain\`), which is surface-pair-agnostic. The one known extension needed: the chain repair currently fits only a line or a circle through the chain; genuinely freeform junctions need a third arm that fits a B-spline curve through the chain vertices (\`GeomAPI_PointsToBSpline\`, binding verified) with the same accept-if-it-fits-the-chain-better rule. The repair already degrades gracefully (keeps the better curve), so this can be added when the first freeform-junction model demands it.
433	- *What NURBS will not stress — don't build for it:* seams, winding loops, degenerate pole edges, seam-anchor planning, and edge splitting all apply only to periodic/wrapped faces; non-periodic B-spline patches never take those paths.
434	- *Bindings verified present (2026-07-08):* \`geom_api::PointsToBSplineSurface\` (grid constructor \`new_array2ofpnt_int2_shape_real\`), \`geom_api::PointsToBSpline\` (curve fit), \`shape_analysis::Surface::{new_handlegeomsurface, value_of_uv, next_value_of_uv, gap}\`, \`geom::BSplineSurface\`; the generic \`geom::Surface::{u_iso, v_iso, bounds, d0, d1}\` all work on B-splines.
435	- *Test models first.* ccad cannot emit freeform surfaces (and the installed ccad segfaults on \`ccad build\` anyway); extend \`gen-test-models\` (src/bin/gen_test_models.rs) to write height-field STLs alongside reference STEPs built with \`PointsToBSplineSurface\` from the same grid. The \`--compare\` gates are now hard errors (volume >1%, round-trip re-read, surface distance), so NURBS reconstruction gets real pass/fail coverage from the first model — a green run means the geometry is actually right, not merely that nothing crashed.
436	
437	---
438	
439	### Algorithm Reference
440	
441	Surface fitting math details (plane fitting, cylinder fitting, sphere fitting, cone fitting, torus fitting) and algorithmic techniques (Unified SOR Framework, Gaussian Map Classification, Medial Axis / Tube Center Method, Quadric Fitting) are documented in [SURFACE_FITTING.md](SURFACE_FITTING.md).
442	
443	---
444	
445	### Stage 3: Surface Reconstruction
446	
447	Build OCCT B-Rep topology (faces, edges, vertices) from the selected surfaces. This is the most complex stage — surface intersections in 3D are numerically delicate, and small perturbations can cause large changes in intersection curves or cause them to disappear.
448	
449	**Core data structures:**
450	
451	A vector of \`FaceDescriptor\` structs, one per selected surface:
452	- \`selected_surface_idx: usize\` — Index into the selected surfaces from stage 2.6.
453	- \`surface: OwnedPtr<HandleGeomSurface>\` — Infinite OCCT surface, type-erased (created in 3.1).
454	- \`adjacent_faces: Vec<usize>\` — Indices of adjacent FaceDescriptors, ordered topologically around this face's boundary. A face may appear multiple times if it shares multiple edges with this face (e.g., a cylindrical face adjacent to itself via a seam edge).
455	- \`edge_indices: Vec<usize>\` — ReconEdge indices. \`edge_indices[i]\` is the edge between this face and \`adjacent_faces[i]\`.
456	- \`vertex_indices: Vec<usize>\` — BRepVertex indices at corners. \`vertex_indices[i]\` is the vertex between \`edge_indices[i]\` and \`edge_indices[(i+1) % N]\`.
457	- The \`TopoDS_Face\` objects built from these descriptors live in \`Stage3Output.faces\` (parallel to \`face_descriptors\`), populated in 3.4, with \`Stage3Output.concave_faces\` flagging faces whose natural normal points into the material.
458	
459	A vector of \`ReconEdge\` structs:
460	- \`face_indices: [usize; 2]\` — Indices of the two adjacent FaceDescriptors.
461	- \`vertex_indices: [usize; 2]\` — Indices of the two BRepVertices at each end. For closed-loop edges (no vertices), both are \`usize::MAX\`.
462	- \`curve_3d: Option<OwnedPtr<HandleGeomCurve>>\` — 3D intersection curve, trimmed to vertex endpoints (populated in 3.3).
463	- \`pcurves: [Option<OwnedPtr<HandleGeom2dCurve>>; 2]\` — pcurve on each adjacent face's surface, parallel to \`face_indices\` (populated in 3.4 by the shared-edge assembler).
464	- \`tangent: bool\` — Whether the adjacent surfaces are tangent along this edge (detected in 3.2).
465	- \`mesh_boundary_vertices: Vec<usize>\` — Mesh vertex indices along this boundary, ordered along the boundary.
466	
467	A vector of \`BRepVertex\` structs:
468	- \`point: [f64; 3]\` — 3D position: the mesh vertex position, refined for sharp corners by cyclic projection onto the adjacent fitted surfaces (see stage 2.6 refitting notes).
469	- \`adjacent_faces: Vec<usize>\` — Indices of FaceDescriptors meeting at this vertex, in topological order.
470	- \`adjacent_edges: Vec<usize>\` — Indices of ReconEdges meeting at this vertex, in topological order.
471	- \`uv_coords: Vec<(f64, f64)>\` — UV coordinates of this vertex on each adjacent face's surface, parallel to \`adjacent_faces\` (populated in 3.4).
472	- Per-vertex tolerances live on the shared \`TopoDS_Vertex\` objects, raised adaptively in 3.4 to cover each vertex's distance from its curve endpoints.
473	
474	#### 3.1 Create OCCT surface objects and build adjacency graph
475	
476	**Surface creation** (\`create_occt_surface\`):
477	- For each selected surface, create the corresponding infinite OCCT surface:
478	    - Planar → \`geom::Plane::new_pnt_dir\` with \`gp::Pnt\` at centroid and \`gp::Dir\` along normal. Wrapped via \`to_handle().to_handle_surface()\`.
479	    - Cylindrical → \`geom::CylindricalSurface::new_ax3_real\` with \`gp::Ax3\` from axis origin/direction and radius. Wrapped via \`to_handle().to_handle_surface()\`.
```

```
1	//! Generates test models that cannot be produced via ccad, using OCCT
2	//! directly. The STL/STEP pairs are written to tests/occt/ and committed to
3	//! the repo, so this tool only needs to be re-run when a model changes.
4	//!
5	//! Usage: gen_test_models [<output_dir>]   (default: tests/occt)
6	//!
7	//! Models:
8	//! - hollow_cube: 20 mm cube with a fully enclosed 10 mm cubic void at its
9	//!   center. Exercises multi-shell solid construction: the mesh has two
10	//!   closed shells and the STEP output must be ONE solid with an internal
11	//!   cavity (volume 7000 mm³), not two nested solids.
12	//! - full_torus: complete donut (R=10, r=3). Exercises the doubly-periodic
13	//!   seam handling in stage 3.4: a complete torus face needs both a U seam
14	//!   (around the major circle) and a V seam (around the tube).
15	
16	use opencascade_sys::{b_rep_algo_api, b_rep_mesh, b_rep_prim_api, gp, message, stl_api, topo_ds};
17	
18	fn write_pair(shape: &topo_ds::Shape, dir: &str, name: &str) {
19	    // Tessellate for STL (also used by STEP viewers, harmless for STEP).
20	    let _mesh = b_rep_mesh::IncrementalMesh::new_shape_real_bool_real_bool(
21	        shape, 0.1, false, 28.6_f64.to_radians(), false,
22	    );
23	
24	    let stl_path = format!("{dir}/{name}.stl");
25	    let mut writer = stl_api::Writer::new();
26	    *writer.ascii_mode() = false;
27	    let progress = message::ProgressRange::new();
28	    if !writer.write(shape, &stl_path, &progress) {
29	        panic!("failed to write {stl_path}");
30	    }
31	    println!("wrote {stl_path}");
32	
33	    let step_path = format!("{dir}/{name}.step");
34	    brepper::write_step_file(shape, &step_path).expect("failed to write STEP");
35	    println!("wrote {step_path}");
36	}
37	
38	fn hollow_cube(dir: &str) {
39	    let mut outer = b_rep_prim_api::MakeBox::new_real3(20.0, 20.0, 20.0);
40	    let inner_corner = gp::Pnt::new_real3(5.0, 5.0, 5.0);
41	    let mut inner = b_rep_prim_api::MakeBox::new_pnt_real3(&inner_corner, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0);
42	
43	    let progress = message::ProgressRange::new();
44	    let mut cut = b_rep_algo_api::Cut::new_shape2_progressrange(
45	        outer.shape(),
46	        inner.shape(),
47	        &progress,
48	    );
49	    assert!(cut.is_done(), "hollow_cube boolean cut failed");
50	    write_pair(cut.shape(), dir, "hollow_cube");
51	}
52	
53	fn full_torus(dir: &str) {
54	    let mut torus = b_rep_prim_api::MakeTorus::new_real2(10.0, 3.0);
55	    write_pair(torus.shape(), dir, "full_torus");
56	}
57	
58	fn main() {
59	    let dir = std::env::args().nth(1).unwrap_or_else(|| "tests/occt".to_string());
60	    std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir).expect("failed to create output dir");
61	    hollow_cube(&dir);
62	    full_torus(&dir);
63	}
64	
```

```
This directory contains test STL files organized by source:

## Directory Structure

- \`manual/\` - Hand-written ASCII STL files for basic testing
- \`generated/\` - STL files exported from CAD programs (Fusion 360, Onshape)

## Manual Test Files

### cube.stl
A unit cube (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) with 12 triangles. Used for basic import and sampling tests.

## Recommended Test Models to Export

When exporting from Fusion 360 or Onshape, use the following models to test different surface types and mesh densities:

### Basic Geometric Primitives
1. **sphere_25mm.stl** - 25mm diameter sphere
   - Tests: spherical surface fitting, uniform curvature
   - Export at: Fine mesh (many small triangles)

2. **cylinder_10x30mm.stl** - 10mm diameter, 30mm height cylinder
   - Tests: cylindrical surface fitting, flat end caps
   - Export at: Normal mesh

3. **cone_15x20mm.stl** - 15mm base diameter, 20mm height cone
   - Tests: conical surface fitting, point singularity
   - Export at: Normal mesh

### Multi-Surface Models
4. **rounded_cube_10mm_r2.stl** - S cube with 2mm edge fillets
   - Tests: plane + cylindrical fillet detection, surface transitions
   - Export at: Fine mesh to capture fillets

5. **pipe_elbow_10mm.stl** - 90° pipe elbow, 10mm inner diameter
   - Tests: toroidal surfaces, cylindrical surfaces
   - Export at: Fine mesh

6. **bracket_simple.stl** - L-bracket with holes
   - Tests: multiple planes at angles, cylindrical holes
   - Export at: Normal mesh

### Varying Triangle Sizes
7. **plate_with_hole_100x50.stl** - 100x50mm plate with 10mm center hole
   - Tests: large flat faces vs small curved facesc
   - Important: Do NOT use adaptive mesh - want to see large triangles on plate
   - Export at: Coarse mesh

8. **stepped_block.stl** - Block with steps of varying sizes
   - Tests: many parallel planes at different heights
   - Export at: Coarse mesh (want clean planar triangles)

### Complex Surfaces
9. **dome_hemisphere_20mm.stl** - 20mm diameter hemisphere
   - Tests: large curved surface recognition
   - Export at: Fine mesh

10. **chamfered_cube_10mm_c1.stl** - 10mm cube with 1mm edge chamfers
    - Tests: angled plane detection, small faces
    - Export at: Normal mesh

## Export Settings

### Fusion 360
- Format: STL (ASCII or Binary)
- Refinement: Choose based on test needs:
  - Coarse: For testing large face handling
  - Medium: General testing
  - Fine: For testing curved surface detail
- Units: Millimeters (default)

### Onshape
- Format: STL
- Units: Millimeters
- Resolution:
  - Coarse: For flat surfaces
  - Medium: General testing  
  - Fine: For curved surfaces
- Triangle count: Note the count for expected behavior

## Naming Convention

\`\`\`
<shape>_<dimension_mm>[_<feature>].stl
\`\`\`

Examples:
- \`sphere_25mm.stl\`
- \`cylinder_10x30mm.stl\` (diameter x height)
- \`cube_10mm_r2_fillet.stl\` (10mm cube, 2mm fillet radius)

## Adding New Test Files

When adding new test STL files:
1. Place in appropriate subdirectory (\`manual/\` or \`generated/\`)
2. Update this README with:
   - Filename and dimensions
   - What surface types it tests
   - Export settings used
3. Consider adding a corresponding unit test if testing new functionality
```

```
7:opencascade-sys = { path = "../opencascade-rs/crates/opencascade-sys" }
#!/bin/bash
# Run all STL test files through brepper and generate tests/RESULTS.md
# Usage: ./scripts/run_test_table.sh [<brepper_binary>]
# Default binary: ./target/release/brepper

set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

BREPPER="${1:-./target/release/brepper}"

if [ ! -x "$BREPPER" ]; then
    echo "Error: brepper binary not found at $BREPPER" >&2
    echo "Build with: cargo build --release" >&2
    exit 1
fi

OUTPUT="tests/RESULTS.md"

# Map STL file to its corresponding STEP file
find_step() {
    local stl="$1"
    local dir=$(dirname "$stl")
    local base=$(basename "$stl" .stl)

    # Strip .ascii suffix if present
    base="${base%.ascii}"

    # Try exact match first
    if [ -f "$dir/$base.step" ]; then
        echo "$dir/$base.step"
        return
    fi

    # Strip resolution suffixes (_coarse, _medium, _fine, _low, _high)
    local stripped=$(echo "$base" | sed -E 's/_(coarse|medium|fine|low|high)$//')
    if [ -f "$dir/$stripped.step" ]; then
        echo "$dir/$stripped.step"
        return
    fi

    echo ""
}

# Special flags for specific tests
get_extra_flags() {
    local stl="$1"
    case "$stl" in
        *rounded_cube_10_r2_coarse*)
            echo "--angular-tolerance 20"
            ;;
        *)
            echo ""
            ;;
    esac
}

# Count totals
total=0
pass_count=0
fail_count=0
bad_count=0

# Collect results into arrays for two-pass output
declare -a all_stls all_steps all_statuses all_times all_dirs

for stl in $(find tests -name '*.stl' | sort); do
    step=$(find_step "$stl")
    extra_flags=$(get_extra_flags "$stl")

    if [ -z "$step" ]; then
        compare_flag=""
    else
        compare_flag="--compare $step"
    fi

    tmpout=$(mktemp)
    # Write a real STEP file so stage 4.1's round-trip re-read and volume
    # comparison actually run (-o /dev/null cannot be re-read and fails).
    outstep="$tmpout.step"
    start_time=$(python3 -c 'import time; print(time.monotonic())')

    if timeout 120 "$BREPPER" "$stl" -o "$outstep" $compare_flag $extra_flags > "$tmpout" 2>&1; then
        status="✓"
        is_pass=1
    else
        exitcode=$?
        is_pass=0
        if [ $exitcode -eq 124 ]; then
            status="FAIL: timeout"
        else
            # Extract failure info from output
            last_line=$(tail -5 "$tmpout" | grep -iE "error|panic|fail|abort|thread" | tail -1 || true)
            if [ -n "$last_line" ]; then
                status="FAIL: $(echo "$last_line" | head -c 80)"
            else
                status="FAIL (exit $exitcode)"
            fi
        fi
    fi

    end_time=$(python3 -c 'import time; print(time.monotonic())')
    elapsed=$(python3 -c "print(f'{$end_time - $start_time:.2f}')")

    relpath="${stl#tests/}"
    stl_dir=$(dirname "$relpath")

    all_stls+=("$stl")
    all_steps+=("$step")
    all_statuses+=("$status")
    all_times+=("$elapsed")
    all_dirs+=("$stl_dir")

    total=$((total + 1))
    if [[ "$stl_dir" == "bad" ]]; then
        bad_count=$((bad_count + 1))
    elif [[ $is_pass -eq 1 ]]; then
        pass_count=$((pass_count + 1))
    else
        fail_count=$((fail_count + 1))
    fi

    # Print progress to stderr
    echo "  $status ($elapsed s) $stl" >&2

    rm -f "$tmpout" "$outstep"
done

# Generate RESULTS.md
{
    cat <<'HEADER'
<!-- This file is generated by scripts/run_test_table.sh — do not edit manually.
     To regenerate: ./scripts/run_test_table.sh [path/to/brepper]
     Default binary: ./target/release/brepper -->

# Test Results

Each STL test file is run through brepper with \`--compare\` against
its corresponding STEP file (when available):

\`\`\`
brepper <input.stl> -o <tmpfile>.step --compare <input.step>
\`\`\`

Special flags:
- \`rounded_cube_10_r2_coarse\`: \`--angular-tolerance 20\`

HEADER

    echo "Tests last run: $(date +%Y-%m-%d)."
    echo ""

    # Group by directory
    current_dir=""
    for i in "${!all_stls[@]}"; do
        stl="${all_stls[$i]}"
        step="${all_steps[$i]}"
        status="${all_statuses[$i]}"
        elapsed="${all_times[$i]}"
        dir="${all_dirs[$i]}"

        if [[ "$dir" != "$current_dir" ]]; then
            if [[ -n "$current_dir" ]]; then
                echo ""
            fi
            echo "## ${dir}"
            echo ""
            echo "| Test File | Status | Time | Notes |"
            echo "|-----------|--------|------|-------|"
            current_dir="$dir"
        fi

        basename=$(basename "$stl")
        if [[ "$status" == "✓" ]]; then
            echo "| $basename | ✓ | ${elapsed}s | |"
        else
            # Extract notes from the status
            notes="${status#FAIL: }"
            if [[ "$notes" == "$status" ]]; then
                echo "| $basename | $status | ${elapsed}s | |"
            else
                echo "| $basename | FAIL | ${elapsed}s | $notes |"
            fi
        fi
    done

    echo ""
    echo "## Summary"
    echo ""
    echo "- **Total test files**: $total"
    echo "- **Passing**: $pass_count / $total"
    echo "- **Expected failures (bad/)**: $bad_count"
    echo "- **Failing non-bad tests**: $fail_count"

} > "$OUTPUT"

echo "" >&2
echo "Results written to $OUTPUT" >&2
echo "Total: $total, Passing: $pass_count, Bad: $bad_count, Failing: $fail_count" >&2
```

```
#!/bin/zsh

# Run step-measure-tolerance on all STL/STEP pairs under tests/ and print a table
# with per-group (suffix) summary rows.
# Distances displayed in mm. OCCT converts STEP units to mm internally.
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
PROJECT_DIR="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.." && pwd)"
BINARY="$PROJECT_DIR/target/release/step-measure-tolerance"

# Build release binary
echo "Building step-measure-tolerance (release)..." >&2
cargo build --release --bin step-measure-tolerance --manifest-path "$PROJECT_DIR/Cargo.toml" 2>&1 | tail -1 >&2

ROW_FMT="%-40s %12s %12s %12s %12s %10s %10s %10s %8s %8s %10s %10s %10s %10s\n"

print_header() {
    printf "$ROW_FMT" "Test Case" "Vtx Max mm" "Vtx Avg mm" "Ctr Max mm" "Ctr Avg mm" "Max Dim" "Ang Max °" "Ang Avg °" "Nodes" "Faces" "STEP Area" "STL Area" "STEP Vol" "STL Vol"
    print_sep
}

print_sep() {
    printf "$ROW_FMT" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..40})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..12})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..12})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..12})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..12})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..10})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..10})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..10})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..8})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..8})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..10})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..10})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..10})" \
        "$(printf '%0.s-' {1..10})"
}

# Format vertex distance (mm, 6 decimal places)
fmt_vtx() {
    awk "BEGIN { v = $1 + 0; if (v == 0) printf \"0\"; else printf \"%.6f\", v }"
}

# Format centroid distance (mm, 3 decimal places)
fmt_ctr() {
    awk "BEGIN { v = $1 + 0; if (v == 0) printf \"0\"; else printf \"%.3f\", v }"
}
# Format angular deviation (degrees, 4 decimal places)
fmt_ang() {
    awk "BEGIN { v = $1 + 0; if (v == 0) printf \"0\"; else printf \"%.4f\", v }"
}


# Collect all STL files into an array (avoids subshell from pipe)
stl_files=(${(f)"$(find "$PROJECT_DIR/tests" -name '*.stl' -not -name '*.ascii.stl' | sort)"})

# Track per-group maximums
typeset -A group_vtx_max group_vtx_avg group_ctr_max group_ctr_avg group_ang_max group_ang_avg
```
</details>

```
# Instructions for LLM Coding Assistants

This file contains guidelines for AI/LLM coding assistants working on this project. Read ALL of AGENTS.md - no just the first 100 lines.

The shell is zsh. Use zsh quoting conventions. "echo ===" will fail, and globs in flags must be quoted.

### Commit Checklist (MANDATORY — verify before every commit)

- \`cargo clippy\` emits no warnings.
- Build passes with no errors or warnings.

## Project Layout

This is a Rust project. Key locations:

- \`README.md\` - Program usage. Read it.
- \`DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md\` - Development plan. Read it.
- \`Cargo.toml\` — Rust project manifest
- \`src/\` — Rust source files
  - \`bin/brepper.rs\` — the main program
  - \`bin/step_measure_tolerance.rs\` — utility to measure distances from STL to correpsonding STEP
  - \`bin/viewer.rs\` — GUI to visualize STL or STEP files
- \`scripts/\` — shell scripts for batch operations over test data
  - \`step_distance_table.sh\` - runs \`step_measure_tolerance\` over all STL/STEP pairs and summarizes statistics
- \`tests/\` — STL and STEP test file pairs
  - \`manual/\` — handcrafted simple models
  - \`onshape/\` — models exported from Onshape
  - \`ccad/generated/\` — models generated via CodeCAD

### OCCT / opencascade-rs

The project uses the \`opencascade-sys\` crate (auto-generated Rust FFI bindings to OpenCASCADE Technology) via a path dependency. MANDATORY: All useful C++ OCCT APIs should be available in the binding - if you want to use one that doesn't seem to be bound, complain loudly about it AND STOP.

\`\`\`
../opencascade-rs/crates/opencascade-sys   ← Rust FFI bindings (8700+ types)
../opencascade-rs/crates/opencascade-sys/PORTING.md  ← Naming conventions & usage patterns
../opencascade-rs/crates/opencascade-sys/generated/  ← All generated .rs modules
../opencascade-rs/crates/occt-sys/OCCT/src/  ← OCCT C++ source (for reading docs/headers)
../opencascade-rs/crates/occt-sys/OCCT/dox/  ← OCCT C++ documentation
\`\`\`

The \`builtin\` feature (default) compiles OCCT from source — first build takes ~8 minutes. Subsequent builds are fast.

## Commit Messages

All commit messages must include:

1. **A clear description** of the changes made
2. **The AI agent/model** used to generate the changes (e.g., "Claude Sonnet 4 (Anthropic, 2025)")
3. **The user prompts** that led to the changes

Format:
\`\`\`
<descriptive commit title>

<detailed description of changes>

---
Generated with assistance from <model name> (<provider>, <year>)
```
</details>

```
## Development Plan Maintenance

Keep DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md up to date with each commit:

1. **Mark completed items** - Check off (\`[x]\`) any Implementation Phases items that are completed by the commit
2. **Add new tasks** - If work reveals new tasks or sub-tasks not in the plan, add them to the appropriate phase
3. **Modify existing tasks** - If a planned approach changes (e.g., different algorithm, new dependency), update the relevant sections
4. **Include in commit** - Changes to DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md should be part of the same commit as the implementation work

## README Maintenance

Keep README.md up to date when changes affect user-facing behavior:

1. **New dependencies** - Add to the dependencies list with installation instructions
2. **New CLI options** - Update the usage examples and options documentation
3. **Changed defaults** - Document any changes to default parameter values
4. **New features** - Add brief descriptions of significant new capabilities
5. **Include in commit** - README updates should be part of the same commit as the feature work

### IMPORTANT: Time Builds and Tests

**Always** prefix build and test commands with \`time\`. When they take more than 2 minutes ask the user whether to speed them up.

Correct: \`time make -j4 2>&1\`
Correct: \`time ctest --output-on-failure -j4 2>&1\`

## Temporary Test Code

When writing temporary code for debugging or testing:

1. **Put files in \`tmp/\`** - This directory is in the project root and ignored by git. Don't use \`/tmp\` or other directories outside the workspace.

2. **Don't delete temporary code** - Leave it in \`tmp/\` in case it's useful later.

## Library Reuse

Before implementing non-trivial functionality (text rendering, file parsing, data structures, etc.), search for existing open-source libraries that provide that functionality. Evaluate whether using a library will be better for code simplicity and maintainability than writing it from scratch. Consider factors like: compatibility with existing dependencies, maintenance status, API complexity, and how well the library fits the use case. Then go with your decision — either use the library or implement it yourself — and briefly explain why.

## Generating CodeCAD Test Models

Test models can be generated with ccad - see \`../codecad/docs\` for documentation. To regenerate the STL and STEP files for CodeCAD-based tests:

\`\`\`bash
# Requires 'ccad' tool installed (https://codecad.xyz)
./tests/ccad/generate_models.sh
\`\`\`
```
