//=================================================================================================

void GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface::Init(const TColgp_Array2OfPnt&        Points,
                                          const Approx_ParametrizationType ParType,
                                          const Standard_Integer           DegMin,
                                          const Standard_Integer           DegMax,
                                          const GeomAbs_Shape              Continuity,
                                          const Standard_Real              Tol3D,
                                          const Standard_Boolean           thePeriodic)
{
  Standard_Integer Imin = Points.LowerRow();
  Standard_Integer Imax = Points.UpperRow();
  Standard_Integer Jmin = Points.LowerCol();
  Standard_Integer Jmax = Points.UpperCol();

  Standard_Real Tol2D = Tol3D;

  // first approximate the U isos:
  Standard_Integer add = 1;
  if (thePeriodic)
  {
    add = 2;
  }
  AppDef_MultiLine Line(Jmax - Jmin + 1);
  Standard_Integer i, j;

  for (j = Jmin; j <= Jmax; j++)
  {
    AppDef_MultiPointConstraint MP(Imax - Imin + add, 0);
    for (i = Imin; i <= Imax; i++)
    {
      MP.SetPoint(i, Points(i, j));
    }
    if (thePeriodic)
    {
      MP.SetPoint(Imax + 1, Points(1, j));
    }
    Line.SetValue(j, MP);
  }

  Standard_Integer nbit       = 2;
  Standard_Boolean UseSquares = Standard_False;
  if (Tol3D <= 1.e-3)
    UseSquares = Standard_True;

  AppDef_BSplineCompute
    TheComputer(DegMin, DegMax, Tol3D, Tol2D, nbit, Standard_True, ParType, UseSquares);

  switch (Continuity)
  {
    case GeomAbs_C0:
      TheComputer.SetContinuity(0);
      break;

    case GeomAbs_G1:
    case GeomAbs_C1:
      TheComputer.SetContinuity(1);
      break;

    case GeomAbs_G2:
    case GeomAbs_C2:
      TheComputer.SetContinuity(2);
      break;

    default:
      TheComputer.SetContinuity(3);
  }

  if (Tol3D <= 0.0)
  {
    TheComputer.Interpol(Line);
  }
  else
  {
    TheComputer.Perform(Line);
  }

  const AppParCurves_MultiBSpCurve& TheCurve = TheComputer.Value();

  Standard_Integer               VDegree = TheCurve.Degree();
  TColgp_Array1OfPnt             Poles(1, TheCurve.NbPoles());
  const TColStd_Array1OfReal&    VKnots = TheCurve.Knots();
  const TColStd_Array1OfInteger& VMults = TheCurve.Multiplicities();

  Standard_Integer nbisosu = Imax - Imin + add;
  AppDef_MultiLine Line2(nbisosu);

  for (i = 1; i <= nbisosu; i++)
  {
    TheCurve.Curve(i, Poles);
    AppDef_MultiPointConstraint MP(Poles.Upper(), 0);
    for (j = 1; j <= Poles.Upper(); j++)
    {
      MP.SetPoint(j, Poles(j));
    }
    Line2.SetValue(i, MP);
  }

  // approximate the resulting poles:

  AppDef_BSplineCompute
    TheComputer2(DegMin, DegMax, Tol3D, Tol2D, nbit, Standard_True, ParType, UseSquares);
  if (Tol3D <= 0.0)
  {
    if (thePeriodic)
    {
      TheComputer2.SetPeriodic(thePeriodic);
    }
    TheComputer2.Interpol(Line2);
  }
  else
  {
    if (thePeriodic && Line2.NbMultiPoints() > 2)
    {
      TheComputer2.SetPeriodic(thePeriodic);
      //
      TColStd_Array1OfReal aPars(1, Line2.NbMultiPoints());
      BuildParameters(Line2, ParType, aPars);
      math_Vector aTang(1, 3 * Poles.Upper());
      BuildPeriodicTangent(Line2, aPars, aTang);
      Standard_Integer ind = 1;
      TheCurve.Curve(ind, Poles);
      AppDef_MultiPointConstraint MP1(Poles.Upper(), 0);
      for (j = 1; j <= Poles.Upper(); j++)
      {
        MP1.SetPoint(j, Poles(j));
        Standard_Integer k = 3 * (j - 1);
        gp_Vec           aT(aTang(k + 1), aTang(k + 2), aTang(k + 3));
        MP1.SetTang(j, aT);
      }
      Line2.SetValue(ind, MP1);
      //
      ind = Line2.NbMultiPoints();
      TheCurve.Curve(ind, Poles);
      AppDef_MultiPointConstraint MP2(Poles.Upper(), 0);
      for (j = 1; j <= Poles.Upper(); j++)
      {
        MP2.SetPoint(j, Poles(j));
        Standard_Integer k = 3 * (j - 1);
        gp_Vec           aT(aTang(k + 1), aTang(k + 2), aTang(k + 3));
        MP2.SetTang(j, aT);
      }
      Line2.SetValue(ind, MP2);
    }
    TheComputer2.Perform(Line2);
  }

  const AppParCurves_MultiBSpCurve& TheCurve2 = TheComputer2.Value();

  Standard_Integer               UDegree = TheCurve2.Degree();
  TColgp_Array1OfPnt             Poles2(1, TheCurve2.NbPoles());
  const TColStd_Array1OfReal&    UKnots = TheCurve2.Knots();
  const TColStd_Array1OfInteger& UMults = TheCurve2.Multiplicities();

  // computing the surface
  TColgp_Array2OfPnt ThePoles(1, Poles2.Upper(), 1, Poles.Upper());
  for (j = 1; j <= Poles.Upper(); j++)
  {
    TheCurve2.Curve(j, Poles2);
    for (i = 1; i <= Poles2.Upper(); i++)
    {
      ThePoles(i, j) = Poles2(i);
    }
  }

  mySurface = new Geom_BSplineSurface(ThePoles, UKnots, VKnots, UMults, VMults, UDegree, VDegree);
  if (thePeriodic && Line2.NbMultiPoints() > 2)
  {
    mySurface->SetUPeriodic();
  }

  myIsDone = Standard_True;
}

//=================================================================================================

void GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface::Init(const TColgp_Array2OfPnt& Points,
                                          const Standard_Real       Weight1,
                                          const Standard_Real       Weight2,

> Looking at the OCCT source code, I can see the convention is confirmed: periodic along U means the row index is the first array index. The code appends a copy of the first row at the end, and with the constraint setup using `Imax - Imin + add` where add equals 2, it creates the proper number of points for the periodic dimension.
> 
> The interpolation path calls `SetUPeriodic()` unconditionally when the periodic flag is set and there are more than 2 multi-points — for a ring of ~93 points that's 94 points total, which easily satisfies this condition.
> 
> In the first pass, the algorithm approximates the U isos by creating an AppDef_MultiLine where each MultiPoint corresponds to a column. So the first fit actually runs along the J direction (columns), producing curves parameterized by V — these are the U isoparametric curves, one per row. The VKnots come from fitting across the J dimension, which makes sense since J maps to the V parameter. When periodic, the MultiPoint includes that extra wrapped point for each row to handle the wraparound.
> 
> Each MultiPoint represents a station along the fit parameter and holds multiple 3D channels that get fitted simultaneously. The fit produces one B-spline per channel (row i), and they all share the same knots and parameters along the J direction. So channel i's resulting curve passes through all the points in row i across the columns — that's the V-direction curve at a fixed U station.
> 
> These rows correspond to U-isos in OCCT terminology — curves at constant U parameter. The comment about approximating U-isos confirms this: rows are constant-U, columns are constant-V. The first fit adds an extra channel that duplicates the first row, so it produces Imax-Imin+2 iso curves total (rows 1 through Imax plus a wrapped copy of row 1), and these become the MultiPoints fed into the second fit.
> 
> The second fit runs along the U direction with periodic boundary conditions, treating the first and last MultiPoints as identical to close the loop. OCCT handles the duplication internally, so the input array shouldn't duplicate the closing row — the library adds that itself. The chord-length parametrization along U then comes from fitting over the pole positions of these iso curves.
> 
> For the interpolation path when Tol3D ≤ 0, I need to verify that AppDef_BSplineCompute honors SetPeriodic during the Interpol call, since the tangent-building branch only runs during Perform. A test will show empirically whether periodic interpolation produces C2 continuity across the closure.
> 
> Regarding knot multiplicities at the seam: if the periodic surface has multiplicity 1 there, C2 continuity follows by construction. I should also confirm that SetUKnots on a periodic surface handles affine scaling of knots correctly—it should, since the basis functions scale exactly with affine transformations.

//! Probe: conventions of GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface::Interpolate with
//! thePeriodic=true, for the §2.7 closed-band periodic pipeline
//! (DEVELOPMENT_PLAN "Path to the non-compromised design").
//!
//! Questions answered:
//!  1. Periodic along which array index? (expected: U = first index, rows,
//!     closing row omitted — OCCT appends the wrap copy itself)
//!  2. Is the result IsUPeriodic, and is closure C2?
//!  3. Does the surface interpolate the input points?
//!  4. Does SetUKnots rescale to [0, 2π] exactly (geometry unchanged)?
//!  5. Does ShapeAnalysis_Surface return principal U in [0, 2π) afterwards?
//!  6. Does UIso(0) pass through the first input row (the seam gauge)?
//!  7. Does IntSS(plane, periodic surface) return a usable closed curve?

use opencascade_sys::{
    approx, gp, geom, geom_api, shape_analysis, t_col_std, t_colgp,
};

const TWO_PI: f64 = 2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI;

fn pt(p: [f64; 3]) -> opencascade_sys::OwnedPtr<gp::Pnt> {
    gp::Pnt::new_real3(p[0], p[1], p[2])
}

fn dist(a: &gp::Pnt, b: [f64; 3]) -> f64 {
    ((a.x() - b[0]).powi(2) + (a.y() - b[1]).powi(2) + (a.z() - b[2]).powi(2)).sqrt()
}

fn main() {
    // Synthetic closed band: elliptical rings (a=27, b=10, h=18 — the
    // elliptical_cylinder model's proportions), n_around stations WITHOUT
    // the closing duplicate, n_across height stations.
    let (n_around, n_across) = (24usize, 5usize);
    let (a, b, h) = (27.0, 10.0, 18.0);
    let ring_pt = |i: usize, j: usize| -> [f64; 3] {
        let th = TWO_PI * i as f64 / n_around as f64;
        [a * th.cos(), b * th.sin(), h * j as f64 / (n_across - 1) as f64]
    };

    // First index (rows) = around/periodic axis; second = across.
    let mut pts = t_colgp::Array2OfPnt::new_int4(1, n_around as i32, 1, n_across as i32);
    for i in 0..n_around {
        for j in 0..n_across {
            pts.set_value(i as i32 + 1, j as i32 + 1, &pt(ring_pt(i, j)));
        }
    }
    let mut fit = geom_api::PointsToBSplineSurface::new();
    fit.interpolate_array2ofpnt_parametrizationtype_bool(
        &pts,
        approx::ParametrizationType::Chordlength,
        true,
    );
    println!("Q1/Q2 fit: is_done={}", fit.is_done());
    let surface = fit
        .surface()
        .to_handle_surface()
        .downcast_to_b_spline_surface()
        .expect("downcast");
    {
        let bs = surface.get();
        let (mut u0, mut u1, mut v0, mut v1) = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
        bs.bounds(&mut u0, &mut u1, &mut v0, &mut v1);
        println!(
            "  u_periodic={} v_periodic={} deg=({},{}) poles=({},{}) bounds=({:.6},{:.6})x({:.6},{:.6})",
            bs.is_u_periodic(),
            bs.is_v_periodic(),
            bs.u_degree(),
            bs.v_degree(),
            bs.nb_u_poles(),
            bs.nb_v_poles(),
            u0, u1, v0, v1,
        );
        print!("  u_knots ({}):", bs.nb_u_knots());
        for k in 1..=bs.nb_u_knots().min(6) {
            print!(" {:.4}(m{})", bs.u_knot(k), bs.u_multiplicity(k));
        }
        println!(
            " ... {:.4}(m{})",
            bs.u_knot(bs.nb_u_knots()),
            bs.u_multiplicity(bs.nb_u_knots())
        );

        // Closure continuity: D2 at u0 vs u1 (same v).
        let vm = 0.5 * (v0 + v1);
        let eval = |u: f64| {
            let mut p = gp::Pnt::new_real3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
            let (mut d1u, mut d1v, mut d2u, mut d2v, mut d2uv) = (
                gp::Vec::new(),
                gp::Vec::new(),
                gp::Vec::new(),
                gp::Vec::new(),
                gp::Vec::new(),
            );
            bs.d2(u, vm, &mut p, &mut d1u, &mut d1v, &mut d2u, &mut d2v, &mut d2uv);
            (
                [p.x(), p.y(), p.z()],
                [d1u.x(), d1u.y(), d1u.z()],
                [d2u.x(), d2u.y(), d2u.z()],
            )
        };
        let (p_lo, d1_lo, d2_lo) = eval(u0);
        let (p_hi, d1_hi, d2_hi) = eval(u1);
        let dd = |x: [f64; 3], y: [f64; 3]| {
            ((x[0] - y[0]).powi(2) + (x[1] - y[1]).powi(2) + (x[2] - y[2]).powi(2)).sqrt()
        };
        println!(
            "  closure: |P(u0)-P(u1)|={:.3e} |D1U delta|={:.3e} |D2U delta|={:.3e}",
            dd(p_lo, p_hi),
            dd(d1_lo, d1_hi),
            dd(d2_lo, d2_hi),
        );
    }

    // Q3: interpolation quality at the input points.
    {
        let erased = surface.to_handle_surface();
        let mut sas = shape_analysis::Surface::new_handlegeomsurface(&erased);
        let mut max_d = 0.0_f64;
        for i in 0..n_around {
            for j in 0..n_across {
                let p = ring_pt(i, j);
                let uv = sas.value_of_uv(&pt(p), 1e-7);
                let _ = uv;
                max_d = max_d.max(sas.gap());
            }
        }
        println!("Q3 interpolation: max gap at input points = {max_d:.3e}");
    }

    // Q4: rescale U knots to [0, 2*pi]; geometry must be unchanged.
    let mut before: Vec<([f64; 3], f64, f64)> = Vec::new(); // (point, u_frac, v)
    {
        let bs = surface.get();
        let (mut u0, mut u1, mut v0, mut v1) = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
        bs.bounds(&mut u0, &mut u1, &mut v0, &mut v1);
        for k in 0..7 {
            let uf = k as f64 / 7.0;
            let v = v0 + (v1 - v0) * (k as f64 / 6.0);
            let mut p = gp::Pnt::new_real3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
            bs.d0(u0 + (u1 - u0) * uf, v, &mut p);
            before.push(([p.x(), p.y(), p.z()], uf, v));
        }
    }
    {
        let bs = surface.get_mut();
        let nk = bs.nb_u_knots();
        let (k_first, k_last) = (bs.u_knot(1), bs.u_knot(nk));
        let mut arr = t_col_std::Array1OfReal::new_int2(1, nk);
        for k in 1..=nk {
            let scaled = (bs.u_knot(k) - k_first) / (k_last - k_first) * TWO_PI;
            arr.set_value(k, &scaled);
        }
        bs.set_u_knots(&arr);
        let (mut u0, mut u1, mut v0, mut v1) = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
        bs.bounds(&mut u0, &mut u1, &mut v0, &mut v1);
        println!(
            "Q4 rescale: new bounds=({:.6},{:.6})x({:.6},{:.6}) (want u=(0,{:.6}))",
            u0, u1, v0, v1, TWO_PI,
        );
        let mut max_d = 0.0_f64;
        for (p, uf, v) in &before {
            let mut q = gp::Pnt::new_real3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
            bs.d0(u0 + (u1 - u0) * uf, *v, &mut q);
            max_d = max_d.max(dist(&q, *p));
        }
        println!("  geometry drift across rescale at 7 samples: {max_d:.3e}");
    }

    // Q5: principal U from ShapeAnalysis after the rescale.
    {
        let erased = surface.to_handle_surface();
        let mut sas = shape_analysis::Surface::new_handlegeomsurface(&erased);
        let mut u_min = f64::MAX;
        let mut u_max = f64::MIN;
        for i in 0..n_around {
            let p = ring_pt(i, 2);
            let uv = sas.value_of_uv(&pt(p), 1e-7);
            u_min = u_min.min(uv.x());
            u_max = u_max.max(uv.x());
        }
        println!("Q5 ShapeAnalysis principal U range over a ring: [{u_min:.4}, {u_max:.4}]");
    }

    // Q6: UIso(0) should be the seam gauge through the first input row.
    {
        let bs = surface.get();
        let iso = bs.u_iso_real(0.0);
        let c = iso.get();
        let mut max_d = 0.0_f64;
        for j in 0..n_across {
            let target = ring_pt(0, j);
            // Sample the iso densely and take the min distance (cheap check).
            let (f, l) = (c.first_parameter(), c.last_parameter());
            let mut best = f64::MAX;
            for s in 0..200 {
                let t = f + (l - f) * s as f64 / 199.0;
                best = best.min(dist(&c.value(t), target));
            }
            max_d = max_d.max(best);
        }
        println!("Q6 UIso(0) max distance to first input row: {max_d:.3e}");
    }

    // Q7: IntSS with the cap plane z=0.
    {
        let origin = gp::Pnt::new_real3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
        let normal = gp::Dir::new_real3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0);
        let plane = geom::Plane::new_pnt_dir(&origin, &normal);
        let plane_h = geom::Plane::to_handle(plane).to_handle_surface();
        let surf_h = surface.to_handle_surface();
        let int_ss = geom_api::IntSS::new_handlegeomsurface2_real(&plane_h, &surf_h, 1e-7);
        println!("Q7 IntSS(plane z=0, surface): done={} nb_lines={}",
            int_ss.is_done(), int_ss.nb_lines());
        for li in 1..=int_ss.nb_lines() {
            let curve = int_ss.line(li);
            let c = curve.get();
            let (f, l) = (c.first_parameter(), c.last_parameter());
            let p_f = c.value(f);
            let p_l = c.value(l);
            let closed = dist(&p_f, [p_l.x(), p_l.y(), p_l.z()]) < 1e-6;
            let mut max_d = 0.0_f64;
            for i in 0..n_around {
                let target = ring_pt(i, 0);
                let mut best = f64::MAX;
                for s in 0..400 {
                    let t = f + (l - f) * s as f64 / 399.0;
                    best = best.min(dist(&c.value(t), target));
                }
                max_d = max_d.max(best);
            }
            println!(
                "  line {li}: params [{f:.4},{l:.4}] closed={closed} periodic={} \
                 max dist to bottom ring pts={max_d:.3e}",
                c.is_periodic(),
            );
        }
    }
}

/// Which unit-square axis runs around a seam-cut band (from cut copy to cut
/// copy): the cut vertices sit at that axis's parameter extremes.
fn cut_around_axis(region: &Region, uv: &[(f64, f64)]) -> Result<bool, String> {
    let cut_uv = region
        .loops
        .iter()
        .flatten()
        .find(|&&(_, out)| out == CUT_OUTSIDE)
        .map(|&(li, _)| uv[li])
        .ok_or("seam-cut region has no cut boundary")?;
    Ok(cut_uv.0.min(1.0 - cut_uv.0) < cut_uv.1.min(1.0 - cut_uv.1))
}

    uv: &[(f64, f64)],
) -> Result<Vec<BSplineHypothesis>, String> {
    // The around axis runs from cut copy to cut copy: cut vertices sit at
    // that axis's parameter extremes.
    let cut_uv = region
        .loops
        .iter()
        .flatten()
        .find(|&&(_, out)| out == CUT_OUTSIDE)
        .map(|&(li, _)| uv[li])
        .ok_or("seam-cut region has no cut boundary")?;
    let around_u = cut_uv.0.min(1.0 - cut_uv.0) < cut_uv.1.min(1.0 - cut_uv.1);

    // Orient the grid so the fitted surface's natural normal (d1u × d1v)
    // points outward, matching the mesh winding normals. Fixing the
    // convention at fit time (one row flip) beats recovering it later with
    // per-face heuristics.
    let idx = |i: usize, j: usize| i * n_v + j;
    let (ci, cj) = (n_u / 2, n_v / 2);
    let du = sub3(grid[idx(ci + 1, cj)], grid[idx(ci - 1, cj)]);
    let dv = sub3(grid[idx(ci, cj + 1)], grid[idx(ci, cj - 1)]);
    let grid_n = cross3(du, dv);
    let center = grid[idx(ci, cj)];
    let mesh_n = region_normal_near(mesh, region, center);
    let flip = dot3(grid_n, mesh_n) < 0.0;

    for i in 0..n_u {

            let pnt = gp::Pnt::new_real3(p[0], p[1], p[2]);

    // Orient the grid so the fitted surface's natural normal (d1u × d1v)
    // points outward, matching the mesh winding normals. Fixing the
    // convention at fit time (one row flip) beats recovering it later with
    // per-face heuristics.
    let idx = |i: usize, j: usize| i * n_v + j;
    let (ci, cj) = (n_u / 2, n_v / 2);
    let du = sub3(grid[idx(ci + 1, cj)], grid[idx(ci - 1, cj)]);
    let dv = sub3(grid[idx(ci, cj + 1)], grid[idx(ci, cj - 1)]);
    let grid_n = cross3(du, dv);
    let center = grid[idx(ci, cj)];
    let mesh_n = region_normal_near(mesh, region, center);
    let flip = dot3(grid_n, mesh_n) < 0.0;

    // Array layout: the fitted surface's U is the array's FIRST index. A
    // periodic fit needs the around-the-band axis there (transpose when the
    // around axis is v), with its closing station — the second cut copy,
    // whose column duplicates the first — omitted: OCCT's periodic
    // Interpolate appends the wrap-around copy of the first row itself
    // (probed, see DEVELOPMENT_PLAN §2.7). Orientation: transposing negates
    // d1u×d1v, so the outward flip reverses the SECOND index and accounts
    // for the transpose.
    let (n_a, n_b, transpose) = match around {
        Some(false) => (n_v - 1, n_u, true),
        Some(true) => (n_u - 1, n_v, false),
        None => (n_u, n_v, false),
    };
    let flip_b = flip != transpose;
    let mut pts = t_colgp::Array2OfPnt::new_int4(1, n_a as i32, 1, n_b as i32);
    for a in 0..n_a {
        for b in 0..n_b {
            let bb = if flip_b { n_b - 1 - b } else { b };
            let (i, j) = if transpose { (bb, a) } else { (a, bb) };
            let p = grid[idx(i, j)];
            let pnt = gp::Pnt::new_real3(p[0], p[1], p[2]);
            pts.set_value(a as i32 + 1, b as i32 + 1, &pnt);
        }
    }

    } else {

                        &pts,

                        3,
                        8,
                        geom_abs::Shape::C2,
                        tol3d,
                    )

            Ok(Some(s)) => s,
            Ok(None) => {
                last_err = "GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface did not converge".to_string();
                continue;
            }
            Err(_) => {
                last_err = "GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface raised an exception".to_string();
                continue;
            }
        };
        if around.is_some() {
            // Rescale the periodic (around) axis's knots to exactly [0, 2π]
            // — an exact affine reparameterization (probed: geometry drift
            // ~1e-15). Stage 3.4's wrapped-face machinery (branch unwrap,
            // winding, pcurve shifts, seam placement) hard-codes that
            // period.
            let bs = surface.get_mut();
            if !bs.is_u_periodic() {
                last_err = "periodic interpolation returned a non-periodic surface".to_string();
                continue;
            }
            let nk = bs.nb_u_knots();
            let (k0, k1) = (bs.u_knot(1), bs.u_knot(nk));
            let mut knots = t_col_std::Array1OfReal::new_int2(1, nk);
            for k in 1..=nk {
                let scaled = (bs.u_knot(k) - k0) / (k1 - k0) * std::f64::consts::TAU;
                knots.set_value(k, &scaled);
            }
            bs.set_u_knots(&knots);
        }
        match validate_fit(
            mesh, region, sampler.uv, maps, around, flip_b, surface, n_u, n_v, &grid, config,
        ) {
            Ok(hyp) => return Ok(hyp),
            Err(e) => last_err = e,
        }
    }
    Err(last_err)
}

/// Validate a fitted surface: every region vertex and face centroid must
/// lie within surface tolerance. Each projection is seeded from the
/// vertex's own Floater UV (`uv`, indexed like `region.verts`), the one
/// reliable way to find the true nearest point on a many-knot surface.
#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]
fn validate_fit(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    region: &Region,
    uv: &[(f64, f64)],
    maps: &AxisMaps,
    flip: bool,
    surface: OwnedPtr<geom::HandleGeomBSplineSurface>,
    n_u: usize,
    n_v: usize,
    grid: &[[f64; 3]],
    config: &Config,
) -> Result<BSplineHypothesis, String> {
    // Hypothesis vertices are unique GLOBAL mesh vertices (region.verts may
    // repeat globals for seam-cut clones).
    let mut hyp_verts = region.verts.clone();
    hyp_verts.sort_unstable();
    hyp_verts.dedup();
    let mut hyp = BSplineHypothesis::new(surface, region.faces.clone(), hyp_verts);
    let tol = config.surface_tolerance_mm;
    // The fit's parameter is ~linear in arc fraction (the grid stations
    // equalize arc), and its v axis is reversed when the grid was flipped
    // for outward orientation.
    let seed_of = |li: usize| -> (f64, f64) {
        let (u, v) = uv[li];
        let gu = AxisMaps::arc_fraction(&maps.u_profile, u);
        let gv = AxisMaps::arc_fraction(&maps.v_profile, v);
        (gu, if flip { 1.0 - gv } else { gv })
    };
```

**After:**
```
/// Validate a fitted surface: every region vertex and face centroid must
/// lie within surface tolerance. Each projection is seeded from the
/// vertex's own Floater UV (`uv`, indexed like `region.verts`), the one
/// reliable way to find the true nearest point on a many-knot surface.
#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]
fn validate_fit(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    region: &Region,
    uv: &[(f64, f64)],
    maps: &AxisMaps,
    around: Option<bool>,
    flip_b: bool,
    surface: OwnedPtr<geom::HandleGeomBSplineSurface>,
    n_u: usize,
    n_v: usize,
    grid: &[[f64; 3]],
    config: &Config,
) -> Result<BSplineHypothesis, String> {
    // Hypothesis vertices are unique GLOBAL mesh vertices (region.verts may
    // repeat globals for seam-cut clones).
    let mut hyp_verts = region.verts.clone();
    hyp_verts.sort_unstable();
    hyp_verts.dedup();
    let mut hyp = BSplineHypothesis::new(surface, region.faces.clone(), hyp_verts);
    hyp.u_periodic = around.is_some();
    let tol = config.surface_tolerance_mm;
    // The fit's parameter is ~linear in arc fraction (the grid stations
    // equalize arc). Map the Floater axes onto the fitted surface's axes:
    // transposed when the band's around axis is v (the surface's U is
    // always the array's first index), with the second axis reversed when
    // the grid was flipped for outward orientation.
    let seed_of = |li: usize| -> (f64, f64) {
        let (u, v) = uv[li];
        let gu = AxisMaps::arc_fraction(&maps.u_profile, u);
        let gv = AxisMaps::arc_fraction(&maps.v_profile, v);
        let (ga, gb) = if around == Some(false) { (gv, gu) } else { (gu, gv) };
        (ga, if flip_b { 1.0 - gb } else { gb })
    };

/// True when the two faces are B-spline halves of one fitted surface (the
/// deliberate seam-split of a closed freeform band): edges between them —
/// and the corner vertices those edges end at — are reconstruction
/// artifacts with no counterpart in a reference model, which represents
/// the band as a single periodic face with a seam.
fn is_seam_cut_pair(
    fi0: usize,
    fi1: usize,
    face_descriptors: &[FaceDescriptor],
    stage2: &Stage2Output,
) -> bool {
    let s0 = &stage2.selected_surfaces[face_descriptors[fi0].selected_surface_idx];
    let s1 = &stage2.selected_surfaces[face_descriptors[fi1].selected_surface_idx];
    match (s0, s1) {
        (SelectedSurface::BSpline(a), SelectedSurface::BSpline(b)) => {
            a != b
                && stage2.bspline_hypotheses[*a].shared_surface_group.is_some()
                && stage2.bspline_hypotheses[*a].shared_surface_group
                    == stage2.bspline_hypotheses[*b].shared_surface_group
        }
        _ => false,
    }
}

> The full-circle reconstruction logic checks whether the span deviates significantly from 2π to determine if we're dealing with a partial arc that needs circle fitting from three points. In our case, the IntSS returned a span of exactly 2π, so the deviation check passes and we skip the circle reconstruction entirely—which is good because fitting a circle to an elliptical junction would be incorrect. For a general freeform band,  a partial-arc result on a closed junction would trigger circle reconstruction and likely fail the chain deviation check, pushing it toward the B-spline repair arm, but that's a deferred concern since the closed-chain periodic interpolation isn't needed for this model.
>

    // Ground-truth validation: the mesh boundary chain lies on the true
    // junction within chordal tolerance, so the trimmed curve must pass
    // close to the chain. When it doesn't — the classic complementary-arc
    // trap on a periodic junction, a degenerate IntSS result with an odd
    // parameterization, or a straight-line stand-in for a curved junction —
    // rebuild the curve as the circle through the chain and re-trim with a
    // chain-supported arc. The chain is the one representation available
    // for every junction, so this guard is uniform across surface pairs.
    let final_curve = repair_edge_curve_from_boundary(
        final_curve, edge, vertices, mesh, config, fi0, fi1,
    );

    // Closed-loop edges must carry a PERIODIC curve: stage 3.4's seam
    // planning re-anchors them with MakeEdge over [t, t + period] at an
    // arbitrary seam azimuth. Analytic closed junctions (circles) already
    // are; IntSS junctions against a fitted B-spline surface arrive as
    // closed-but-non-periodic trimmed curves and are converted (exact —
    // probed at ~1e-14).
    let final_curve = if edge.vertex_indices[0] == usize::MAX
        && edge.vertex_indices[1] == usize::MAX
    {
        periodicize_closed_curve(final_curve, config, fi0, fi1)
    } else {
        final_curve
    };

    edge.curve_3d = Some(final_curve);
    Ok(())
}

/// Convert a closed-loop edge's closed-but-non-periodic curve into a
/// periodic Geom_BSplineCurve (same geometry, same parameter range). Keeps
/// the input curve when it is already periodic, is not actually closed, or
/// the conversion fails.
fn periodicize_closed_curve(
    curve: OwnedPtr<geom::HandleGeomCurve>,
    config: &Config,
    fi0: usize,
    fi1: usize,
) -> OwnedPtr<geom::HandleGeomCurve> {
    {
        let c = curve.get();
        if c.is_periodic() {
            return curve;
        }
        let p = c.value(c.first_parameter());
        let q = c.value(c.last_parameter());
        let gap = ((p.x() - q.x()).powi(2) + (p.y() - q.y()).powi(2) + (p.z() - q.z()).powi(2))
            .sqrt();
        if gap > config.vertex_tolerance_mm {
            return curve; // not closed; nothing to periodicize
        }
    }
    let converted = std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(|| {
        let mut bsc = geom_convert::curve_to_b_spline_curve_handlegeomcurve_parameterisationtype(
            &curve,
            convert::ParameterisationType::Tgtthetaover2,
        );
        bsc.get_mut().set_periodic();
        bsc.to_handle_curve()
    }));
    match converted {
        Ok(periodic) => {
            if config.verbose {
                eprintln!(
                    "    Edge (f{fi0},f{fi1}): closed junction curve made periodic \
                     for seam re-anchoring"
                );
            }
            periodic
        }
        Err(_) => {
            if !config.quiet {
                eprintln!(
                    "  Warning: edge (f{fi0},f{fi1}): could not make the closed junction \
                     curve periodic; seam re-anchoring may keep its original start"
                );
            }
            curve
        }
    }
}

static void BuildParameters(const Standard_Boolean         PeriodicFlag,
                            const TColgp_Array1OfPnt&      PointsArray,
                            Handle(TColStd_HArray1OfReal)& ParametersPtr)
{
  Standard_Integer ii, index;
  Standard_Real    distance;
  Standard_Integer num_parameters = PointsArray.Length();
  if (PeriodicFlag)
  {
    num_parameters += 1;
  }
  ParametersPtr = new TColStd_HArray1OfReal(1, num_parameters);
  ParametersPtr->SetValue(1, 0.0e0);
  index = 2;
  for (ii = PointsArray.Lower(); ii < PointsArray.Upper(); ii++)
  {
    distance = PointsArray.Value(ii).Distance(PointsArray.Value(ii + 1));
    ParametersPtr->SetValue(index, ParametersPtr->Value(ii) + distance);
    index += 1;
  }
  if (PeriodicFlag)
  {
    distance =
      PointsArray.Value(PointsArray.Upper()).Distance(PointsArray.Value(PointsArray.Lower()));
    ParametersPtr->SetValue(index, ParametersPtr->Value(ii) + distance);
  }
}

    // For closed-loop edges, IntSS may return partial arcs (e.g., semicircles)
    // when the intersection circle passes through the sphere's UV poles (the
    // intersection plane contains the sphere axis). In UV space, such a circle
    // splits into two disconnected arcs, which IntSS returns separately.
    // Detect this and reconstruct the full circle from sampled curve points.
    // Partiality is decided by the endpoint gap, NOT the parameter span: a
    // closed junction with a B-spline surface comes back as a closed curve
    // over an arbitrary range (observed [0,1]), and treating it as a
    // partial arc would replace the true junction with a bogus circle.
    let full_circle_curve: Option<OwnedPtr<geom::HandleGeomCurve>> =
        if edge.vertex_indices[0] == usize::MAX && edge.vertex_indices[1] == usize::MAX {
            let c = initial_curve_handle.get();
            let span = c.last_parameter() - c.first_parameter();
            let p_first = c.value(c.first_parameter());
            let p_last = c.value(c.last_parameter());
            let endpoint_gap = ((p_first.x() - p_last.x()).powi(2)
                + (p_first.y() - p_last.y()).powi(2)
                + (p_first.z() - p_last.z()).powi(2))
            .sqrt();
            if endpoint_gap > 10.0 * config.vertex_tolerance_mm {
                // Partial arc — reconstruct full circle from 3 sampled points
                let fp = c.first_parameter();
                let p0 = c.value(fp);
                let p1 = c.value(fp + span * 0.25);
                let p2 = c.value(fp + span * 0.75);

/// elliptical_cylinder: a closed freeform wall (annulus topology) is
/// seam-cut, fitted once, and split into two B-spline faces sharing the
/// fitted surface — tagged as one shared-surface group so stage 3 treats
/// the edges between them as reconstruction artifacts.
#[test]
fn nurbs_elliptical_cylinder_stage27_selection() {
    let stl = format!("{}/tests/nurbs/elliptical_cylinder.stl", manifest_dir());
    let step = format!("{}/tests/nurbs/elliptical_cylinder.step", manifest_dir());
    let config = config_for_compare_stage27(&stl, &step);
    let output = run_stage2(&config);
    let (planar, bspline) = planar_bspline_selection_counts(&output);
    assert_eq!(bspline, 2, "closed wall should split into two B-spline faces");
    assert_eq!(planar, 2, "top and bottom caps");
    let groups: Vec<Option<usize>> = output
        .bspline_hypotheses
        .iter()
        .map(|h| h.shared_surface_group)
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(groups[0], groups[1], "both halves carry one group tag");
    assert!(groups[0].is_some(), "the halves must be tagged as seam-split");
}
```

/// elliptical_cylinder: a closed freeform wall (annulus topology) is

/// wrapped face with a real seam edge — the same form CAD kernels write.
#[test]
fn nurbs_elliptical_cylinder_stage27_selection() {
    let stl = format!("{}/tests/nurbs/elliptical_cylinder.stl", manifest_dir());
    let step = format!("{}/tests/nurbs/elliptical_cylinder.step", manifest_dir());

    assert_eq!(bspline, 1, "closed wall is ONE periodic B-spline face");
    assert_eq!(planar, 2, "top and bottom caps");
    let hyp = &output.bspline_hypotheses[0];
    assert!(hyp.u_periodic, "closed-band fit must be U-periodic");
}

Quads are split along the v0–v2 diagonal for weighting and sampling. **Closed bands** (a second boundary loop of extent ≥ half the largest — a small hole floats freely, a comparable second loop means the region wraps, e.g. the wall of a closed prism) are first **seam-cut** into a disk along a shortest vertex path between the two loops (`cut_region_seam`): the path follows FACE perimeter edges only (a path along a quad's split diagonal would tear that quad across the cut), its vertices are duplicated, right-side triangle fans switch to the clones, and the boundary re-chains into one loop whose two cut copies carry a `CUT_OUTSIDE` id — corner detection then lands the 4 corners exactly at the cut endpoints. The clones keep their originals' positions, so the sampled parameter-extreme grid columns carry identical data and the fitted (clamped, non-periodic) surface closes exactly: its two boundary iso-curves share a pole column and coincide.
```

215	**Curvature-guided seed ordering**: Start faces are processed in ascending order of a per-face *curvature-difference score* rather than mesh index order. The score is computed once per mesh (in stage 2, shared by all surface stages):
216	
217	1. **Per-face curvature summary**: for each mesh edge between adjacent faces, the discrete normal curvature along the crossing direction is κ ≈ θ/d (dihedral angle over centroid distance). A face's summary is the maximum κ over its edges — approximately its largest principal curvature.
218	2. **Neighbor difference**: a face's raw score is the maximum |summary difference| against its edge neighbors. Interior faces of any uniform surface (plane, cylinder, cone, sphere, torus) score ≈ 0 — curvature is locally constant even where it is nonzero — while faces at surface transitions score high. Crucially, this includes **tangent junctions** (fillet↔plane, fillet↔cylinder), which are G1-continuous and therefore invisible to dihedral-angle checks, but G2-discontinuous: curvature jumps from 0 to 1/r.
219	3. **Diffusion**: 3 Jacobi passes of neighbor averaging (new = ½·self + ½·mean(neighbors)) spread the junction signal a few hops, so ordering prefers deep-interior faces whose seed neighborhoods (1-ring / fan, radius ≈ 1–2) cannot touch a junction.
220	4. **Junction mask**: separately from the diffused ordering score, faces whose RAW score exceeds 50% of the local curvature magnitude (max of own and neighbors' summaries) are flagged as junction faces. The criterion is local-relative, not mesh-global: sharp creases dominate a global maximum and tangent junctions — the primary target — would fall below any fraction of it.
221	
222	Effect: interior seeds run first and commit large, correctly-fitted hypotheses; junction faces are usually absorbed by BFS growth before they ever become start faces (committed faces do not seed). **Seed gathering exclusion**: in pass 1, junction faces are also excluded from seed neighborhoods (conical fans, spherical 1-rings, toroidal hop-expansion), so seeds stay on one surface; a second pass retries remaining undeduced faces without the filter so surfaces composed entirely of transition faces (one-row fillets) still seed. Toroidal gathering hop-expands (up to 3 hops, targeting ≥ 16 faces) since small fillet tubes have little interior across the tube but extend along the fillet axis. Ordering and masks are deterministic: ties break by face index.
223	
224	**Computational cost**: For each starting face, the number of seed trials is typically small (1 for planar/spherical/toroidal, 1–6 for conical/cylindrical). Each trial BFS covers the connected surface region. Since most faces on the same surface will discover the same region, the work is dominated by the first few faces that discover the region before their neighbors get committed. The curvature field costs O(N) plus three O(N) diffusion passes — negligible next to LM fitting.
225

227	  - For each hypothesis, compute the centroid of each member face.
228	  - Project each centroid onto the fitted surface (nearest point on the surface).

230	  - If any projected centroid exceeds \`--surface-tolerance\`, report an error.
231	  - Note: centroid-to-surface distance measures both fitting accuracy and tessellation sagitta ($\approx h^2 / 8R$ for curvature radius $R$ and chord length $h$). For typical tessellations this is small relative to \`--surface-tolerance\`.

236	- \`normal: [f64; 3]\` — Unit normal vector pointing outward from the shell/solid.
237	- \`distance: f64\` — Signed distance from origin to plane along the normal (plane equation: normal · p = distance).
238	- \`error_max, error_min: f64\` — Maximum (positive) and minimum (most negative) signed distance from any vertex to the plane.
239	- \`error_abs_sum: f64\` — Sum of absolute vertex-to-plane distances.

244	
245	**Surface fit**: Area-weighted normal averaging. Each face's unit normal is weighted by the face's triangle area, then the weighted sum is normalized. The plane distance is the mean of \`normal · vertex\` over all vertices. This gives larger faces more influence on the plane orientation. See [SURFACE_FITTING.md](SURFACE_FITTING.md) for detailed fitting math.
246	
247	**Distance metric**: Signed distance from vertex to plane: \`d = normal · vertex - distance\`. All vertices must satisfy \`|d| ≤ vertex_tolerance\`.

    let (mut planar_hypotheses, planar_quit) = bfs::generate_hypotheses::<PlanarSurface>(&mut mesh, &bfs_config, viz_21);

    // Record which faces belong to blob-like planar regions so the
    // curved-surface stages can exclude flat facets from seed gathering
    // (a top-face quad pulled into a corner vertex-blend torus seed poisons
    // the fit). Neither size nor multi-face-ness distinguishes a real plane
    // from a flat strip lying on a curved surface: strips along straight
    // small-radius fillets are long, exactly planar, and legitimately
    // needed by torus seeds. The discriminator is SHAPE: a real plane
    // region is a 2D blob with interior faces (>= 3 neighbors in the same
    // hypothesis), while a strip is a 1-wide chain with none.
    bfs_config.multiface_planar = {
        let mut interior_counts = vec![0_usize; planar_hypotheses.len()];
        for face in &mesh.faces {
            let pi = face.planar_hypothesis;
            if pi < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
            let same_neighbors = face.neighbors[..vc]
                .iter()
                .filter(|&&ni| ni >= 0 && mesh.faces[ni as usize].planar_hypothesis == pi)
                .count();
            if same_neighbors >= 3 {
                interior_counts[pi as usize] += 1;
            }
        }
        mesh.faces
            .iter()
            .map(|f| {
                let pi = f.planar_hypothesis;
                pi >= 0
                    && planar_hypotheses[pi as usize].faces.len() >= 8
                    && interior_counts[pi as usize] * 5 >= planar_hypotheses[pi as usize].faces.len()
            })
            .collect()
    };
    // EXPERIMENT: multiface_planar neutralized for per-mask timing attribution.
    bfs_config.multiface_planar = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
```

Ordering and masks are deterministic: ties break by face index.
```

That's recorded in [TODO.md](TODO.md) as a probe-then-delete item rather than folded into this change.

> I'm trying to understand why the plane-bspline intersection is failing with zero lines—this suggests the surfaces aren't actually intersecting where they should be. The cube likely has embossed or engraved text (like "XYZ" markings), so where planar faces meet the freeform bspline surfaces of the text, the intersection calculation is breaking down, which then cascades into BRepCheck failures for those specific faces.
> 
> When the exact intersection curve can't be computed, the code falls back to using a mesh-boundary chain—essentially interpolating vertices from the mesh boundary directly. This approximation only guarantees proximity to the boundary but doesn't lie exactly on both surfaces, so when these chain-based edges are projected onto the surface parameter space as pcurves, they don't form a watertight trimming loop. The edges may not align perfectly with the surface, causing self-intersecting or invalid wires that BRepCheck flags as problematic.
> 
> I should look at how BRepCheck constructs its warning messages to understand the exact failure mode better.

3389	        let g1 = if v1 != usize::MAX {
3390	            vertex_group.get(&v1).copied()

3393	        };

3398	                groups.push(vec![ei]);

> I'm skipping the formal task tracking since this is a quick diagnostic investigation. Let me examine faces 3, 4, 9, 11 and 49, 50, 52, 53 to see what's happening geometrically—the STL file appears to be a calibration cube with X, Y, Z letters embossed on different faces to test 3D printer axis orientation and alignment.
> 
> With 566 vertices and 1128 faces plus 6 B-spline surfaces covering 66 faces (likely the raised letter geometry on three or six faces), the issue becomes clearer: at the boundary where a planar cube face meets a B-spline letter surface, there's a geometric mismatch. The planar face uses an infinite mathematical plane, while the B-spline surface is a bounded patch fitted only to the letter's geometry, so the parametric domain of the spline doesn't actually extend far enough to intersect with the plane—the fitted surface only covers the letter itself and doesn't reach the plane boundary.
> 
> More likely, embossed letters have a thin vertical wall (a separate planar extrusion) connecting the letter's top to the cube face, so the B-spline captures only the curved/sloped parts while the vertical wall is its own face. This means the B-spline and plane only touch along their boundary curve, and since they're tangent there rather than transversally intersecting, IntSS returns zero intersection lines because the algorithm expects curves that cross, not just touch. The tangency detection finding 8 of 147 edges as tangent aligns with this—these are likely the boundary curves where surfaces meet but don't cross. r a fit that's slightly off or doesn't reach the plane exactly. This aligns with a known OCCT limitation where surface approximation can overshoot tolerance — the raised letters (likely split into multiple faces per character) were fit as B-spline surfaces that don't quite intersect the base plane mathematically, so IntSS correctly finds zero intersection curves because the surfaces genuinely don't cross in 3D space.
> 
> The real issue is that five edges between the planar cube faces and the fitted letter surfaces fail to construct because the two surfaces meet nearly tangentially rather than at a sharp crease, and OCCT's surface-surface intersection numerics can't seed a valid intersection curve in that smooth blending region.
> 
> The code falls back to building a curve directly from the mesh boundary polyline, which succeeds for all five edges with deviation under 5.3e-2mm, so Stage 3.3 reports all 147 curves computed — it's a warning, not an error, since the fallback worked. But downstream, this mesh-boundary approximation doesn't lie exactly on either surface or their parametric curves, which creates a downstream problem. The fallback chain-based edge curve causes BRepCheck failures because the projected pcurve doesn't align properly with the bspline surface trim, likely creating self-intersections in parameter space—especially for face 3's "intersecting wires" error. I'm investigating whether the pcurve projection to the bspline surface has special handling or if it fails because the 3D chain curve doesn't actually lie on the surface geometry.

> So the fallback approach is working as intended—when a straight-line chord deviates too much from the actual boundary chain, it switches to fitting either a circular arc or B-spline through the vertices, which brings the deviation down to acceptable levels in the 1-2 centimeter range. This gives a reasonably accurate geometric representation of the curved mesh boundary. But there's a critical issue emerging that I need to think through.
> 
> The problem is that this fitted 3D curve, while close to the mesh boundary polyline, isn't actually constrained to lie on either the planar surface or the fitted B-spline surface itself. It's just a curve through the 3D vertices. When Stage 3.4 tries to project this curve onto each surface to create the 2D parametric curves needed for trimming, the projection can fail or produce self-intersecting loops if the original 3D curve doesn't sit precisely on the surfaces—which is likely given fabrication noise and the fact that the B-spline surface was fit independently with its own tolerance. This mismatch between the 3D boundary curve and the actual surfaces is what's causing the "intersecting wires" and "invalid wire" errors I'm seeing. ompletely, leaving a gap where the mesh boundary should snap to both surfaces simultaneously. The fallback edge curve bridges this gap by approximating the mesh vertices, but it doesn't actually lie on either surface with the precision OCCT requires, so when Stage 3.4 tries to build trimmed faces using these edges, the 2D parameter-space curves become inconsistent or self-intersecting. This cascades into invalid-wire and unorientable-face errors across the 8 faces sharing those 5 problem edges, which then fails the solid's BRepCheck validation.
> 
> I need to verify this by examining the actual mesh geometry at the affected faces and checking the curve deviations more carefully, but the core issue is clear: the B-spline fit doesn't meet the plane with enough geometric precision, and the fallback recovery strategy sacrifices surface-conformance for mesh-fidelity, breaking STEP validity.
> 
> The real question is whether the final output is still usable in practice — I should run a volume comparison check to see if the geometry remains functionally sound despite the BRepCheck failures.

(2) For cylinders: project vertices perpendicular to the axis, fit a 2D circle for axis position and radius. For cones: estimate half-angle and apex from vertex positions along the axis. (3) LM refinement minimizing vertex-to-surface distances, with vertices **recentered** around their centroid for numerical stability (parameters shifted back after fitting), and \`patience=500\` to ensure convergence well below vertex tolerance. With \`--verbose 4\` or higher, each seed fit logs both the cone and cylinder fit attempts along with their max vertex/surface errors and rejection reasons. ## Diagnosis

The warnings all trace back to **5 edges where a fitted B-spline patch meets a tiny planar sliver face**, at the raised/engraved letter geometry on this test cube. Two independent tools ran on `tests/downloaded/xyz-cube-test-20mm.stl`: the `brepper` conversion itself, and `step-measure-tolerance` on the resulting STEP, to check whether the warnings represent a real geometric defect or just a validity nag.

**Root cause (Stage 3.2/3.3).** `GeomAPI_IntSS` returns zero intersection lines for 5 plane↔bspline pairs (edges 48, 68, 84, 86, 109 → faces 3/4/9/11 planar vs. 49/50/52/53 bspline), at [stage3.rs:1349](src/stage3.rs:1349). This is a *known, expected* failure mode, already documented at [DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md:444](DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md:444): a fitted freeform patch usually meets its planar neighbor near-tangentially, and `IntSS` can't seed a transversal intersection walk on a near-tangent pair. The pattern here fits: faces 3/4/9/11 are tiny single-triangle "leftover" planar slivers (stage 2.7's own log says "32 below 4 faces" — too small to be grouped or fit with a surface), sitting right at the edge of the fitted letter surfaces.

**First fallback (works fine).** [`edge_curve_from_boundary_chain`](src/stage3.rs:2063) → [`repair_edge_curve_from_boundary`](src/stage3.rs:1891) rebuilds each of these 5 edges directly from the raw mesh polyline (best of line/circle/C2 B-spline fit), landing 1.6e-2–5.3e-2 mm from the true mesh boundary — good enough that Stage 3.3 reports 147/147 curves computed, no failures. But by construction this curve is *mesh-truth*, not *surface-truth*: it isn't constrained to lie exactly on either the plane or the bspline patch.

**Second-order failure (Stage 3.4).** When that off-surface curve gets trimmed into pcurves for both adjacent faces, the mismatch — negligible on a normal-sized face — is large relative to these sub-mm sliver triangles, producing self-intersecting/invalid wires and an unorientable face on exactly the 8 faces touching those 5 edges. That invalidity then propagates into the shell/solid check ("solid 0 failed BRepCheck").

One extra detail worth noting: face 9 and face 49 each appear in *two* of the five bad edges — they're a pinch point where two bspline patches and a sliver converge (likely where two strokes of a letter meet, e.g. an "X" crossing), which is why they're doubly implicated.

**Practical severity.** I converted the file and cross-checked geometry:
- Volume: STEP 7657.0 mm³ vs. STL 7682.4 mm³ → 0.33% off, well inside the 1% gate.
- Vertex/centroid deviation: max 0.036 mm / 0.335 mm on a 20mm cube.
- Area: STEP 2696.0 mm² vs. STL 2471.7 mm² — **~9% high**, consistent with those invalid/self-intersecting slivers double-covering small patches of surface at the letter edges. This is the one number that shows the defect isn't purely cosmetic.

So: the file is still readable and volumetrically close, but 8 of 54 faces are topologically invalid B-rep at the letter-engraving boundaries — a strict downstream CAD validator would flag/reject those faces even though a mesh-volume comparison wouldn't catch it. This isn't a regression from recent work; it's an un-hardened edge of the documented "tangent junction → boundary-chain fallback" path when the adjacent face is a near-degenerate sliver.

| `#8618` | Y letter (patch 3) | **x 13.85, z −17.2** | severe |

The cube is only 20mm (±10mm in x/y, 0–20 in z). A control point at `(9.000006, −72.516, −154.141)` — I traced this to a specific edge curve shared by faces 3/49 (`stage3.rs`) — is ~150mm from anything in the model. That's your "letter almost missing" (severely distorted faces get dropped/collapsed on import) and "slivers extending far beyond the cube" (the milder overshoots on `#4056`/`#9102` are exactly the kind of stray wing a viewer renders as a spike). Notably: the Z letter used **zero** B‑spline surfaces (all-planar per the log), and both its faces are undamaged — so the defect tracks precisely with which regions went through the B‑spline fitter.

## Why it happens

Stage 2.7's fitting grid is built by [`axis_stations`](src/stage2/bspline.rs:1493). Per design (§2.7 rule 5), the "base" stations are pinned exactly at the region's boundary mesh vertices, then evenly subdivided *within each segment* between adjacent vertices up to a density target:

```rust
let k = (target.saturating_sub(1)).div_ceil(base.len() - 1).max(1);
for w in base.windows(2) {
    for step in 0..k { out.push(w[0] + (w[1] - w[0]) * step as f64 / k as f64); }
}
```

`k` is one constant for the whole axis. If the mesh's own boundary tessellation is uneven — finely faceted where the letter has a slight fillet, coarsely faceted where it's genuinely flat (matches your observation: "purely planar... maybe some slight curvature") — one segment ends up many times longer in 3D than its neighbors, but gets subdivided by the *same* `k`. That unevenness goes straight into [`PointsToBSplineSurface::Interpolate`](src/stage2/bspline.rs:1630) with chord-length parametrization. A big jump in consecutive knot spacing is exactly the condition that ill-conditions that interpolation's linear solve — OCCT reports `is_done() == true` and hands back a surface whose control polygon has spurious far-flung points compensating for the near-singularity, even though the curve/surface still passes through the real data points at the knots (interpolation guarantees that part). Between those knots, it bulges catastrophically — which is what you're seeing.

This is why it's invisible in the tool's own logs: `validate_fit`'s "residual vs own grid" check (printed as e.g. `max 6.583e-14 mm`) only samples the fitted surface *at the same discrete nodes it was built from*. An interpolant reproduces those by construction, so the check is structurally blind to inter-node bulging — a surface can log a "perfect" 1e‑14mm fit and still contain a 150mm-off control point.

## Answering your specific questions

- **Small triangles not fit into their planar surface?** No — that's not it. All 641 mesh faces get assigned a surface; nothing is orphaned or misclassified.
- **Points too close together?** Not quite "too close" — it's the opposite pairing: many *very short* boundary segments (fine tessellation on a slightly curved stretch) sitting next to one *much longer* segment (coarse tessellation on a flat stretch) in the same fitting grid. That spacing *ratio* is what ill-conditions the interpolation, not raw proximity.
- **Something else** — yes: a gap in validation. The fit-quality check only evaluates at the interpolation nodes themselves, so a wildly oscillating "successful" fit passes silently.

## Where I'd point a fix

Either constrain `axis_stations` to equalize *3D arc length* per station (like `AxisMaps`/`axis_profile` already does elsewhere in the same file, which was built to fix a related "near-coincident stations" oscillation on the saddle model — see the comment at [stage2/bspline.rs:1040](src/stage2/bspline.rs:1040)) rather than mesh-vertex-index spacing, or add a bounding-box sanity check on the fitted surface's control points (reject/retry if any pole falls far outside the region's own bounding box) so this fails loudly in Stage 2.7 instead of silently exporting garbage. I haven't made either change — want me to implement one of these, or dig further into exactly which mesh segment triggers the bad row first?


## 👤 User

Investigate the mesh segments that cause this. Are they truly non-planar? Is a NURBS surface truly a good way to represent them?

## Are they truly non-planar?

No. All six regions are flat to within **0.012–0.025mm** of a single best-fit plane — a couple hundredths of a millimeter, well under a typical FDM layer height (0.1–0.3mm) and well under this pipeline's own `--surface-tolerance` default (0.4mm) that's used to accept *other* surface types. The 1.5°–3.7° face-normal wobble is consistent with ordinary STL export/mesh-processing noise on flat facets, not real design curvature — and it's essentially the same magnitude across all six regions, whether they ended up garbage or clean. There's no curvature signal correlating with which ones broke; the two "clean" surfaces (Y patch 1/2) are if anything *less* flat than some of the broken ones. This reads as flat, straight-walled embossed/engraved lettering — exactly what you said it looked like by eye.

## Is NURBS the right tool here?

No — and I found exactly why the pipeline chose it anyway. Stage 2.7 has a guard for precisely this case ([stage2/bspline.rs:2141-2161](src/stage2/bspline.rs:2141)):

```rust
// Nearly planar regions get a plane, not a B-spline that overfits noise.
let plane_tol = 10.0 * config.vertex_tolerance_mm;
```

`vertex_tolerance_mm` defaults to `5e-5`mm, so `plane_tol` = **0.0005mm**. All six regions measured 0.012–0.025mm — roughly **25–50× over** that gate — so every one of them fell through to the B-spline fitter instead of being accepted as a plane. The threshold is calibrated for "on-surface exactness" (matching CAD-exact meshes down near machine precision), not for real-world STL noise, so it never fires for data like this.

That's the actual root cause, one level up from what I found last time: the interpolation ill-conditioning I diagnosed before is a real bug, but it's only reachable because a region that should have been trivially accepted as a plane gets routed into the numerically fragile NURBS path instead. Fix the gate, and these regions never reach `axis_stations`/`Interpolate` at all — no ill-conditioning to trigger, no garbage control points, smaller/simpler STEP output, and the "why does this look flat but got fit with a curve" mismatch you noticed goes away at the source.

I'd size `plane_tol` off `surface_tolerance_mm` (or at least a much larger multiple of `vertex_tolerance_mm`) rather than touching the interpolation code — it fixes the actual mismatch between the model's geometry and the fitter chosen for it, rather than just hardening a fitter that shouldn't have run in the first place. # Instructions for LLM Coding Assistants

This file contains guidelines for AI/LLM coding assistants working on this project. Read ALL of AGENTS.md - no just the first 100 lines.

The shell is zsh. Use zsh quoting conventions. "echo ===" will fail, and globs in flags must be quoted.

### Commit Checklist (MANDATORY — verify before every commit)

- \`cargo clippy\` emits no warnings.
- Build passes with no errors or warnings.

## Project Layout

This is a Rust project. Key locations:

- \`README.md\` - Program usage. Read it.
- \`DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md\` - Development plan. Read it.
- \`Cargo.toml\` — Rust project manifest
- \`src/\` — Rust source files
  - \`bin/brepper.rs\` — the main program
  - \`bin/step_measure_tolerance.rs\` — utility to measure distances from STL to correpsonding STEP
  - \`bin/viewer.rs\` — GUI to visualize STL or STEP files
- \`scripts/\` — shell scripts for batch operations over test data
  - \`step_distance_table.sh\` - runs \`step_measure_tolerance\` over all STL/STEP pairs and summarizes statistics
- \`tests/\` — STL and STEP test file pairs
  - \`manual/\` — handcrafted simple models
  - \`onshape/\` — models exported from Onshape
  - \`ccad/generated/\` — models generated via CodeCAD

### OCCT / opencascade-rs

The project uses the \`opencascade-sys\` crate (auto-generated Rust FFI bindings to OpenCASCADE Technology) via a path dependency. MANDATORY: All useful C++ OCCT APIs should be available in the binding - if you want to use one that doesn't seem to be bound, complain loudly about it AND STOP.

\`\`\`
../opencascade-rs/crates/opencascade-sys   ← Rust FFI bindings (8700+ types)
../opencascade-rs/crates/opencascade-sys/PORTING.md  ← Naming conventions & usage patterns
../opencascade-rs/crates/opencascade-sys/generated/  ← All generated .rs modules
../opencascade-rs/crates/occt-sys/OCCT/src/  ← OCCT C++ source (for reading docs/headers)
../opencascade-rs/crates/occt-sys/OCCT/dox/  ← OCCT C++ documentation
\`\`\`

The \`builtin\` feature (default) compiles OCCT from source — first build takes ~8 minutes. Subsequent builds are fast.

## Commit Messages

All commit messages must include:

1. **A clear description** of the changes made
2. **The AI agent/model** used to generate the changes (e.g., "Claude Sonnet 4 (Anthropic, 2025)")
3. **The user prompts** that led to the changes

Format:
\`\`\`
<descriptive commit title>

<detailed description of changes>

---
Generated with assistance from <model name> (<provider>, <year>)

User prompt(s):
- "<prompt 1>"
- "<prompt 2>"
  (include context for prompts that reference previous options/decisions)
\`\`\`

## Development Plan Maintenance

Keep DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md up to date with each commit:

1. **Mark completed items** - Check off (\`[x]\`) any Implementation Phases items that are completed by the commit
2. **Add new tasks** - If work reveals new tasks or sub-tasks not in the plan, add them to the appropriate phase
3. **Modify existing tasks** - If a planned approach changes (e.g., different algorithm, new dependency), update the relevant sections
4. **Include in commit** - Changes to DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md should be part of the same commit as the implementation work

## README Maintenance

Keep README.md up to date when changes affect user-facing behavior:

1. **New dependencies** - Add to the dependencies list with installation instructions
2. **New CLI options** - Update the usage examples and options documentation
3. **Changed defaults** - Document any changes to default parameter values
4. **New features** - Add brief descriptions of significant new capabilities
5. **Include in commit** - README updates should be part of the same commit as the feature work

### IMPORTANT: Time Builds and Tests

**Always** prefix build and test commands with \`time\`. When they take more than 2 minutes ask the user whether to speed them up.

Correct: \`time make -j4 2>&1\`
Correct: \`time ctest --output-on-failure -j4 2>&1\`

## Temporary Test Code

When writing temporary code for debugging or testing:

1. **Put files in \`tmp/\`** - This directory is in the project root and ignored by git. Don't use \`/tmp\` or other directories outside the workspace.

2. **Don't delete temporary code** - Leave it in \`tmp/\` in case it's useful later.

## Library Reuse

Before implementing non-trivial functionality (text rendering, file parsing, data structures, etc.), search for existing open-source libraries that provide that functionality. Evaluate whether using a library will be better for code simplicity and maintainability than writing it from scratch. Consider factors like: compatibility with existing dependencies, maintenance status, API complexity, and how well the library fits the use case. Then go with your decision — either use the library or implement it yourself — and briefly explain why.

# Requires 'ccad' tool installed (https://codecad.xyz)
./tests/ccad/generate_models.sh

<!-- msg_011Cd5C5vPZ32cja7W1boCSp -->

I have the full picture now. Let me reason through the fix design before writing code.

**Root cause, precisely:** `axis_stations` pins grid stations at boundary-vertex positions, and this boundary mixes fine facets (0.175mm chords, on the slightly-curved stretches) with one long straight chord (3.66mm) — a 21:1 spacing jump fed directly into chord-length-parametrized C2 cubic interpolation. A C2 interpolant's overshoot at a knot-spacing discontinuity grows roughly with the *square* of the adjacent-gap ratio (21² ≈ 440× amplification of the mesh's ~0.02–0.3mm flatness noise ≈ 10–130mm — matching the observed 150mm poles). The existing `k`-subdivision divides *every* segment equally, so it can never fix a ratio. And validation only samples at/near data points, so inter-node spikes ship silently.

**The fix, two independent layers:**
1. **Prevention** — condition the station spacing in `axis_stations`, in 3D-arc measure (the `AxisMaps` profile already provides exactly this): merge near-coincident stations (the known "singular interpolation" failure), and subdivide long segments until no gap exceeds ~2× its smaller neighbor (graded spacing, like mesh grading). Subdivision goes uniform-in-arc, not uniform-in-UV. Boundary vertices keep their exact pinned positions (the arch rule stays intact — and mid-segment stations on a *long* segment are safe by construction: a long boundary chord only exists where the mesh is flat).
2. **Detection** — a pole sanity check in `fit_grid`: a B-spline surface lies in the convex hull of its control points, so any pole far outside the data grid's bounding box proves the surface swings far off the mesh. Reject such fits (→ retry ladder / planar fallback) instead of shipping them. This makes the failure mode impossible to ship silently for *any* input.

I deliberately avoid switching to centripetal parametrization (would perturb every model's fit globally); graded stations achieve uniformity directly with zero effect on well-tessellated models.

/// Grid stations for one axis. The base stations are the boundary
/// vertices' own pinned positions (averaged between the two opposite
/// sides — structured or not, the boundary is where the region has exact
/// on-surface data at exact parameters): stations *between* the vertices
/// of a coarse profile sample chord interiors and pin the interpolant to
/// the chordal prism (a 1.7% volume deficit on the arch, the mesh's own
/// chordal error). The base is then evenly subdivided up to the interior-
/// density target when the boundary is coarser than the region it bounds
/// (flat margins tessellate coarsely: hill_with_hole has 8-vertex sides on
/// a 946-vertex region). Sides with mismatched vertex counts fall back to
/// arc-length-uniform stations.
fn axis_stations(
    side_a: &[f64],
    side_b: &[f64],
    target: usize,
    profile: &[(f64, f64)],
) -> Vec<f64> {
    if side_a.len() != side_b.len() || side_a.len() < 2 {
        return AxisMaps::stations(profile, target);
    }
    let base: Vec<f64> = side_a
        .iter()
        .zip(side_b)
        .map(|(a, b)| ((a + b) / 2.0).clamp(0.0, 1.0))
        .collect();
    let k = (target.saturating_sub(1)).div_ceil(base.len() - 1).max(1);
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity((base.len() - 1) * k + 1);
    for w in base.windows(2) {
        for step in 0..k {
            out.push(w[0] + (w[1] - w[0]) * step as f64 / k as f64);
        }
    }
    out.push(*base.last().unwrap());
    out
}

/// Grid stations for one axis. The base stations are the boundary
/// vertices' own pinned positions (averaged between the two opposite
/// sides — structured or not, the boundary is where the region has exact
/// on-surface data at exact parameters): stations *between* the vertices
/// of a coarse profile sample chord interiors and pin the interpolant to
/// the chordal prism (a 1.7% volume deficit on the arch, the mesh's own
/// chordal error). The base is then evenly subdivided up to the interior-
/// density target when the boundary is coarser than the region it bounds
/// (flat margins tessellate coarsely: hill_with_hole has 8-vertex sides on
/// a 946-vertex region). Sides with mismatched vertex counts fall back to
/// arc-length-uniform stations.
///
/// Station spacing is CONDITIONED in 3D-arc measure (the axis profile):
/// chord-length-parametrized C2 interpolation amplifies data noise by
/// roughly the square of the adjacent knot-spacing ratio, so a boundary
/// mixing fine facets with one long straight chord (the xyz-cube letter
/// walls: a 21× jump) turns a 0.02 mm-flat ribbon into control points
/// 150 mm off the part — while passing through every grid node exactly.
/// Near-coincident stations (the other conditioning failure: a
/// near-singular system) are merged; every segment is then subdivided
/// until no piece exceeds GRADE_RATIO× the pieces of either neighbor
/// segment. Subdivision is uniform in arc, not UV (the Floater map
/// compresses high-curvature areas, so UV-uniform substations cluster
/// in 3D). Surviving boundary-vertex stations keep their exact pinned
/// positions; new substations land only inside long segments, where a
/// long boundary chord means the mesh itself is flat and mid-segment
/// samples lie on the true surface (the arch's chordal-prism deficit
/// came from stations between vertices on CURVED stretches).
fn axis_stations(
    side_a: &[f64],
    side_b: &[f64],
    target: usize,
    profile: &[(f64, f64)],
) -> Vec<f64> {
    if side_a.len() != side_b.len() || side_a.len() < 2 {
        return AxisMaps::stations(profile, target);
    }
    /// Merge stations closer (in arc) than this fraction of the median gap.
    const MERGE_FRAC: f64 = 0.25;
    /// Max allowed piece size relative to either neighbor segment's pieces.
    const GRADE_RATIO: f64 = 2.0;
    /// Hard cap on stations per axis (cost guard; the control-point bound
    /// check in `fit_grid` still protects if grading is cut short).
    const MAX_STATIONS: usize = 257;

    // (uv, arc-fraction) base stations.
    let base: Vec<(f64, f64)> = side_a
        .iter()
        .zip(side_b)
        .map(|(a, b)| {
            let uv = ((a + b) / 2.0).clamp(0.0, 1.0);
            (uv, AxisMaps::arc_fraction(profile, uv))
        })
        .collect();

    // Merge pass: drop interior stations far closer than the median gap to
    // their kept predecessor (corner stations always survive).
    let mut gaps: Vec<f64> = base.windows(2).map(|w| w[1].1 - w[0].1).collect();
    gaps.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap());
    let median_gap = gaps[gaps.len() / 2].max(f64::EPSILON);
    let merge_tol = MERGE_FRAC * median_gap;
    let mut kept: Vec<(f64, f64)> = vec![base[0]];
    for &s in &base[1..base.len() - 1] {
        if s.1 - kept.last().unwrap().1 >= merge_tol {
            kept.push(s);
        }
    }
    let last = *base.last().unwrap();
    if kept.len() > 1 && last.1 - kept.last().unwrap().1 < merge_tol {
        kept.pop();
    }
    kept.push(last);

    // Per-segment piece counts: the uniform density target, then graded
    // subdivision to a fixpoint so no piece exceeds GRADE_RATIO× the
    // (current) pieces of either neighbor segment.
    let seg_arc: Vec<f64> = kept
        .windows(2)
        .map(|w| (w[1].1 - w[0].1).max(f64::EPSILON))
        .collect();
    let k = (target.saturating_sub(1)).div_ceil(seg_arc.len()).max(1);
    let mut pieces: Vec<usize> = vec![k; seg_arc.len()];
    for _ in 0..32 {
        let mut changed = false;
        for i in 0..seg_arc.len() {
            let eff = |j: usize| seg_arc[j] / pieces[j] as f64;
            let mut cap = f64::INFINITY;
            if i > 0 {
                cap = cap.min(GRADE_RATIO * eff(i - 1));
            }
            if i + 1 < seg_arc.len() {
                cap = cap.min(GRADE_RATIO * eff(i + 1));
            }
            if !cap.is_finite() {
                continue;
            }
            let total: usize = pieces.iter().sum();
            let headroom = MAX_STATIONS.saturating_sub(total + 1);
            let want = ((seg_arc[i] / cap).ceil() as usize).min(pieces[i] + headroom);
            if want > pieces[i] {
                pieces[i] = want;
                changed = true;
            }
        }
        if !changed {
            break;
        }
    }

    // Emit: kept stations at their exact pinned uv; substations uniform in
    // arc within each segment, mapped back through the profile.
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(pieces.iter().sum::<usize>() + 1);
    for (w, &np) in kept.windows(2).zip(&pieces) {
        out.push(w[0].0);
        for step in 1..np {
            let t = w[0].1 + (w[1].1 - w[0].1) * step as f64 / np as f64;
            out.push(uv_at_arc(profile, t).clamp(w[0].0, w[1].0));
        }
    }
    out.push(kept.last().unwrap().0);
    out
}

/// Invert an axis profile: the uv whose arc fraction is `t` (piecewise-
/// linear interpolation of the profile's (uv, arc) samples).
fn uv_at_arc(profile: &[(f64, f64)], t: f64) -> f64 {
    let k = profile
        .partition_point(|&(_, g)| g < t)
        .clamp(1, profile.len() - 1);
    let (u0, g0) = profile[k - 1];
    let (u1, g1) = profile[k];
    let s = if g1 > g0 {
        ((t - g0) / (g1 - g0)).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
    } else {
        0.0
    };
    u0 + s * (u1 - u0)
}

5. **Resample a grid** through the flattened triangulation (uniform-bin point location; numeric misses near corner slivers are clamped to the nearest triangle within one bin — feeding them to the hole membrane extrapolates garbage). Grid stations per axis are the boundary vertices' own pinned positions (stations *between* the vertices of a coarse profile sample chord interiors and pin the fit to the chordal prism — a 1.7% volume deficit on the arch, the mesh's own chordal error), subdivided up to an interior-density target of ~1.5·√(region vertices) (a flat margin tessellates coarsely: hill_with_hole has 8-vertex sides on a 946-vertex region). Station spacing is **conditioned in 3D-arc measure** (`axis_stations`): chord-length-parametrized C2 interpolation amplifies data noise by roughly the square of the adjacent knot-spacing ratio, so a boundary mixing fine facets with one long straight chord (the xyz-cube letter walls: a 21× jump) turned a 0.02 mm-flat ribbon into control points 150 mm off the part while passing through every grid node exactly. Near-coincident stations (< 0.25× the median arc gap — the near-singular end of the same conditioning problem) are merged, and segments are subdivided to a fixpoint where no piece exceeds 2× either neighbor segment's pieces, uniformly in arc rather than UV (the Floater map compresses high-curvature areas). Surviving boundary-vertex stations keep their exact pinned positions; new substations land only inside long segments, where a long boundary chord means the mesh itself is flat and mid-segment samples lie on the true surface. Genuine hole interiors are filled with a Laplacian membrane so the fitter sees smooth data. The grid is flipped if needed so d1u×d1v matches the mesh's outward normals: B-spline faces are always `concave = false`.
