## Which case

`stepped_block_toroidal_fillets`, fine mesh. The model's real geometry at those spots is a **perimeter fillet cylinder** (r = 0.5 or 1 mm) running along an edge of an end face, meeting a **corner-blend torus** where the profile turns. Competition committed six extra tori straddling those fillets:

| | R | r | sweep |
|---|---|---|---|
| the 18 real corner blends | exactly 2.0000 / 2.5000 / 14.0000 | 0.5 or 1 | 84.7°–103.4° |
| the 6 impostors | 20, 26, 29, 37, 87, 114 | 0.5 or 1 | 3.1°–6.7° |

At seed 24459 the cylinder grew 94 faces (area 2.284) and the torus grew 180 (area 2.714), so the torus won. Same shape at seeds 24588 (95 vs 150), 24615 (67 vs 90), 11638 (160 vs 260).

## Why a torus can nearly always win on area

A torus is a tube of radius *r* whose centre sweeps a circle of radius *R*. As R → ∞ the spine straightens and the torus **becomes** a cylinder — the cylinder is literally the R = ∞ member of the family. So anything a cylinder covers, a torus can cover too, just by setting R huge. Area(best torus) ≥ area(best cylinder) *structurally*.

And it does better than tie. At a tangent junction the two surfaces touch, so one tessellation row past it the neighbour has only departed by ~h²/2r — a very small distance. A cylinder is rigid and must stop there; a torus with two spare degrees of freedom can lean its spine slightly and keep going. It wins the contest by construction, not by being right.

## Why it's the wrong surface anyway

**The parameter isn't determined, so it isn't really "a torus".** Over a 3–7° sweep about the axis, R is essentially free — the data cannot see the revolution. The tell is in the numbers above: the real blends recover R to the reference's exact values, repeatedly, while the impostors report six unrelated magnitudes spanning 20 to 114 mm. An identified parameter lands on the true value; an unidentified one lands wherever the optimizer stops. So the fit isn't "a torus that fits better" — it's a cylinder plus an arbitrary bend.

**The extra area is stolen, not explained.** Those 180 faces are a fillet cylinder's ~94 *plus* ~86 that belong to the adjacent corner blend. Locally and greedily, all 180 are within tolerance of the impostor. Globally, 86 of them belong to a surface that hasn't been committed yet. Claim resolution can't undo it either, because it only arbitrates *contested* faces, and the true owner's flood had already stalled — nobody else claimed them.

**The damage is to the neighbours and the boundaries.** With the impostors present we got 24 tori and 7 real planes against the reference's 18 and 16: fillets fragmented, wall strips eaten, and every shared boundary displaced by a row. That displacement is what the stage-3 reference-edge compare was measuring.

## Why the tessellation would look different

A tessellator subdivides to hold a chordal sag ε, so the step it takes in a given direction is set by the radius of curvature *in that direction*: roughly Δs ≈ 2√(2ερ). A genuine torus of R ≈ 113 mm would therefore be sampled along its spine with one large, **uniform** step everywhere along it — because ρ = R ± r·cos φ ≈ R is constant along the sweep.

What's actually there instead is two different B-rep faces meshed independently: a fillet cylinder swept along a *straight* edge, where the sweep direction has infinite radius and needs essentially no subdivision, joined to a corner blend of R = 2–2.5 mm, which needs many steps around its 90°. So the sampling along the impostor's claimed spine is sparse over the first part and dense over the second — clustered, as you say.

## The numbers from this session

On the medium mesh, the five triangles of one r = 0.5 arc (faces 379/384/387/389/390) span **~8.9 mm in z in a single span**, while their steps *across* the arc are 0.16–0.21 mm. That's ~45:1 anisotropy. On the fine mesh the 30-face blob I probed was 0.4 × 0.4 × **0.0** mm — every centroid at z = −20.506, i.e. one row, many columns across the arc, with cross-arc steps of ~0.022 mm.

The real corner blends look nothing like that: 1296–1533 faces each, spread over both the 90° sweep and the tube arc, roughly comparable in the two directions — near-isotropic, as a torus with R = 2.5 and r = 0.5 should be.

So the mesh anisotropy is a direct fossil of "straight along here, curved across there", and it flatly contradicts R = 113.

## Two related signals in the same family

The impostors' axes came out tilted at odd angles — [−0.223, −0.975, 0], [0.418, −0.903, −0.101]. A real surface of revolution leaves *rings* in its tessellation perpendicular to its axis; those claimed axes bear no relation to the mesh's actual sampling directions.

And there's a stronger fact already established in this project's notes: CAD tessellators **seam B-rep edges even where the surfaces are tangent** — probed directly on nosecone, where 0 triangles straddle the cone–sphere tangency circle and 104 vertices lie exactly on the ring. If that holds generally, the true face partition is always a *subset of the mesh edges*, and the impostor's support demonstrably crosses one of those seams.

## The honest caveats

- Tessellators vary; a Delaunay-style mesher carries less of this structure than Parasolid's. The corpus is mostly Onshape plus generated models, so it may be flattering.
- Density also varies for reasons unrelated to curvature — max-edge-length caps, aspect-ratio limits, proximity to small features. A straight fillet often does get subdivided along its length for those reasons, so the signal is "grossly non-uniform", not "no subdivision at all".
- Stage 1.3's quad fusion already merges triangle pairs, which partly normalizes the raw pattern.

## Algorithm and Implementation

OpenCASCADE package BRepMesh can compute the Delaunay's triangulation with the algorithm of Watson. It can be used for 2d plane or on surface by meshing in UV parametric space.

## Application to Surface Faceting

For surface triangulation, OpenCASCADE uses an incremental approach. The default meshing algorithm BRepMesh_IncrementalMesh has two major options to define triangulation -- linear and angular deflections. At the first step all edges from a face are discretized according to the specified parameters. At the second step, the faces are tessellated. Linear deflection limits the distance between a curve and its tessellation, whereas angular deflection limits the angle between subsequent segments in a polyline.

## Meshing Approach

The system triangulates surfaces by working in parametric UV space and then mapping the results back to 3D model space. Classes BRepMesh_DelaunayNodeInsertionMeshAlgo and BRepMesh_SweepLineNodeInsertionMeshAlgo implement algorithm-specific functionality related to addition of internal nodes, and BRepMesh_DelaunayDeflectionControlMeshAlgo extends functionality of BRepMesh_DelaunayNodeInsertionMeshAlgo by additional procedure controlling deflection of generated triangles.

I found several results related to Parasolid faceting and tessellation. Here are the key findings:

## Parasolid Faceting and Tessellation

PK_TOPOL_facet returns a tabular representation of the part's topology and geometry, defining the facet mesh in terms of connected facet, fin and vertex indices.

### Vertex Matching (Edges Shared Between Faces)

The vertex matching strategy at edges corresponds to the value that will be passed to PK_TOPOL_facet_mesh_o_t.match. Parasolid offers different matching approaches:

- Facets can meet exactly but be topologically disjoint, or they can meet exactly and have the same topology
- The topology matching option matches facet vertices across a common edge, where the boundaries of neighboring facet meshes (generally) meet exactly but are topologically disjoint

### Tabular Output

Parasolid can create facet information in tabular format, defining the facet mesh in terms of connected facet strip, facet, fin and vertex indices, and unlike facet output via the GO interface, tabular output of faceting allows you to output connectivity information for a facet mesh.

### Mesh Quality and Conformality

If PK_TOPOL_facet is being used to return tabular facet data, the fin_fin table only matches fins which belong to the same face (the co-fin values of fins on the face mesh boundary are set to a null index value).

The search results provide technical documentation on how Parasolid handles facet tessellation, topology matching, and mesh connectivity through its PK_TOPOL functions.

I found search results related to faceting, tessellation, and STL export for Parasolid and CAD models. Here's what the search revealed:

## Key Findings:

**Parasolid Faceting Parameters:**
The two faceting parameters, chordal angle and chordal deviation factor are used to control the tessellation and control the degree of fineness of the extracted mesh. Faceting parameter input is supported only for Parasolid models imported with the 'Save geometry in database' option.

**STL Export and Tessellation:**
CAD/MCAD models are defined as analytic (numerical) NURBS surfaces which need to be converted into a polygonal mesh through a process called "mesh tessellation". Each geometrical 'part' in a CAD/MCAD model is defined as a solid "body" which consists of one or more geometrical "faces," and for STL export we wish for all the faces within the body to share edges with each other so that the body is considered to be 'water tight'.

**Edge and Face Issues:**
Boundary edges are identified when certain edges in an STL file are connected to only one face rather than two adjacent faces, which indicates the presence of holes in the geometry.

# BRepMesh_IncrementalMesh Workflow

Yes, BRepMesh_IncrementalMesh follows a two-stage discretization process:

## Edge Discretization First

The algorithm begins by processing edges before faces. According to the documentation: "At the first step all edges from a face are discretized according to the specified parameters."

## Face Triangulation in UV Space

After edge processing, the system moves to face meshing: "At the second step, the faces are tessellated. Linear deflection limits the distance between a curve and its tessellation, whereas angular deflection limits the angle between subsequent segments."

## Boundary Preservation

Face boundaries are indeed preserved as triangulation constraints. The documentation explains that during face discretization, "edges tessellation data obtained and processed on previous steps is used to form contours of target faces and passed as input to the triangulation algorithm."

## Per-Face Processing with Shared Edge Data

Each face is processed individually: "Each face is processed separately, thus it is possible to process faces in a parallel mode." However, edge discretization is shared across adjacent faces. The data model maintains "each edge is characterized by a single 3D curve and zero (in case of free edge) or more 2D curves associated with faces adjacent to this edge," allowing synchronized polygon data between neighboring faces.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about Onshape STL export tessellation quality settings:

## Tessellation Quality Parameters

For STL format export, you specify the Chordal tolerance, Angular deviation, and Minimum facet width.

### Chordal Tolerance

Chordal tolerance represents the maximum distance between the actual part surface and the flat plane of the STL triangle. The Chordal Tolerance defines the maximum deviation between the CAD surface and the mesh facet, and lowering this value produces a smoother surface, which is essential for high-quality 3D printing.

### Angular Tolerance (Angular Deviation)

Angular tolerance controls the deviation between the normals of adjacent triangles. Angular deviation puts a limit on the maximum angle between two faces (measured as angle between outward normals), and as you lower that spec, the difference between adjacent triangles approaches locally flat. For organic shapes or tight radii, reducing the angular tolerance ensures a smoother transition, though it significantly increases the triangle count.

## Resolution Presets

For Coarse: Angular deviation 12.5°, Chordal tolerance 0.24 mm, Minimum facet width 0.635 mm; Medium: 6.25°, 0.12 mm, 0.254 mm; Fine: 2.5°, 0.06 mm, 0.0254 mm.

## Relationship to Triangle Count

Tessellation is the conversion of smooth parametric geometry into a mesh composed of discrete triangles. Lower tolerance values result in more triangles for a smoother surface representation.

## Key Findings:

**Refine Mesh Setting:**
When enabled, Rhino uses a recursive process to refine the mesh by subdividing quadrangles until they meet criteria defined by Maximum angle, Minimum edge length, Maximum edge length, and Maximum distance settings. Disabling refinement results in faster meshing, less accurate meshes, lower polygon count, and evenly sized quadrangles for untrimmed surfaces.

**Mesh Creation Algorithm:**
Surfaces are meshed in a two-step process: first a regular quadrangle mesh is created, then refined by splitting some quadrangles into four smaller quadrangles. The first step creates a regular rectangular grid of vertices on the surface, with spacing estimated to roughly meet meshing criteria.

**Mesh Types in Rhino:**
Render meshes are created on NURBS surfaces and polysurfaces for visualization in shaded or rendered viewports, but are not directly user accessible or editable. Meshes created by the Mesh command are visible, editable, and can be exported to polygon mesh formats like STL, DXF, 3DS, and OBJ.

**STL Export:**
Meshing is valuable for export to STL rapid prototyping files. Meshes created during export have the same mesh settings dialogs as other types.

## What kernel is behind each tool

| Tool | Kernel | Faceter style |
|---|---|---|
| Fusion 360, Inventor | ShapeManager (Autodesk's ACIS fork) | quad-tree gridding |
| SolidWorks, Onshape, Solid Edge, Shapr3D, Plasticity | Parasolid | per-face, own faceter |
| **FreeCAD** | **Open CASCADE** | **genuine Delaunay** |
| Rhino | own kernel | regular quad grid + recursive subdivision |
| Tinkercad, OpenSCAD, Blender, SketchUp | none (mesh/CSG-native) | n/a |

One popular blog claims Fusion uses Parasolid server-side; that's wrong — Wikipedia's kernel table lists ShapeManager for both Fusion and Inventor.

## Does anyone use Delaunay? Yes — and it's the one that matters most to you

OCCT's `BRepMesh` computes Delaunay triangulation **by Watson's algorithm**, in UV parametric space. That's FreeCAD's mesher — and FreeCAD is the fastest-growing free option now that Fusion's personal tier caps cloud documents. It's also, of course, brepper's own mesher.

Rhino is explicitly *not* Delaunay: it builds "a regular rectangular grid of vertices on the surface" then recursively splits quads. ACIS uses "a new quad tree gridding algorithm". Both produce highly structured, grid-like, strongly anisotropic meshes — the best case for your density argument.

## Would they all preserve tangent edges? The B-rep ones: yes, structurally

This is the strong result. Every B-rep faceter uses the same two-stage architecture, and OCCT's docs state it plainly:

> "At the first step all edges from a face are discretized… At the second step, the faces are tessellated."

and

> "edges tessellation data obtained and processed on previous steps is used to form contours of target faces and passed as input to the triangulation algorithm" — with "each face processed separately".

So even the *Delaunay* case is a **constrained** Delaunay whose constraints are the pre-discretized face boundaries. ACIS is described as "maintaining the edge consistency between adjacent faces"; Parasolid's whole matching machinery exists so "all the faces within the body share edges… so that the body is watertight".

That's not a stylistic choice a vendor might change — it's *how they guarantee watertightness*. A tangent edge is an edge in the topology, so it gets discretized like any other, and no triangle can straddle it. This project already measured exactly that on Parasolid output: nosecone's cone–sphere tangency has 0 straddling triangles and 104 vertices lying exactly on the ring, and this session I saw the same on stepped_block, where face 11548 has one vertex at exactly y = −164.00000, on the tangency, with the rest one row in.

## The two signals are not equally reliable

Your original observation actually contains two separable claims, and the research separates them:

- **Boundary preservation** (a tangent B-rep edge is always a chain of mesh edges) — architecture-guaranteed across *every* B-rep faceter, Delaunay included. Robust.
- **Density/anisotropy** (spacing reflects curvature per direction) — faceter-dependent. Very strong for Rhino/ACIS grid meshers and for Parasolid; **weakest exactly for OCCT's Delaunay**, which fills the interior with inserted nodes rather than a grid. Since OCCT is FreeCAD's mesher and brepper's own, that's not a corner case.

So if this became a technique, the seam/ring structure is the dependable half and density is the corroborating half.

## Where it breaks entirely

A large share of Thingiverse content never had a B-rep. OpenSCAD — one of the two dominant formats on Thingiverse alongside STL — is CSG over polyhedra via CGAL, with curves approximated by `$fn`/`$fa`/`$fs` segments; Tinkercad, Blender and SketchUp are mesh-native. There is no "tangent edge" because there are no faces, and often no analytic surface to recover in the first place. Add to that any model that's been through repair or decimation (Meshmixer, netfabb, slicer auto-repair), which destroys the original triangulation structure wholesale.

One in-house caveat too: brepper's own stage 1.3 fuses triangle pairs into quads, which could smear the seam evidence before stage 2 ever sees it. Worth checking before relying on it.

**Net:** for the mechanical-CAD-authored models brepper actually targets, tangent edges are preserved essentially universally, and that's a stronger, more portable signal than the sampling density. Delaunay does occur, but it constrains to the same boundaries.

# Circle Resolution Variables in OpenSCAD

**$fa, $fs, and $fn** control the number of segments used to render circles and arcs:

- **$fa** (minimum angle): "The default value is 12 (i.e. 30 line segments for a full circle)."
- **$fs** (minimum segment size): "The default value is 2"
- **$fn** (segment count): When greater than zero, it overrides the other two variables.

## Formula for Fragment Count

The exact calculation is provided in C code:

\`\`\`c
int get_line_segments_from_r(double r, double fn, double fs, double fa)
{
  if (r < GRID_FINE) return 3;
  if (fn > 0.0) return (int)(fn >= 3 ? fn : 3);
  return (int)ceil(fmax(fmin(360.0 / fa, r*2*M_PI / fs), 5));
}
\`\`\`

An OpenSCAD equivalent is provided: \`ceil(max(min(360/$fa,r*2*PI/$fs),5))\`

This means the fragment count is the maximum of either the angle-based calculation (360/$fa) or the size-based calculation (r×2π/$fs), with a minimum of 5 segments.
```

## 🤖 Assistant
<!-- msg_011CdUdjALixLyz1kHnyCDyu -->

Concrete answer: **no, and for a stronger reason than in B-rep CAD — but the signal you'd want to exploit disappears.**

## Why triangles can't span them

OpenSCAD has no smooth surfaces at any stage. A `cylinder()` is a prism from the moment it is created; a `sphere()` is a polyhedron. CSG runs on polyhedra (CGAL, or the newer Manifold backend). So every facet in the output is planar by construction, and a planar triangle cannot straddle two non-coplanar facets. Any change in surface orientation is *necessarily* a mesh edge. That's a stronger guarantee than Parasolid's or OCCT's, which rely on the edge-first faceting architecture to achieve the same thing.

## But there are no tangent edges to preserve

What would be a C¹ tangency in a real CAD model becomes a junction with a **finite dihedral of one discretization step**. OpenSCAD's rule is

```
n = ceil(max(min(360/$fa, r*2*PI/$fs), 5))
```

with defaults `$fa = 12`, `$fs = 2`. So a prism side-to-side dihedral is 360/n, and with defaults n is capped at 30 — meaning **every curve carries a dihedral of at least 12°**.

Against brepper's default `--angular-tolerance` of 25°, that gives a sharp crossover:

- **$fn ≥ 15** (or, on defaults, radius ≳ 4.5 mm, where `ceil(πr) ≥ 15`) → dihedral ≤ 24° → read as **smooth**, regions merge, brepper fits an analytic surface.
- **$fn ≤ 14** → dihedral ≥ 25.7° → read as **sharp**, kept as a genuine prism.

So `$fn=6` for a hex nut correctly stays a hexagonal prism, and the near-universal `$fn=100` at the top of a file gives 3.6° steps that read as smooth.

## The fit will succeed, and easily

This is worth knowing: OpenSCAD inscribes its polygons, so a prism's vertices lie **exactly on the ideal cylinder of radius r** — which is why holes print undersized. brepper validates by vertex distance (5e-5 mm), so that test passes with essentially zero residual. The binding constraint is the *centroid* test against `--surface-tolerance` (0.4 mm), where the sagitta is r(1−cos(180/n)):

| | sagitta | vs 0.4 mm |
|---|---|---|
| r=5, n=16 | 0.096 mm | passes |
| r=20, n=30 | 0.11 mm | passes |
| r=100, n=30 | 0.55 mm | **fails** |

So large-radius curves at default resolution are the OpenSCAD failure mode — brepper would reject the cylinder and fall back to per-facet planes.

## The real implication: the fossil carries no information

Here's what changes for the idea you raised. In a B-rep mesh the tangent seam is a *distinguished* line — the tessellator started a new face there, vertices align in a ring, and the sampling density typically changes across it. In OpenSCAD output, the junction edge exists but looks **exactly like every other edge in the fan**: going around a Minkowski-rounded corner you get 12° steps, and the step onto the flat face is also 12°. Every edge is a facet boundary, so "is this edge a face boundary?" is trivially true everywhere and distinguishes nothing.

The junction is still detectable — but by *curvature*, not combinatorics: the dihedral is constant at 12° through the fillet and drops to 0° on the flat, which is precisely the curvature-jump signal. So on OpenSCAD models you're back to the jet, with none of the mesh-structure corroboration.

Anisotropy does survive, though, and strongly: `linear_extrude` produces a single span along the extrusion direction with no subdivision, so a prism side is one quad — the same "curved across, straight along" fossil, arguably cleaner than any B-rep faceter's.

## And the ambiguity is genuine

A 15-gon prism and a coarsely-tessellated cylinder are the *same mesh*. Nothing in the file says which the designer meant. brepper's angular tolerance is the arbiter, which makes it a policy dial rather than a measurement — worth documenting as such, since for OpenSCAD-sourced input a user might reasonably want to lower it to keep intended prisms, or raise it to recover intended cylinders.

=== assumptions section
## Assumptions

- Assumes the vertices of the mesh lie precisely on the CAD surfaces, modulo numerical error/stability.
- Assumes transitions between shapes always have a seam — verified to hold
  even for tangent transitions (see Design Principles #2).
- Assumes manifold mesh (each edge shared by exactly 2 faces).
- Assumes consistent face orientation (all normals point outward).

Fails noisily if any of the assumptions are violated, after stage 1.2's
repair pass has fixed what can be fixed without moving a vertex
(\`--strict-mesh\` disables repair).

## Dependencies

| Library | Purpose | Version |
|---------|---------|---------|
=== 300-315
- **The tangent frame comes from a PCA of own + 1-ring vertices, not the
  facet normal** — the smallest-variance direction of the neighborhood IS
  the local normal and stays accurate on strips. Own vertices dominate the
  frame (weight \`OWN_WEIGHT\`).
- **The face's own vertices anchor the fit** (weight \`OWN_WEIGHT = 50\`).
  Tessellators never straddle a B-rep boundary with a triangle, so a face's
  own corners always lie on its own surface. There is **no outlier
  rejection** (rejection forces arbitrary one-side reads that vary face to
  face — measured); sharp-crease neighbors are excluded from the point set,
  and tangent-junction mixing is allowed — junction rows read intermediate
  values, which is fine because no decision ever keys on them.

*Estimator history, for context:* per-edge κ = θ/d failed on irregular
tessellation (the centroid distance doesn't measure arc length in the
rotation direction — the 65:1 sliver fillet of rounded_cube_10_r2_fine
read ~100× low and fragmented ~50×). The neighbor-normal tensor fixed
strips and slivers but deadlocked on balanced-mix junction rings
(stepped_block's blend zones). The jet subsumes both — as a *measurement*;
as a junction *detector* the whole family is dead (see Resolution).

the expected failure mode (sagitta 0.55 mm at r = 100, n = 30, against a 0.4 mm

The ambiguity is *genuine* — a 15-gon prism and a coarse cylinder are the same
mesh — so this is a policy choice rather than something measurable, which
argues for an explicit flag over silent auto-detection. TODO.md carries that as
a future item, with the two detection signals worth trying if we go the other
way (a constant dihedral of exactly 360/n around a whole revolution, and
vertices exactly on the circumscribed circle).

<!-- msg_011CdUeMypjfjEEoVuLuLw2f -->

Let me think this through properly, because I think the assumption is currently under-exploited in a way that explains most of the parameter pile.

## Two different ways to use it

Worth separating up front, because they have very different risk profiles:

- **As a constraint** — "the answer's boundaries must be chains of mesh edges." Provenance-independent: true for every B-rep faceter, and trivially true for OpenSCAD too.
- **As a detector** — "here is where the seams are." Provenance-*dependent*: strong for grid faceters, weak for OCCT's Delaunay, information-free for mesh-native sources.

Stage 2 currently uses it as **neither**. It's cited as justification for partition-then-classify, but nothing in stage 2 either finds seams or requires boundaries to look like seams. Stage 2.1 finds only *sharp* edges; tangent seams are invisible, regions merge across them, and stage 2.3 competition re-derives the partition from scratch by fitting.

Stage 3, by contrast, exploits it fully — the §3.x design note "shared-edge topological assembly instead of geometric sewing." That's the proof of concept worth remembering: using the assumption **deleted** a whole heuristic-laden alternative (tolerance-driven geometric sewing).

## The size of the prize

Nearly the entire parameter pile is the price of not knowing the tangent seams. If the partition were known, each region goes to the whole-region DOF ladder — `classify_one_region`, which already exists and whose few constants are cost-control (subsampling, refit rounds) rather than decision thresholds. The evidence is already in hand: **sharp-edged models pass the ladder with 0 competition regions**, no tuning involved.

Everything that exists only because the partition is unknown:

`SEED_PATCH_CAP` · `MAX_PATCH_DEPTH` · `PATCH_RADII` · `PATCH_TRIM_ROUNDS` · `MIN_CONDITION_FACES` · `MAX_GROW_ROUNDS` · `GROW_VTOL_FACTOR` · `RESIDUAL_SIGMAS` · `MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG` · `MAX_TORUS_RADIUS_RATIO` · `BEND_PATCH_DEPTH` · `BEND_PATCH_CAP` · `MAX_TORUS_STARTS` · `LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX` · `MERGE_MAX_SMALL` · `SMALL_SELECTION_ABSORB_FACES` · relabel's 2× margin and 10-round cap · the freeform island rules

That's roughly **two-thirds of stage 2's behavioural thresholds**, all downstream of one missing fact. Seed ordering, patch conditioning, claim resolution, relabel, merge, re-split and the degeneracy guards are all machinery for guessing a boundary the mesh already contains.

## Exploits, ranked

**1. Snap shared boundaries to mesh-edge chains.** Every remaining `--compare` failure has been a boundary one tessellation row off. Once two adjacent surfaces are fitted, their true intersection or tangency curve is computable — and the assumption guarantees the correct boundary *exists as a mesh-edge chain*. So pick the chain nearest that curve. Deterministic, provenance-independent, and it retires relabel's 2× margin and round cap along with the whole class of failure. This is TODO #5, and the assumption is precisely what licenses it: you're not searching, you're selecting from a guaranteed-nonempty set.

**2. Self-calibrate the chordal tolerance.** `--surface-tolerance` defaults to 0.4 mm, set by a hand edit in March with no recorded rationale, and measured to be 10–15× above actual tessellation sag. But the exporter used *one* deflection setting for the whole body, and the mesh's own centroid-to-surface distances are a sample of it. Estimating it per-model — the same move that worked for the vertex tolerance — replaces a magic number with a measurement. The provenance research is what justifies the premise that a single global value exists.

**3. Reformulate competition as alternating partition/fit.** The assumption says face-level assignment is the right granularity, which is exactly the setting for Lloyd-style iteration (this is Variational Shape Approximation: alternate assign-faces-to-proxies and refit-proxies). I stumbled into half of it this session — relabel + refit converged and took stepped_block from 73 surfaces to exactly 71. Done properly it subsumes seed ordering, patch conditioning, claim resolution, relabel, merge and re-split into one loop with an error criterion and no seeds. Big change, but it's a known algorithm rather than an invention.

**4. Seam detection proper — genuinely hard, and I'd be careful here.** The project already measured that *curvature-based* detection fails: no threshold separates real junctions from real curvature gradients, the classes overlap. What's new is that *structural* signals were never tried — grid-direction discontinuity, density change, vertices lying on a discretized curve rather than scattered by surface meshing. But those are exactly the provenance-dependent ones: near-absent on OCCT's Delaunay interiors, which is FreeCAD's mesher and brepper's own. So a detector would be an **accelerator with fallback to competition**, not a replacement — which means it wouldn't actually delete the parameters. Lower value than it first appears.

## What it can't do

The assumption says where boundaries *can* be, not which candidate partition is right. It doesn't touch the degenerate-torus problem (that fit's support is a perfectly valid union of mesh faces), and it says nothing about surface *type*. And its detector form is worthless on mesh-native input.

## If I were choosing

**#1 first.** It's narrow, provenance-independent, attacks the only failure class still standing, and removes a heuristic rather than adding one. **#2** next, as a small independent win against a documented arbitrary constant. **#3** is where the real simplification lives, but it's a rewrite of stage 2.3–2.4 and should follow the sweep harness (#6 on the list) so the before/after is measurable across more than the handful of models I inspect by hand.

Good question — the circularity is the crux, and it's breakable because of an asymmetry the mesh already gives us for free.

## First, what `--surface-tolerance` actually is

It's used as `centroid_distance(fit, centroid[f]) ≤ stol` in face validation, merge, and the ladder. The physical quantity it bounds is the **chordal sag**: a planar facet chords a curved surface, so its centroid sits *inside* the true surface.

For a facet whose vertices lie on a surface of radius R, with circumradius ρ measured perpendicular to the axis:

```
depth = R − √(R² − ρ²) ≈ ρ²/(2R)
```

And the tessellator chose the facet size precisely so this stays under its **deflection setting** ε. So `--surface-tolerance` isn't really a fitting tolerance at all — it's a stand-in for a parameter the exporter used and then discarded.

How far off is the default? Stage 1's `--compare` already measures the true sag against reference surfaces: **8.9e-4 mm** on stepped_block fine, **9.5e-4 mm** on rounded_cube fine. Against a default of 0.4 mm. That's roughly **400× too loose**, on a constant whose history is a hand edit in March with no recorded rationale.

## The asymmetry that makes it measurable

This is the same one that made the acceptance tolerance self-calibrating: **vertices lie on the true surface (~1e-6 mm), centroids sit inside by the sag.** The mesh therefore contains both a sample of the true surface *and* a sample of the chord. It is its own reference — no STEP needed.

## Three estimators, increasingly independent

**(a) Fit-based, bootstrapped from the unambiguous regions.** Sharp-bounded regions are solved by the whole-region ladder with no tolerance choices beyond vertex validation — they're the part of the model where nothing is in doubt. For every facet in a committed surface, the distance from its centroid to *its own fit* is a direct sag measurement. Take a high quantile across those. On stepped_block fine that's the end caps and walls, a few hundred faces, all available before competition runs.

**(b) Fit-free, from the mesh's own second-order structure.** For two adjacent facets on a cylinder of radius R, each spanning arc angle θ (the dihedral) with width h = Rθ:

```
sag ≈ (h/2)²/(2R) = h²/(8R) = h·θ/8
```

So **sag ≈ dihedral × facet size / 8**, computable per facet from the mesh alone — no fits, no jet inversion, available in stage 2.1. A high quantile over the model gives ε.

**(c) Cross-check.** (a) and (b) should agree. If they don't, the provenance premise is violated — a decimated, repaired, or remeshed STL — which is itself worth knowing and worth telling the user.

## How to prove the estimator before trusting it

This is the part I'd insist on: the corpus **has** reference STEPs, and stage 1's `--compare` already reports the true centroid max distance. So run the reference-free estimator across the corpus and check it reproduces those numbers (8.9e-4 on stepped_block fine, 9.5e-4 on rounded_cube fine, and whatever medium/coarse give). The reference is the validation instrument, never the production input — exactly the right use of it.

## The bonus: the same argument retires `--angular-tolerance`

`--angular-tolerance` (25°) is *also* a stand-in for an exporter setting — its own doc comment says so: "Medium-resolution CAD exports step small-radius fillets up to ~24° between rows… the default must admit those." Onshape's presets expose it directly (12.5° / 6.25° / 2.5°).

And it's recoverable the same way, as a **clustering** rather than a threshold: the dihedral distribution across a CAD mesh should be strongly bimodal — a mass of tessellation steps near zero, and a separate population of real sharp edges. Find the gap (Otsu-style) instead of fixing 25°. On stepped_block fine, 384 of 51603 edges are called sharp, so the populations are lopsided enough that a gap should be visible; I'd plot it before believing it.

That also drops the OpenSCAD detector out for free: a faceted-by-construction model has a *constant* dihedral around each revolution, so the distribution is spiky rather than bimodal-with-a-gap — the absence of a clean gap is the signal.

## Risks I'd want measured first

- **ε is not truly global.** Exporters also cap angular deviation and minimum facet width, so different features are bound by different constraints. A single ε is an upper bound, not a uniform value — fine for our use, but the estimator must take a high quantile or max, never a median, or it will reject legitimate faces.
- **Tightening 0.4 → ~1e-3 is a 400× change** and will move behaviour everywhere. `REFIT_GIVE_UP` is defined as 8×stol; merge's centroid gate uses it; so does every `face_validates`. This wants the sweep harness (TODO #6) in place first.
- **Coarse meshes genuinely have larger sag** — that's the whole point of measuring per model, but it means the corpus's coarse variants are the real test.
- **A repaired or decimated STL breaks the premise entirely.** The cross-check in (c) is the guard, and detecting that case is arguably as valuable as the tolerance itself.

Net: `--vertex-tolerance` is a genuine precision request from the user and should stay a flag. `--surface-tolerance` and `--angular-tolerance` are both attempts to guess what the exporter did, and both are measurable from the mesh — so they should become *estimates with an override*, not defaults.

Target is stepped_block medium; fine must stay passing.

**B — estimate the two exporter-derived tolerances from the mesh.** The asymmetry that makes it reference-free (vertices on the surface, centroids inside by the sag), the derivations `depth ≈ ρ²/(2R)` and fit-free `sag ≈ dihedral × facet size / 8`, three estimators with a cross-check that doubles as a decimated-mesh detector, the measured evidence that 0.4 mm is ~400× too loose, and the insistence that reference STEPs are the *validation instrument, never the production input*. **C — VSA / alternating partition-fit.** Named as the literature algorithm, with the evidence half of it already works here (relabel+refit took stepped_block fine 73→71), what it subsumes, and the instruction to do it last, after the sweep harness.

**Then the simplification protocol** — the part that's easy to skip. Candidates ordered most-likely-dead first, ending with whether the jet still has a job beyond rung ordering. 11	  **Rewrite Roadmap** in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md and the **Stage-2 Retrospective**
12	  for rationale. Remaining classification-quality gaps (disabled test
13	  blockers) are listed in the item below; the obsolete old-BFS-pipeline TODO
14	  items (absorb pass, \`--skip-stage\`, planar-only mode) were pruned 2026-07-23.
15	
16	- **NEXT MAJOR WORK — exploit the seam assumption. Read this first.** This is
17	  the recommended plan for the next several sessions, in order (A → B → C).
18	  Background reading before starting: **Mesh provenance and the seam
19	  assumption** and **Identifiability is not model selection** in
20	  DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md, plus the ranked list in the item below (which records
21	  two ideas already tried and refuted — do not re-derive them).
22	
23	  **The framing.** The assumption is that a B-rep face boundary is always a
24	  chain of mesh edges, tangent junctions included. There are two ways to use
25	  it, with very different risk: as a **constraint** ("the answer's boundaries
26	  must be mesh-edge chains" — provenance-independent, true for every faceter)
27	  or as a **detector** ("here is where the seams are" — provenance-dependent,
28	  weak on OCCT's Delaunay interiors, information-free on mesh-native input).
29	  **Stage 2 currently uses it as neither.** Stage 3 uses it fully, and is the
30	  proof of concept: §3.x "shared-edge topological assembly instead of geometric
31	  sewing" *deleted* a heuristic-laden alternative outright.
32	
33	  **The prize, quantified.** Almost every tuned parameter in stage 2 is the
34	  price of not knowing the tangent seams. If the partition were known, each
35	  region goes to the whole-region DOF ladder (\`classify_one_region\`, which
36	  already exists and whose few constants are cost-control — subsampling, refit
37	  rounds — not decision thresholds). The evidence is already in hand: **sharp-
38	  edged models pass the ladder with 0 competition regions and no tuning at
39	  all.** Everything below exists only because tangent seams are invisible:
40	  \`SEED_PATCH_CAP\`, \`MAX_PATCH_DEPTH\`, \`PATCH_RADII\`, \`PATCH_TRIM_ROUNDS\`,
41	  \`MIN_CONDITION_FACES\`, \`MAX_GROW_ROUNDS\`, \`GROW_VTOL_FACTOR\`,
42	  \`RESIDUAL_SIGMAS\`, \`MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG\`, \`MAX_TORUS_RADIUS_RATIO\`,
43	  \`BEND_PATCH_DEPTH\`, \`BEND_PATCH_CAP\`, \`MAX_TORUS_STARTS\`,
44	  \`LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX\`, \`MERGE_MAX_SMALL\`, \`SMALL_SELECTION_ABSORB_FACES\`,
45	  relabel's 2× margin and 10-round cap, and the freeform island rules —
46	  roughly **two-thirds of stage 2's behavioural thresholds**.
47	
48	  ---
49	
50	  **A. Snap shared region boundaries to mesh-edge chains.** *Start here:
51	  narrow, provenance-independent, and it removes a heuristic rather than adding
52	  one.*
53	
54	  Every remaining \`--compare\` failure has been a boundary sitting one
55	  tessellation row off, and nothing in the pipeline reasons about where a
56	  boundary *should* be — it falls out of flood plus claim resolution. The
57	  assumption guarantees the correct boundary **exists** as a mesh-edge chain,
58	  so this is selection from a guaranteed-nonempty set, not a search.
59	
60	  - Once two adjacent surfaces are committed, compute the curve where they
61	    meet, then reassign the boundary faces by which side of it they fall on,
62	    choosing the mesh-edge chain that best follows it.
63	  - **The hard case is exactly the one that matters.** At a *tangent* junction
64	    the surfaces graze rather than cross, so \`GeomAPI_IntSS\` is the wrong tool
65	    — it is numerically fragile there and that fragility is what produced the
66	    original 4.4e-2 mm error (a plane offset δ moves its intersection with a
67	    torus it should graze by √(2rδ), so tiny fit error is hugely amplified).
68	    For tangency, find the locus of minimum distance between the two fitted
69	    surfaces instead — for a plane grazing a torus that is the tangency circle,
70	    computable in closed form from the fitted parameters. Consider handling
71	    tangent and transversal junctions by different code paths; stage 3.2
72	    already classifies edges as tangent, and stage 3's compare already exempts
73	    tangent edges to the chordal tolerance for this reason.
74	  - Note OCCT gotchas already recorded in DONE/DEVELOPMENT_PLAN: \`IntSS\`
75	    construction can *throw* (knots too close) rather than report \`!IsDone\`.
76	  - **Retires:** relabel's 2× anti-flapping margin and 10-round cap, probably
77	    \`MERGE_MAX_SMALL\`.
78	  - **Validation:** \`stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_medium\` is the target (a
79	    1.6e-1 mm reference-edge compare, \`#[ignore]\`d in stage4_integration);
80	    fine must stay passing. Use \`tmp/probe.sh\` first, full suite to decide.
81	
82	  ---
83	
84	  **B. Estimate \`--surface-tolerance\` and \`--angular-tolerance\` from the mesh
85	  instead of defaulting them.** Both are stand-ins for settings the *exporter*
86	  used and then discarded; neither is a property of the fitting problem.
87	  \`--vertex-tolerance\` is different — it is a genuine precision request from
88	  the user and should stay a plain flag.
89	
90	  *Why it is measurable without a reference STEP.* The mesh is its own
91	  reference, because **vertices lie on the true surface (~1e-6 mm) while
92	  centroids sit inside it by the chordal sag**. For a facet whose vertices lie
93	  on a surface of radius R, with circumradius ρ perpendicular to the axis:
94	  \`depth = R − √(R² − ρ²) ≈ ρ²/(2R)\`. The tessellator sized the facet so this
95	  stays under its deflection setting ε, so the sag distribution over the mesh
96	  *is* a sample of ε.
97	
98	  *How far off the default is:* stage 1's \`--compare\` already reports the true
99	  sag — **8.9e-4 mm** on stepped_block fine, **9.5e-4 mm** on rounded_cube
100	  fine — against a default of **0.4 mm**, i.e. ~400× too loose. (0.4 was a hand
101	  edit in March 2026 with no recorded rationale; see the tolerance-history
102	  notes.) Earlier measurements: worst centroid sag 0.026 mm Onshape-coarse,
103	  0.038 mm Fusion-low.
104	
105	  Three estimators, increasingly independent:
106	  1. **Fit-based, bootstrapped from the unambiguous regions.** Sharp-bounded
107	     regions are solved by the ladder with no tolerance choices beyond vertex
108	     validation. For each of their facets, distance from centroid to its own
109	     committed fit is a direct sag sample. High quantile → ε. Available before
110	     competition runs.
111	  2. **Fit-free, from the mesh's second-order structure.** For adjacent facets
112	     on a cylinder of radius R spanning dihedral θ with width h = Rθ:
113	     \`sag ≈ (h/2)²/(2R) = h²/(8R) = h·θ/8\`. So **sag ≈ dihedral × facet size /
114	     8**, per facet, no fits and no jet inversion — computable in stage 2.1.
115	  3. **Cross-check.** (1) and (2) should agree. Disagreement means the
116	     provenance premise is violated — a decimated, repaired or remeshed STL —
117	     which is itself worth detecting and reporting.
118	
119	  *Prove it before trusting it:* the corpus has reference STEPs and stage 1
120	  \`--compare\` reports the true centroid max distance, so run the reference-free
121	  estimator across the corpus and check it reproduces those numbers. The
122	  reference is the **validation instrument, never the production input**.
123	
124	  *The angular tolerance falls out of the same reasoning.* Its own doc comment
125	  admits it is a stand-in ("Medium-resolution CAD exports step small-radius
126	  fillets up to ~24° between rows… the default must admit those"), and Onshape
127	  exposes the setting directly (12.5° / 6.25° / 2.5° for coarse/medium/fine).
128	  Recover it as a **clustering** rather than a threshold: the dihedral
129	  distribution should be bimodal — tessellation steps near zero, real sharp
130	  edges well separated — so find the gap (Otsu-style). Plot it before
131	  believing it; on stepped_block fine only 384 of 51603 edges are called sharp,
132	  so the populations are very lopsided. **Bonus:** the absence of a clean gap,
133	  or a spiky constant-dihedral distribution, is exactly the OpenSCAD
134	  faceted-by-construction detector described in the item below.
135	
136	  *Risks to measure first:*
137	  - ε is not truly global — exporters also cap angular deviation and minimum
138	    facet width, so different features are bound by different constraints. Take
139	    a high quantile or max, **never a median**, or legitimate faces get
140	    rejected.
141	  - Tightening 0.4 → ~1e-3 is a 400× change that moves behaviour everywhere.
142	    \`REFIT_GIVE_UP\` is defined as 8×stol; merge's centroid gate and every
143	    \`face_validates\` use it. Do the sweep harness (item 6 below) first.
144	  - Coarse meshes genuinely have larger sag — the corpus's coarse variants are
145	    the real test, not the fine ones.
146	
147	  ---
148	
149	  **C. Reformulate competition as alternating partition/fit.** *The big one —
150	  where the real simplification lives. Do it last, and only after the sweep
151	  harness, because it is a rewrite of stage 2.3(b)–2.4 and the before/after
152	  must be measurable on more than the handful of models one inspects by hand.*
153	
154	  The assumption says face-level assignment is the right granularity, which is
155	  exactly the setting for Lloyd-style iteration — this is **Variational Shape
156	  Approximation** (Cohen-Steiner et al.): alternate (assign faces to proxies)
157	  and (refit proxies) to a fixpoint. Half of it already exists and is known to
158	  work here: \`relabel_boundaries\` + \`refit_geometry\` converged this session and
159	  took stepped_block fine from 73 surfaces to exactly the reference's 71.
160	
161	  - **Subsumes:** seed ordering (\`neighbor_jet_mismatch\`), \`seed_patch\`,
162	    \`condition_patch\`, \`grow\`/\`grow_from\`/\`flood\`, \`resolve_claims\`,
163	    \`relabel_boundaries\`, \`merge_regions\`, \`resplit_disconnected\`.
164	  - **Needs:** an error metric (vertex distance, self-calibrated as in
165	    \`acceptance_tol\`); a proxy-count rule (add a proxy where regional error is
166	    worst, drop one whose faces are all absorbed); and the existing DOF ladder
167	    to choose each proxy's *type*.
168	  - **Keep:** the DOF ladder itself, \`axis_normals_consistent\`, and the
169	    identifiability guards until measured inert (see below).
170	  - Beware the known failure mode of greedy selection that VSA is meant to fix:
171	    a richer model stealing a neighbour's support. Global iteration should
172	    dissolve it — that is the main hypothesis to test.
173	
174	  ---
175	
176	  **After A/B/C: measure how much of the rest can be deleted.** Do not guess —
177	  this session found three of five guards already inert. Protocol, per
178	  candidate, one at a time:
179	  1. Disable it (set the constant to a no-op value, or short-circuit the
180	     predicate) and rebuild.
181	  2. \`./tmp/probe.sh\` — per-model plane/cyl/cone/sphere/torus/bspline
182	     breakdown over 14 models; diff against a saved baseline. **Surface counts
183	     alone are not enough: a 3-torus regression once hid behind an unchanged
184	     total of 71.**
185	  3. Full suite (\`cargo test --release --no-fail-fast\`, ~2.5 min) — decisive.
186	  4. Inert on both ⇒ delete it, and record in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN what it was for
187	     and what superseded it, so the knowledge is not lost with the code.
188	
189	  Re-test in roughly this order, most-likely-dead first:
190	  - \`MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG\`, \`MAX_TORUS_RADIUS_RATIO\` — degeneracy guards that
191	    exist because competition builds wrong supports; correct supports should
192	    make them unnecessary.
193	  - \`LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX\` — its rationale is that an analytic surface islanded in
194	    a jagged per-facet blob makes invalid wires; if boundaries are clean chains
195	    after A, that rationale may simply evaporate.
196	  - \`GROW_VTOL_FACTOR\` + \`RESIDUAL_SIGMAS\` — both belong to flood, which C
197	    replaces.
198	  - The whole \`PATCH_*\` / \`SEED_PATCH_CAP\` / \`MIN_CONDITION_FACES\` family —
199	    gone with seeds.
200	  - \`MERGE_MAX_SMALL\`, \`SMALL_SELECTION_ABSORB_FACES\` and the freeform island
201	    rules (\`enclosed\`, \`islands_split_a_patch\`).
202	  - \`MIN_CYLINDER_FACES\` / \`MIN_SPHERE_FACES\` / \`MIN_TORUS_FACES\`.
203	  - Finally, ask whether the **jet** is still needed at all beyond the
204	    ladder's rung ordering (\`region_is_developable\`). It was demoted to a prior
205	    in the 2026-07-20 pivot; C may remove its last real job.
206	
207	  Track the constant count as a headline number: stage 2 carried **35** at the
208	  time of writing (\`grep -h "^const \|^pub(crate) const \|^pub(super) const "
209	  src/stage2/*.rs | wc -l\`). Report it in the commit each time it moves.
210	
211	  *Deliberately not recommended:* seam **detection** proper (finding tangent
212	  seams directly). Curvature-based detection was measured dead in the
213	  2026-07-20 pivot — no threshold separates real junctions from real curvature
214	  gradients, the classes overlap. Structural signals (grid-direction
215	  discontinuity, density change) were never tried but are provenance-dependent
216	  and near-absent on OCCT's Delaunay interiors, so a detector would have to
217	  fall back to competition anyway and would not retire any parameter.
218	
219	- **Faceted-by-construction sources (OpenSCAD, Tinkercad, Blender): a flag or
220	  auto-detection.** Not a bug today, and not being worried about yet — recorded
221	  so the eventual decision is informed. These have no B-rep at any stage, so
222	  there are no tangent junctions to recover, only discretization steps, and the
223	  seam assumption that carries the whole pipeline holds trivially but conveys
224	  no information (every edge is a facet boundary). Full findings, with the
225	  fragment-count arithmetic and the thresholds, are under **Mesh provenance and
226	  the seam assumption** in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md. The headlines:
227	  - \`--angular-tolerance\` (default 25°) silently decides whether an OpenSCAD
228	    revolution comes out as an analytic surface or as the prism it literally
229	    is: \`$fn ≥ 15\` reads smooth, \`$fn ≤ 14\` reads sharp. On OpenSCAD's own
230	    defaults that is radius ≳ 4.5 mm. A \`$fn = 6\` hex nut is handled correctly
231	    by accident of the same rule.
232	  - The ambiguity is *genuine* — a 15-gon prism and a coarse cylinder are the
233	    same mesh — so this is a policy choice, not something to be measured. That
234	    argues for an explicit flag over silent auto-detection, or at least for
235	    auto-detection that reports what it decided.
236	  - Expected failure mode where a fit *is* attempted: large radii at default
237	    resolution, where the sagitta \`r(1 − cos(180/n))\` breaks
238	    \`--surface-tolerance\` (0.55 mm at r = 100, n = 30) and the surface falls to
239	    per-facet planes. Vertex validation never fails, because OpenSCAD inscribes
240	    its polygons and the vertices sit exactly on the ideal surface.
241	  - Detection signals if we go that way: a constant dihedral of exactly 360/n
242	    all the way around a revolution (B-rep tessellation steps vary, and density
243	    changes at seams), and vertices exactly on the circumscribed circle.
244	  - Worth a corpus model or two before deciding anything.
245	
246	- **Make the stage-2 decomposition robust rather than tuned.** Stage 2 carries
247	  ~25 behavioural thresholds, and several sit one step from catastrophe: on
248	  \`stepped_block_toroidal\` medium, four *unrelated* knobs — \`GROW_VTOL_FACTOR\`
249	  ×3.3, \`MIN_CONDITION_FACES\` 6→4, \`PATCH_TRIM_ROUNDS\` 16→32, and capping the
250	  fallback seed patch — each flip the model from 83 surfaces to a full collapse
251	  to per-facet planes. When unrelated parameters all sit on a cliff the values
252	  are not the problem, the structure is. (This is the same failure mode the
253	  2026-07-17 pivot was called for; it re-grew on the new architecture within a
254	  fortnight, so it is worth watching for deliberately.) Ranked candidates, each
255	  aimed at *replacing* guards rather than adding one:
256	  1. **Self-calibrating acceptance tolerance — DONE 2026-07-27**
257	     (\`acceptance_tol\`, compete.rs). See the DEVELOPMENT_PLAN section
258	     "Calibrate acceptance on the fit, not on a constant". Note what it did and
259	     did not achieve: the operative bar is now scale-free and insensitive to its
260	     parameter over a 3× range, but it did not remove a constant —
```

#!/bin/zsh
# Per-model surface-type breakdown: the acceptance corpus for stage-2 guards.
for m in \
  onshape/stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_fine onshape/stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_medium \
  onshape/rounded_cube_10_r2_fine onshape/part_rounded_cube_10_r2_coarse \
  onshape/pipe_elbow_10_medium onshape/nosecone_medium \
  onshape/pill_fine onshape/chamfered_cube_10_c1_medium \
  ccad/generated/cone_cylinder ccad/generated/filleted_cylinder ccad/generated/filleted_pipe \
  nurbs/bspline_wave nurbs/elliptical_arch nurbs/elliptical_cylinder ; do
  b=$(./target/release/dump_regions tests/$m.stl surfaces 2>/dev/null \
      | awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="plane")p++; else if($i=="cyl")c++; else if($i=="cone")k++;
              else if($i=="sphere")s++; else if($i=="torus")t++; else if($i=="bspline")b++}
             END{printf "%d/%d/%d/%d/%d/%d", p+0,c+0,k+0,s+0,t+0,b+0}')
  printf "%-17s %s\n" "$(basename $m | cut -c1-17)" "$b"
done

//! Stage 2: Segmentation & Classification (partition-then-classify)
//!
//! Sub-stage numbering (DEVELOPMENT_PLAN):
//!
//! 2.1: Sharp-edge classification (fit-free) + osculating-jet prior
//!      (\`edges.rs\`).
//! 2.2: Region extraction — connected components over interior edges
//!      (\`regions.rs\`).
//! 2.3: Per-region surface discovery (\`classify.rs\` driver) — whole-region
//!      DOF ladder (2.3(a)) then scoped fit competition (2.3(b), \`compete.rs\`)
//!      with bent-tube/torus promotion (2.3(c)) for the tangent chains the
//!      ladder cannot explain, and B-spline fitting of the leftover components
//!      (2.3(e), \`bspline.rs\`). Whatever remains degrades to per-facet planes.
//! 2.4: Resolution & repair — relabel / merge / re-split + invariants
//!      (\`repair.rs\`).
//! 2.5: Selected-surface output.
//!
//! The analytic fitters (\`planar.rs\`, \`conical.rs\`, \`spherical.rs\`,
//! \`toroidal.rs\`) share the \`surface::SurfaceType\` trait, driven generically
//! by the ladder and competition. The old BFS hypothesis-generation pipeline
//! that predated this rewrite was removed (Rewrite Roadmap step 7).

/// Minimum number of mesh faces required to accept a cylindrical hypothesis.
/// Any real CAD tessellation of a cylinder produces at least 3 facets around
/// the circumference; this rejects spurious 2-face fits (e.g. adjacent torus
/// facets that locally approximate a cylinder).
pub(crate) const MIN_CYLINDER_FACES: usize = 3;

/// Minimum number of mesh faces required to accept a spherical hypothesis.
/// Sphere fitting has 4 degrees of freedom (cx, cy, cz, r), so at least 4
/// non-degenerate faces are needed for a well-determined fit. This also rejects
/// spurious fits from small patches that are consistent with many surface types.
pub(crate) const MIN_SPHERE_FACES: usize = 4;

/// Minimum number of mesh faces required to accept a toroidal hypothesis.
/// A torus has 7 degrees of freedom (center xyz, axis direction 2, R, r),
/// so at least 7 faces are needed for a well-determined fit.
pub(crate) const MIN_TORUS_FACES: usize = 7;

/// Maximum sphere radius as a multiple of the mesh bounding-box diagonal.
/// With solid-angle coverage validation and surface-tolerance validation during
/// BFS, this no longer needs to be tight — those checks prevent pathological
/// growth. A large value serves as a numerical guardrail against degenerate fits.
pub(crate) const MAX_SPHERE_RADIUS_FACTOR: f64 = 1000.0;

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Hypothesis data structures
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// A planar surface hypothesis fitted to a set of mesh faces.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct PlanarHypothesis {
    /// Unit normal vector pointing outward from the shell/solid.
    pub normal: [f64; 3],
    /// Signed distance from origin to plane along the normal.
    pub distance: f64,
    /// Set of mesh face indices that fit this hypothesis.
    pub faces: Vec<usize>,
    /// Set of mesh vertex indices on this plane.
    pub vertices: Vec<usize>,
    /// Maximum (positive) distance from any vertex to the plane.
    pub error_max: f64,
    /// Minimum (most negative) distance from any vertex to the plane.
    pub error_min: f64,
    /// Sum of absolute vertex-to-plane distances.
    pub error_abs_sum: f64,
}

/// A cylindrical or conical surface hypothesis fitted to a set of mesh faces.
/// Cylinders are represented as cones with half_angle == 0.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct ConicalHypothesis {
    /// The apex of the cone, or a point on the axis for cylinders.
    pub apex: [f64; 3],
    /// Unit direction vector along the cone/cylinder axis.
    pub axis_direction: [f64; 3],
    /// Half-angle of the cone in radians (0 for cylinders).
    pub half_angle: f64,
    /// Cylinder radius (when half_angle == 0). 0 for true cones.
    pub radius_at_apex: f64,
    /// Whether the surface normal points away from the axis (convex=true) or toward it (concave=false).
    pub convex: bool,
    /// Set of mesh face indices that fit this hypothesis.
    pub faces: Vec<usize>,
    /// Set of mesh vertex indices on this surface.
    pub vertices: Vec<usize>,
    /// Maximum absolute distance from any vertex to the surface.
    pub error_max: f64,

/// Compute the edge curve for a tangent edge.
///
/// For tangent edges, \`GeomAPI_IntSS\` often fails or produces degenerate results.
/// Instead, construct the curve analytically based on the surface pair types:
/// - Plane-cylinder tangent: line parallel to cylinder axis at the tangent point
/// - Sphere-cylinder tangent: circle arc on the sphere, in a plane perpendicular
///   to the cylinder axis through the sphere center's projection on the axis
/// - Cylinder-cylinder tangent: line parallel to shared axis direction
/// - Plane-sphere tangent: degenerate (single point) — construct line from vertices
fn compute_tangent_edge_curve(
    edge: &mut ReconEdge,
    face_descriptors: &[FaceDescriptor],
    vertices: &[BRepVertex],
    stage2: &Stage2Output,
    config: &Config,
) -> Result<(), String> {
    let [fi0, fi1] = edge.face_indices;
    let ss0 = &stage2.selected_surfaces[face_descriptors[fi0].selected_surface_idx];
    let ss1 = &stage2.selected_surfaces[face_descriptors[fi1].selected_surface_idx];

    // Determine which surface types we have
    let has_sphere_cylinder = matches!(
        (ss0, ss1),
        (SelectedSurface::Spherical(_), SelectedSurface::Conical(_))
            | (SelectedSurface::Conical(_), SelectedSurface::Spherical(_))
    );

    let is_closed_loop = edge.vertex_indices[0] == usize::MAX || edge.vertex_indices[1] == usize::MAX;

    if has_sphere_cylinder {
        // Sphere-cone tangencies are NOT great circles on the sphere (the
        // tangent circle sits at radius R·cos α, offset along the cone axis),
        // so handle them with the generic axis-perpendicular circle
        // construction from mesh boundary vertices.
        let cone_axis = match (ss0, ss1) {
            (SelectedSurface::Conical(c), _) | (_, SelectedSurface::Conical(c))
                if !stage2.conical_hypotheses[*c].is_cylinder() =>
            {
                let h = &stage2.conical_hypotheses[*c];
                Some((h.apex, h.axis_direction))
            }
            _ => None,
        };
        if is_closed_loop {
            if let Some((axis_origin, axis_dir)) = cone_axis {
                return compute_tangent_edge_curve_axis_circle_closed(
                    edge, &axis_origin, &axis_dir, stage2, config,
                );
            }
            return compute_tangent_edge_curve_sphere_cylinder_closed(
                edge, ss0, ss1, stage2, config,
            );
        }
        // Open arcs: the circle is constructed from the sphere geometry and
        // the two endpoint vertices, which works for both cylinders and
        // near-cylindrical cones (e.g. fillets fitted as slight cones).
        let v0 = &vertices[edge.vertex_indices[0]];
        let v1 = &vertices[edge.vertex_indices[1]];
        return compute_tangent_edge_curve_sphere_cylinder(
            edge, v0, v1, ss0, ss1, stage2, config,
        );
    }

    // Check for torus involvement
    let has_torus = matches!(ss0, SelectedSurface::Toroidal(_))

    if has_torus {
        if is_closed_loop {
            return compute_tangent_edge_curve_torus_closed(
                edge, ss0, ss1, stage2, config,

        }
        let v0 = &vertices[edge.vertex_indices[0]];
        let v1 = &vertices[edge.vertex_indices[1]];
        return compute_tangent_edge_curve_torus_arc(
            edge, v0, v1, ss0, ss1, stage2, config,
        );
    }

Read TODO.md's first item and did enough reconnaissance to plan. Here's where things stand.

## Next up: item A — snap shared region boundaries to mesh-edge chains

TODO.md's plan is A → B → C, and **A** is explicitly "start here": narrow, provenance-independent, and it *removes* a heuristic instead of adding one. Every remaining `--compare` failure is a boundary sitting one tessellation row off, and nothing in the pipeline reasons about where a boundary *should* be — it falls out of flood plus claim resolution. The seam assumption guarantees the correct boundary exists as a mesh-edge chain, so this is selection from a nonempty set, not a search.

Baseline is clean: working tree has only three untracked `tests/downloaded/` files, HEAD is `d045e8a` (docs-only), stage-2 constant count is **35**.

## Four things I found that should shape how you start

**1. Most of the hard geometry already exists — in stage 3.** [stage3.rs:2353](src/stage3.rs:2353) `compute_tangent_edge_curve` already does exactly the closed-form constructions item A calls for, dispatched by surface-type pair: sphere↔cylinder, torus (closed loop and open arc), axis-perpendicular circle for cones, line-from-vertices fallback for plane↔cylinder. And [stage3.rs:1279](src/stage3.rs:1279) `detect_tangency` classifies an edge as tangent by comparing the two *fitted* normal fields at mesh boundary vertices (2° threshold) — it reads nothing but `Stage2Output` and mesh vertices, so that criterion ports into stage 2 essentially unchanged.

The catch: those functions produce OCCT `Geom_Curve` handles and consume `ReconEdge`/`BRepVertex`. Stage 2 doesn't need a trimmed curve — it needs a **side test**, which is strictly weaker and can be plain f64. So read them as a worked reference for the per-pair math, not as code to call.

**2. There's a sharper argument for the minimum-distance locus than "IntSS is fragile."** The locus is *stable* where the intersection is not. For a plane grazing a torus, the intersection circle moves by √(2rδ) under a plane offset error δ — that's the recorded 4.4e-2 mm amplification. The minimum-distance locus is the set of points where the two normal fields agree, which depends on the plane's *direction* and the torus's own geometry but **not on the plane's offset at all**. A δ error moves it by zero to first order; only normal-direction error moves it, and linearly. That's the property that makes A sound, and it generalizes: for every tangent pair the locus is "where n_A ∥ n_B", which is the same predicate `detect_tangency` already evaluates pointwise.

**3. The thing being replaced is `relabel_boundaries`** ([repair.rs:207](src/stage2/repair.rs:207)). Its two retirable constants are visible in the code: the `d_best < d_own * 0.5` anti-flap margin at line 244 and the `0..10` round cap at line 211. Note it already alternates assignment with refit (lines 261+, added 2026-07-26) — so the loop structure snap needs is in place; what changes is the *criterion* from "compare two local residuals" to "which side of a global locus."

**4. The stated validation target won't flip by itself — plan around that.** The one ignored stage-4 test ([stage4_integration.rs:346](tests/stage4_integration.rs:346)) blames coarse sampling: medium is 82 surfaces vs the reference 71, with ~4 fillet cylinders *missing* and ~14 arc facets still per-facet, blocked on `LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX`. Boundary snapping doesn't create missing surfaces. So use the **continuous** metric instead — `Compare 3.1: edge boundary max dist` ([stage3.rs:340](src/stage3.rs:340)), currently 1.6e-1 mm on medium — and treat "fine stays passing" as the hard constraint.

## Concrete first-session plan

**Step 0 — baseline.** Build release, save `./tmp/probe.sh` output as the diff target, and run the ignored medium test with `--compare` to capture both the 1.6e-1 number and the worst-edge coordinates ([stage3.rs:291](src/stage3.rs:291) prints the worst boundary vertex position, which feeds straight into `dump_regions … at <x> <y> <z>`).

**Step 1 — build it as a diagnostic before it's a behaviour change.** A new `dump_regions` mode that, for each pair of adjacent committed surfaces: classifies tangent vs transversal by the ported normal-agreement test, computes the locus, and reports how many currently-assigned faces sit on the wrong side. This measures the size of the prize with zero regression risk, works on *fine* (which passes) as a correctness check — the answer there should be ≈0 wrong-side faces — and becomes the instrument for judging the real pass later.

**Step 2 — implement `snap_boundaries` as an additive pass in repair.rs**, running after relabel rather than replacing it, alternating with `refit_geometry` the same way relabel does. Keeping both initially isolates snap's effect; probe first, full suite decisive.

**Step 3 — delete the margin and the round cap** only once snap is demonstrably carrying the boundaries, and record in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN what they were for. That's the first movement of the 35-constant headline number.

**Pair coverage to implement first**, driven by what stepped_block actually contains: plane↔torus (the end cap against the perimeter fillet — the exact case that produced 4.4e-2), torus↔cylinder, cylinder↔plane. Anything else falls through to existing relabel behaviour, which keeps the blast radius small.

The one judgment call I'd flag before coding: whether an unhandled or ill-conditioned pair should fall back to relabel silently or refuse to move faces at all. I'd default to falling back, since that makes step 2 strictly additive — but say if you'd rather it be loud.

> I'm designing a geometry module that computes a side function for pairs of committed surfaces sharing a mesh boundary, where the function determines which side of the locus a point belongs to. For transversal junctions, this side function is naturally available from the surface geometry itself.
> 
> The key insight is that for tangent cases, the residual comparison between signed distances becomes ill-conditioned since both distances are small and comparable, but the geometric locus is still well-defined. Instead of relying on residuals, I need to compute genuine geometric side functions based on each point's position relative to the tangency curve itself.
> 
> For the specific case of a plane tangent to a torus, the tangency locus is determined by where the plane's normal aligns with the torus's normal — which happens at the topmost or bottommost circle of the torus's tube. This gives a circular locus of radius R centered at the torus center offset by ±r along the axis, lying in the plane perpendicular to that axis. the axis at the tangency height. For a concave fillet where a wall meets a floor, the torus sits with its axis vertical and touches the floor along a circle of radius R. For plane-torus tangency in general, the normal must be nearly parallel to the axis, and the locus is a circle of radius R positioned at height c·a ± r along the axis. Now I'm setting up a side function for plane-torus that uses the radial distance from a point to the axis. The normal vector at any point on the torus is determined by the tube angle φ, and at the tangency circle where the torus touches the plane, the normal aligns with the plane's normal (φ = ±90°). This is actually an extremum of the axial coordinate, so the torus surface folds back on itself near the tangency point—on one side of φ = 90°, the surface continues over the top and wraps back down.
> 
> For a physical fillet between a floor and wall, the tube only spans a quarter circle from φ = 90° (floor contact) to φ = 180° (wall contact), and beyond the tangency the torus would dip below the floor. The correct approach is to use the signed distance to the plane as the side function, where faces on the fillet sit above the plane by a height that grows quadratically near the tangency—this is the degenerate case where the fillet's height follows a quadratic profile.
> 
> To avoid the amplification problem this creates, I should switch to using the surface normal instead of position. The torus's normal rotates linearly with arclength at rate 1/r, while its position departs quadratically, so the tangency locus is where the torus's normal becomes parallel to the plane's normal. I can define a side function based on the angle between these normals, signed by the direction of φ, and compute it by finding the tube-angle φ(p) at each point through the fitted torus geometry.
> 
> The key stability advantage: errors in the plane's offset don't affect the alignment angle at all, errors in the plane's normal direction shift it linearly, and errors in the torus's axis direction also shift it linearly. This gives a position error of r·Δ instead of the quadratic √(2rδ) scaling. For mesh faces on the plane itself, φ is still well-defined as long as the point isn't on the axis, so the side function works consistently across the entire mesh. the relationship holds near the tangency circle too—the angular offset from the tangency point scales linearly with the radial distance from the circle's center, with the tube radius as the scaling factor.
> 
> The side function elegantly reduces to just the signed radial distance from the torus axis relative to its major radius, which defines the tangency circle itself. Points outside this circle have positive values, points inside have negative ones, and the stability of this function depends on how accurately the fitted torus's axis position and major radius are determined.
> 
> This principle extends beautifully to any surfaces of revolution sharing a common axis—the typical tangency scenario in CAD like a fillet torus meeting a perpendicular plane or a coaxial cylinder. In all these cases, the tangency locus is a circle about the shared axis, and the side function becomes simply the difference between the point's actual distance from the axis and the reference distance, making it clean and numerically robust.
> 
> For a plane perpendicular to the torus axis, the tangency circle has radius R (where the torus normal aligns with the plane normal at φ = ±90°), and the side function is just ρ − R. For a coaxial cylinder, the tangency occurs at ρ = R ± r depending on whether it's outer or inner tangency, and the side function naturally uses the axial coordinate instead. is bad and h is good. The key insight is that I should use whichever coordinate varies linearly across the separation—the one whose gradient aligns with the tangent direction of the locus curve. More formally, the side function is the projection onto the tangent plane: s(p) = (p − p₀) · t̂, where t̂ is perpendicular to the locus within that plane. For the cylinder-torus case, this means choosing either the radial or axial direction depending on which one captures the linear separation.
> 
> For a plane tangent to a cylinder, the locus is a line parallel to the axis, and I need to find the direction perpendicular to both the axis and the plane normal—that's the coordinate that varies linearly away from the tangency line. When a sphere is tangent to a cylinder or cone, the locus becomes a circle, and I'm working through how the side function behaves in that configuration.
> 
> Now looking at degenerate cases: coaxial cylinders with the same radius collapse into the same surface, giving a circle locus but leaving the fit under-determined. Coplanar planes, a plane tangent to a sphere at a single point, and coaxial tori all trigger the LOUD flag because they're either degenerate or don't provide enough constraint information.
> 
> For non-tangent intersections where surfaces cross transversally, the intersection curve is well-behaved since the crossing angle stays bounded away from zero, and signed distances work naturally as the side function. The relabeling already handles these cases fine because the residuals diverge significantly. The real challenge is the tangent case, though in sharp-edged models the boundary is already a mesh edge that stage 2.1 partitions correctly without needing repair.

//!   for tracing a stage-3 compare failure back to stage 2.
//! - \`owner <face>...\` — the surface owning a face and how well its
//!   neighbours' surfaces explain it (the stage-2.4 relabel criterion).

use brepper::config;
use brepper::stage1::ConnectedMesh;
use brepper::stage2::edges::{classify_edges, compute_jet_field, EdgeClass};
use brepper::stage2::regions::extract_regions;
use brepper::stage1;

fn centroid(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, fi: usize) -> [f64; 3] {
    let f = &mesh.faces[fi];
    let vc = f.vertex_count as usize;
    let mut c = [0.0; 3];
    for &vi in &f.vertex_indices[..vc] {
        let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
        c[0] += v.x;
        c[1] += v.y;
        c[2] += v.z;
    }
    let n = vc as f64;
    [c[0] / n, c[1] / n, c[2] / n]
}

/// Area of a mesh face (triangle, or a quad as two triangles).
fn tri_area(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, fi: usize) -> f64 {
    let f = &mesh.faces[fi];
    let p = |k: usize| {
        let v = &mesh.vertices[f.vertex_indices[k]];
        [v.x, v.y, v.z]
    };
    let tri = |a: [f64; 3], b: [f64; 3], c: [f64; 3]| {
        let u = [b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1], b[2] - a[2]];
        let w = [c[0] - a[0], c[1] - a[1], c[2] - a[2]];
        let x = [u[1] * w[2] - u[2] * w[1], u[2] * w[0] - u[0] * w[2], u[0] * w[1] - u[1] * w[0]];
        0.5 * (x[0] * x[0] + x[1] * x[1] + x[2] * x[2]).sqrt()
    };
    let mut a = tri(p(0), p(1), p(2));
    if f.vertex_count == 4 {
        a += tri(p(0), p(2), p(3));
    }
    a
}

/// Distance from a point to a selected surface (analytic types only).
fn dist_to(
    out: &brepper::stage2::Stage2Output,
    sel: &brepper::stage2::SelectedSurface,
    q: [f64; 3],
) -> f64 {
    use brepper::stage2::SelectedSurface as S;
    match sel {
        S::Planar(i) => {
            let h = &out.planar_hypotheses[*i];
            (h.normal[0] * q[0] + h.normal[1] * q[1] + h.normal[2] * q[2] - h.distance).abs()
        }
        S::Conical(i) => {
            let h = &out.conical_hypotheses[*i];
            let d = [q[0] - h.apex[0], q[1] - h.apex[1], q[2] - h.apex[2]];
            let a = h.axis_direction;
            let t = d[0] * a[0] + d[1] * a[1] + d[2] * a[2];
            let perp = [d[0] - t * a[0], d[1] - t * a[1], d[2] - t * a[2]];
            let r = (perp[0].powi(2) + perp[1].powi(2) + perp[2].powi(2)).sqrt();
            if h.half_angle == 0.0 {
                (r - h.radius_at_apex).abs()
            } else {
                (r * h.half_angle.cos() - t * h.half_angle.sin()).abs()
            }
        }
        S::Toroidal(i) => {
            let h = &out.toroidal_hypotheses[*i];
            let d = [q[0] - h.center[0], q[1] - h.center[1], q[2] - h.center[2]];
            let a = h.axis_direction;
            let t = d[0] * a[0] + d[1] * a[1] + d[2] * a[2];
            let perp = [d[0] - t * a[0], d[1] - t * a[1], d[2] - t * a[2]];
            let r = (perp[0].powi(2) + perp[1].powi(2) + perp[2].powi(2)).sqrt();
            (((r - h.major_radius).powi(2) + t * t).sqrt() - h.minor_radius).abs()
        }
        S::Spherical(i) => {
            let h = &out.spherical_hypotheses[*i];
            let d = [q[0] - h.center[0], q[1] - h.center[1], q[2] - h.center[2]];
            ((d[0].powi(2) + d[1].powi(2) + d[2].powi(2)).sqrt() - h.radius).abs()
        }
        S::BSpline(_) => f64::NAN,
    }
}

    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().collect();
    let path = &args[1];
    let mode = args.get(2).map(|s| s.as_str()).unwrap_or("summary");
    let config = config::parse_config_from(["brepper", path, "-q"]).unwrap();
