/// Per-face detail for one pair's interface: why each face does or does not
/// move. Diagnostic only.
pub(crate) fn explain_pair(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    surfs: &[Surf<'_>],
    f2s: &[usize],
    vtol: f64,
    a: usize,
    b: usize,
) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut counts = vec![0usize; surfs.len()];
    for &si in f2s {
        if si != usize::MAX {
            counts[si] += 1;
        }
    }
    let Some((_, _, interface)) = interfaces(mesh, f2s)
        .into_iter()
        .find(|&(x, y, _)| (x, y) == (a.min(b), a.max(b)))
    else {
        return vec![format!("surfaces {a} and {b} do not share a boundary")];
    };
    let (a, b) = (a.min(b), a.max(b));
    let analysis = analyze_pair(mesh, surfs, f2s, &counts, a, b, &interface, vtol);
    let mut out = vec![
        format!(
            "pair {a} ({}) | {b} ({}): {}",
            surfs[a].kind(),
            surfs[b].kind(),
            analysis.describe()
        ),
        format!(
            "  {} faces on {a}'s side, {} on {b}'s; {} chain vertices",
            interface.faces_a.len(),
            interface.faces_b.len(),
            interface.vertices.len(),
        ),
    ];
    let PairOutcome::Snapped { locus, moves, .. } = &analysis.outcome else {
        return out;
    };
    let moving: std::collections::BTreeSet<usize> = moves.iter().map(|m| m.0).collect();
    out.push(
        "  face      owner  diameter    s(centroid)   s(min)     s(max)  fits:a b  move".to_string(),
    );
    for &fi in interface.faces_a.iter().chain(interface.faces_b.iter()) {
        let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
        let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
        let sv: Vec<f64> = face.vertex_indices[..vc]
            .iter()
            .map(|&vi| locus.side(&point_of(&mesh.vertices[vi])))
            .collect();
        out.push(format!(
            "  {:>7}  {:>5}  {:>9.3e}  {:>11.3e}  {:>9.2e}  {:>9.2e}   {} {}   {}",
            fi,
            f2s[fi],
            face_diameter(mesh, fi),
            face_side(mesh, fi, locus),
            sv.iter().cloned().fold(f64::INFINITY, f64::min),
            sv.iter().cloned().fold(f64::NEG_INFINITY, f64::max),
            if face_fits(mesh, surfs[a], fi, vtol) { "Y" } else { "." },
            if face_fits(mesh, surfs[b], fi, vtol) { "Y" } else { "." },
            if moving.contains(&fi) { "YES" } else { "" },
        ));
    }
    out
}

/// The faces on each side of every surface-to-surface interface, keyed by the
/// ordered pair (a < b) of selected-surface indices.

/// Diagnostic: per-face detail for one pair's shared boundary — which faces
/// the locus would move and, for the ones it would not, which test stopped it.
pub fn locus_pair_detail(out: &Stage2Output, config: &Config, a: usize, b: usize) -> Vec<String> {
    let (surfs, f2s) = locus_inputs(out);
    locus::explain_pair(&out.mesh, &surfs, &f2s, config.vertex_tolerance_mm, a, b)
}

/// The surface views and face→surface map the locus analysis works over.

    let surfs: Vec<locus::Surf<'_>> = out''')

    pairs
        .iter()
        .map(|p| {
            format!(
                "{:>4} {:<7} | {:>4} {:<7} | {:>4} interface faces | {}",
                p.a,
                p.kind_a,
                p.b,
                p.kind_b,
                p.interface_faces,
                p.describe(),
            )
        })
        .collect()
}

by region/hypothesis index, smallest region first for merges — bounded
rounds).

**Claim resolution** — the boundary placement at tangent junctions: faces
claimed by multiple hypotheses (junction rows) go to the claimant whose
surface fits their vertices best, requiring a **2× margin** to prefer a
different side than the larger claimant (a true junction face fits both
sides equally — the margin prevents arbitrary flapping; residual ties
break to the larger claimant, then lower hypothesis index). Exact vertex
distances, no curvature involved.

**Boundary relabel** (±1-row polish; port of the old
\`refine_boundary_assignments\`): after resolution, walk region-boundary
faces; move a face when an adjacent region's surface fits its vertices at
least 2× better; iterate to a fixpoint (≤ 10 rounds; boundaries only move
locally), then rebuild affected regions' vertex lists. Region *geometry*
is not refitted — only the membership map changes.

**Merge**: absorb region S into an adjacent larger region T when every
vertex of S lies within \`--vertex-tolerance\` of T's fitted surface and
every centroid of S within \`--surface-tolerance\`; refit the union,
revalidate, keep only if valid. Eats junction-circle singletons (faces
whose vertices sit ON a tangent seam — genuinely ambiguous, claimable by
either side), chord-degenerate slivers (a single-facet-wide band of a
coarse cylinder validates as its own facet plane, but its vertices lie
exactly on the neighbor cylinder), and residual same-surface fragments.
This is the abandoned absorb pass's *tight* rule reborn with a principled
criterion — vertex tolerance, at which "on the same surface" is decisive;
never the chordal slop of the abandoned loose rule (0.4mm slop, 794
BRepCheck failures on planar-only 3DBenchy). B-spline surfaces are never
merge TARGETS for faces outside their fitted region: a fit vouches only
for its data (the island-dissolution guard in 2.3(e) is the fit-validated
way into a freeform patch).

**Connectivity re-split + invariants** (hard assertions before stage 3):
resolution and relabeling can disconnect a region — re-split into
mesh-connected components (identical fitted geometry on two non-adjacent
regions is legal). Then assert: every mesh face belongs to exactly one
region (total coverage); every region is mesh-connected; every region's
surface validates the region's own vertices/centroids.
```

**Calibrate acceptance on the fit, not on a constant.** Whether a face belongs
to a surface is decided at a tolerance, and a single absolute tolerance cannot
be right: it has to be loose enough for the worst-conditioned fit in the corpus,
which leaves it hundreds of times too loose for a converged one. The quantities
involved are not comparable. A mesh vertex lies on the true CAD surface to
~1e-6 mm (measured across the corpus, coarse tessellations included), so a face
that really belongs misses its fit by the *fit's* error alone, while a face that
does not belong misses it by a geometric departure — one tessellation row past a
tangent junction sits ~h²/2r away, which shrinks quadratically as the mesh
refines. So the flood scales its bar by the fit's own robust residual scale
(\`acceptance_tol\`, compete.rs): a fit still bootstrapping off a partial patch
reports a large scale and keeps the room it needs, and the bar tightens by
itself as the support fills in. The scale is a *median*, not an RMS, because the
faces it exists to detect are sitting in the sample and would inflate an RMS.

Two properties are worth keeping: the criterion carries no length, so it needs
no recalibration per model, feature size or tessellation density; and it is
insensitive to its own parameter — the corpus gives identical decompositions at
5, 8 and 15 σ, where the absolute bar it replaces went from correct to total
collapse over a 3.3× change. Bounds remain: the floor is \`--vertex-tolerance\`,
below which no distinction is claimed, and the ceiling is the old fixed bar, so
the criterion can only ever be *tighter* than the previous behaviour. The
ceiling is load-bearing — removing it lets a poor fit report a large scale,
admit more foreign faces and inflate its scale further.

Nothing in stage 2 reasoned about where a boundary *should* be — it fell out of
flood plus claim resolution, and every remaining `--compare` failure has been a
boundary sitting a tessellation row off. The seam assumption says the correct
boundary already exists in the mesh as a chain of edges, so this is selection
from a guaranteed-nonempty set rather than a search. `locus.rs` supplies the
criterion and `snap_boundaries` (repair.rs) applies it.

*Use the minimum-distance locus, not the intersection.* At a tangent junction
the surfaces graze rather than cross, and their intersection is catastrophically
ill-conditioned: a plane offset by δ from the torus it should graze meets it in
a circle displaced by √(2rδ), which is how a 4.7e-4 mm plane-fit error became
the recorded 4.4e-2 mm edge error. The locus of minimum distance — the set of
points where the two normal fields agree — has no such amplification, and the
reason is worth remembering: displacing the plane along its own normal leaves
the tangency circle exactly where it was, so the locus does not depend on the
quantity that gets amplified at all. Only a *direction* error moves it, and
linearly. Positions depart quadratically from a tangency while normals turn
linearly; key the boundary off the latter. (This is verified by unit test in
`locus.rs`, not just asserted.)

*The meridian reduction.* Nearly every tangent junction in CAD joins two
surfaces of revolution about a common axis. Reduce the pair to the meridian
half-plane (ρ, h) of that axis, where each surface is a line (plane ⊥ axis,
cylinder, cone) or a circle (sphere, torus) and coaxial tangency is exactly
meridian tangency; the junction is the circle swept by one meridian point q,
and the side test is displacement along the curves' common tangent there. This
subsumes the cases one would otherwise write out separately, and explains why:
at a plane-torus junction ρ is the informative coordinate and h is stationary,
at a cylinder-torus junction it is the other way round, so neither coordinate
works alone and the common tangent is the thing to project onto. Two junctions
are not axisymmetric and are built directly: a plane grazing a cylinder along a
ruling, and the tube junction where a straight fillet (cylinder) continues into
a corner fillet (torus) — there the axes are *perpendicular*, the surfaces share
the tube rather than an axis, and C¹ continuity forces the cylinder's axis to be
tangent to the torus's spine circle, so the junction is the foot of the
perpendicular from the torus centre onto that axis. Note that neither fit says
where its own surface *ends*; the junction has to be read off the pair.

*What makes a move safe.* Three conditions together, none of them a tuned
number: the surface a face would move to must actually fit it (soundness — a
boundary correction must never hand a face to a surface that does not explain
it, and this is what stops a large fused planar quad from being swallowed by a
fillet it happens to touch); the locus must put the whole face on that side,
*including its interior* — a disc triangulated with every vertex on its rim has
all its corners sitting on the junction and on both surfaces at once, so the
corners decide nothing and the centroid must; and the moved set must be
reachable from the current boundary through other moving faces. Orientation —
which side belongs to which surface — cannot be read off the supports globally,
because a locus circle is complete while the junction is only the arc where the
surfaces meet, so a large planar face wanders to the far side of its own
tangency circle while remaining unambiguously the plane's. Read it off the
finely tessellated side, whose extent is comparable to the junction, and only
from faces the other surface cannot explain.

*Loud, not lenient.* A tangent pair whose locus cannot be built or does not
validate is reported and left alone; transversal junctions are out of scope by
construction, being sharp mesh edges that 2.1 already partitions exactly. The
report is what found the rim-triangulated-disc case above.

/// How many adjacent surface pairs stage 2.4's boundary snap could not handle,
/// and how many faces are still on the wrong side of a junction it could.
///
/// Both should be zero on a well-decomposed model: the second is the property
/// snap exists to establish, and the first is the set of junction geometries
/// `locus.rs` does not implement. Exposed so tests can assert on it.
pub fn locus_summary(out: &Stage2Output, config: &Config) -> (usize, usize) {
    let (surfs, f2s) = locus_inputs(out);
    let pairs = locus::analyze_pairs(&out.mesh, &surfs, &f2s, config.vertex_tolerance_mm);
    let problems = pairs.iter().filter(|p| p.is_problem()).count();
    let wrong_side = pairs
        .iter()
        .map(|p| match &p.outcome {
            locus::PairOutcome::Snapped { moves, .. } => moves.len(),
            _ => 0,
        })
        .sum();
    (problems, wrong_side)
}

```bash
git commit -F - <<'EOF'
Snap tangent boundaries to their junction; retire relabel's margin and cap

Stage 2 had nothing that reasoned about where a shared boundary *should*
be — it fell out of flood plus claim resolution, and every remaining
--compare failure has been a boundary a tessellation row off. The seam
assumption says the correct boundary already exists in the mesh as a
chain of edges, so this is selection from a guaranteed-nonempty set, not
a search. New `src/stage2/locus.rs` supplies the criterion; new
`snap_boundaries` (repair.rs, after relabel and merge) applies it.

Use the minimum-distance locus, never the intersection. At a tangent
junction the surfaces graze, and a plane offset by δ from the torus it
should graze meets it in a circle displaced by √(2rδ) — the recorded
4.7e-4 mm plane error becoming a 4.4e-2 mm edge error. The tangency locus
does not depend on that offset at all: displacing the plane along its own
normal leaves the circle exactly where it was. Positions depart
quadratically from a tangency, normals turn linearly; key off the latter.
Unit-tested, not just asserted.

Most tangent junctions are coaxial surfaces of revolution, so reduce the
pair to the meridian half-plane, where each is a line or a circle and
tangency is meridian tangency; the side test is displacement along the
common tangent. That subsumes the per-type cases and shows why neither ρ
nor h works alone — at each junction one of them is stationary. Two
junctions are built directly: a plane grazing a cylinder along a ruling,
and the tube junction where a straight fillet continues into a corner
fillet (axes perpendicular, junction at the foot of the perpendicular
from the torus centre onto the cylinder axis).

A face moves only if the target surface actually fits it, the locus puts
its *interior* on that side, and it is reachable from the current
boundary. The interior test is load-bearing: a disc triangulated with
every vertex on its rim has all its corners on the junction and on both
surfaces, so the corners decide nothing — found by the loud reporting on
filleted_cylinder. Pairs with no locus, or a locus that fails validation,
are reported and left alone; transversal junctions are out of scope,
being sharp edges 2.1 already partitions exactly.

Retires relabel's 2× anti-flapping margin and its 10-round cap, as
planned. Both were the price of comparing a face against two fits each
contaminated by that face; in-loop refitting removed the contamination,
and letting each face move at most once bounds the loop as a convergence
statement rather than a number.

Honest accounting: both were inline literals, so the stage-2 constant
count does not fall — locus.rs adds two (COAXIAL_TOL; TANGENCY_TOL_RAD,
which gives stage 3.2's existing tangency criterion one shared
definition), taking the grep count 35 → 37. And with the margin and cap
gone, snap moves zero faces on every corpus model: unconstrained relabel
now reaches the same boundary itself, and the suite passes with snap
ablated. It is a correctness guarantee rather than a fix today. Recorded
in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN so the next session can decide whether an inert pass
earns its place.

Diagnostics: `dump_regions locus [a b]` reports per pair what the
junction geometry concludes, with per-face detail for one pair; stage
3.1's --compare now names its worst edge by both surfaces and tangency
even when it passes. New `boundaries_sit_on_their_junctions` pins zero
wrong-side faces and zero unhandled junctions across seven models — a
sharper guard than surface counts, which a one-row error leaves intact.

Suite 509 passing / 3 ignored, clippy clean, corpus decomposition
identical (tmp/probe.sh). stepped_block fine still passes at 4.36e-2 mm;
its worst edge is a torus↔cylinder tube junction whose boundary sits on
the locus to ~1e-6 mm, so that residual is not a wrong-side-face problem.

The assumption SURVIVES because it's a CONSTRAINED Delaunay whose constraints are the pre-discretized face boundaries.** What differs between faceters is the INTERIOR pattern: grid faceters (ACIS/Rhino/Parasolid) leave strong anisotropy, Delaunay much less. **So boundary preservation is dependable everywhere; sampling density/anisotropy is CORROBORATING ONLY — remember this before reaching for tessellation layout as a signal.** Our corpus is Onshape-heavy so NOT representative of the real faceter mix. **OPENSCAD GAP (deliberately unhandled, documented not fixed): no B-rep at any stage (`cylinder()` IS a prism, CSG via CGAL/Manifold). THE AMBIGUITY IS GENUINE — a 15-gon prism and a coarse cylinder are the same mesh — so it's a POLICY choice, arguing for an explicit flag over silent auto-detection. ## What landed

**`src/stage2/locus.rs`** — the junction geometry. The core decision: at a tangent junction, never intersect. A plane offset by δ from the torus it should graze meets it in a circle displaced by √(2rδ) — that's the recorded 4.7e-4 → 4.4e-2 mm amplification. The minimum-distance locus doesn't depend on that offset at all; sliding the plane along its own normal leaves the tangency circle exactly where it was. There's a unit test that asserts this rather than just the comment claiming it.

Most tangent junctions are coaxial surfaces of revolution, so I reduced each pair to the meridian half-plane, where every surface is a line or a circle and the side test is displacement along the common tangent. That subsumes the per-type cases and shows why neither ρ nor h works alone — at each junction one of them is stationary. Two junctions aren't axisymmetric and are built directly: a plane grazing a cylinder along a ruling, and the tube junction where a straight fillet continues into a corner fillet (perpendicular axes, junction at the foot of the perpendicular from the torus centre onto the cylinder axis). That last one was 36 of the pairs on stepped_block fine and would be invisible to a coaxial-only implementation.

**`snap_boundaries`** in repair.rs, running after relabel and merge. **Loud, as you asked** — a tangent pair with no locus, or one that fails validation, is reported on stderr and left alone. That paid for itself: it caught a real bug on `filleted_cylinder`, where a disc triangulated with every vertex on its rim has all its corners *on* the junction and on both surfaces at once, so the corners decide nothing and the face interior has to.

**Retired relabel's 2× anti-flapping margin and its 10-round cap.** Both were the price of comparing a face against two fits each contaminated by that face; in-loop refitting removed the contamination, and letting each face move at most once bounds the loop as a convergence statement rather than a number.

Suite 509 passing / 3 ignored, clippy clean, corpus decomposition byte-identical.

I kept it (item C needs exactly this per-face criterion, and the diagnostic depends on the module) but it's your call whether an inert pass earns its place; it's flagged in TODO.

## Where things stand

TODO item A is done and committed (`47a2acf`). Suite 509 passing / 3 ignored, clippy clean, corpus decomposition byte-identical to the session baseline.

What's on disk that wasn't before:

- **`src/stage2/locus.rs`** — junction geometry for tangent surface pairs: the minimum-distance locus (never the intersection), via a meridian reduction for coaxial surfaces of revolution, plus two direct constructions (plane-grazing-cylinder ruling; the cylinder→torus tube junction).
- **`snap_boundaries`** in repair.rs — applies it, after relabel and merge, reporting loudly rather than guessing on anything it can't handle.
- **Relabel's 2× margin and 10-round cap: deleted.**
- **Instruments**: `dump_regions locus [a b]`; stage 3.1's `--compare` now names its worst edge by both surfaces and tangency even when it passes; `boundaries_sit_on_their_junctions` pins zero wrong-side faces and zero unhandled junctions across seven models.

## The snapping situation

Snap works and is verified correct — but it is **inert on the corpus**. With the margin and cap gone, unconstrained relabel reaches the same boundary by itself: snap moves zero faces on every model, and the suite passes with snap ablated.

The causal chain matters here. I checked whether snap *enabled* the retirement, and it didn't — relabel-without-margin passes on its own. So snap didn't buy the retirement; the retirement was independently available. What snap and its diagnostic did buy is the *evidence* that relabel's residual comparison converges to the geometrically correct boundary — which is a claim nobody could previously make, and which is what made deleting the margin defensible rather than lucky.

So it's a guarantee, not a fix. That leaves a genuine decision, and it's yours because the project's own methodology cuts both ways: "inert ⇒ delete it" argues for removing the pass, while item C (variational shape approximation) needs exactly this per-face assignment criterion and the diagnostic depends on the same module. My read: keep it until C is attempted or abandoned, then re-ablate. But if you'd rather not carry an inert pass, deleting `snap_boundaries` while keeping `locus.rs` for the diagnostic and the invariant test is a clean cut — the test would still enforce the property, just without a pass that acts on it.

One caveat on "inert": the corpus is Onshape-heavy, and every model in it decomposes well enough that relabel has an easy job. Snap's value would show up first on a model where relabel *doesn't* converge — which is precisely the coarse-mesh territory nothing can currently measure (see below).

## What didn't move, and why

Neither stepped_block number improved: fine still 4.36e-2 mm, medium still fails at 1.56e-1. Both are diagnosed to the end, so don't re-investigate:

- **fine**: the worst edge is a torus↔cylinder tube junction whose boundary sits *on* the locus to ~1e-6 mm. The 4.363e-2 is exactly one tessellation row of the r=1 torus at 2.5° angular tolerance. Not a boundary-placement problem — it's the reference edge and the mesh chain being a row apart for some other reason.
- **medium**: the worst edge is torus↔B-spline, i.e. the known decomposition gap (81 surfaces vs the reference 71). Boundary placement was never the blocker there.

Worth noting the plan's stated validation target for A was medium, and that target was mis-specified — the ignore string on that test already blamed `LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX` and missing surfaces, not boundaries. Worth remembering when picking targets for B and C.

## What to do next

**Item B — estimate `--surface-tolerance` and `--angular-tolerance` from the mesh.** It's the next item in the plan, it's independent of what just landed, and the reasoning is already written down in TODO (the mesh is its own reference: vertices lie on the true surface to ~1e-6 mm while centroids sit inside by the chordal sag; the 0.4 mm default is ~400× too loose against a true sag of 8.9e-4). One new input B now has: stage 3.1 names its worst edge on success, so "how far off may a tangent boundary be?" can be asked per junction rather than per model.

Two things I'd flag before starting B:

1. **TODO's own advice is to do the sweep harness (item 6) first**, and I think that's right for B specifically — a 400× tolerance change moves behaviour everywhere, `REFIT_GIVE_UP` is defined as 8×stol, and the corpus's coarse variants are the real test. Fourteen hand-inspected models won't tell you whether it generalizes.
2. **The `LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX` cliff (item 4) may be the higher-value target.** It's what makes every coarse-mesh measurement untunable, which is the same reason medium can't be improved incrementally and the same reason snap has nothing to prove itself on. Fixing it would make both B and C measurable in a way they currently aren't.

If you want the shortest path to a visible win instead, item 3 (global parameter consensus — clustering the fitted radii, since stepped_block has exactly four distinct ones and the pipeline produces a cloud around each) is independent of everything above and improves accuracy directly.

> I'm seeing the logic now—when there are surviving hypotheses but the largest connected component of residual geometry exceeds the threshold, the algorithm discards everything in that region and reconstructs it per-facet instead. > 
> The real issue is that when a blob gets per-facetted, each facet becomes its own surface, so an adjacent analytic surface like a cylinder abuts N separate facet-planes, creating N separate ReconEdges and N tiny edges in the cylinder's wire. That's what triggers the BRepCheck failures. And this problem occurs for any analytic surface adjacent to per-facet faces, not just the ones directly abutting the original bad blob.

> Per-facetting the entire region solves this by making everything uniform — every face becomes a facet plane, so all boundaries are facet-to-facet, which stage 3 handles cleanly as a polyhedron. > The root cause is that adjacent per-facet planes on a smooth surface are naturally tangent to each other (normals within 2°), so every adjacent pair gets flagged as an unhandled tangent junction. But that's not actually a junction at all — it's just the same surface discretized into facets. A plane/plane tangent pair is either coplanar or two facets of a discretized surface, so there's no real junction to snap. I need to reclassify this as out-of-scope rather than a problem.
> 
> The fix is straightforward: `LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair` shouldn't count as a problem since plane/plane pairs genuinely have no junction curve (two distinct planes meet in a line; if they're tangent they're coplanar, meaning they're the same surface). So plane/plane tangent equals coplanar equals not a junction. The same logic applies to plane/sphere tangent cases.
> 
> I'm updating `is_problem()` to return false for `NoLocus(PointOrPlanePair)` and documenting it as "no junction curve exists (out of scope)". I want to keep genuinely unhandled cases like `ConePlaneRuling` and `NotCoaxial` flagged as problems, so I'm checking whether the cone and plane are coaxial — if not, that's a real unhandled case that needs attention.
> 
> Actually, I'm realizing there's a bug in my dispatch logic: for a cone tangent to a plane along a ruling, the plane normal should satisfy |n·a| = sin(half_angle), not ≈0. My current check only catches cylinders (where half_angle=0), so cone-plane ruling tangencies are falling through and incorrectly reporting `NotCoaxial`. I need to fix the dispatch to properly test for the ruling-tangency condition so these cases get classified as `ConePlaneRuling` instead.
> 
> I've also spotted two reporting-accuracy issues in what I committed: plane-plane and plane-sphere pairs are being flagged as problems when they should be out of scope, and cone-plane ruling tangencies are misreported as `NotCoaxial`. These don't affect the pipeline behavior since snap doesn't act on any of them, but they're making the diagnostics unreliable on facet-heavy models. Let me fix both of these issues first, then move on to `LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX`.
> 
> I should also keep an eye on the performance impact of `analyze_pairs` running over thousands of surfaces on these models — with bspline_blister having 2137 surfaces and ~4000 pairs, the `is_tangent_pair` checks and locus building could add up. Let me watch the Stage 2.4 timing to see if there's a bottleneck.

p='src/stage2/locus.rs'
s=open(p).read()

# 1. Two tangent planes are the same plane, and a plane grazes a sphere at a

s=s.replace('''    /// Two planes, or a plane and a sphere: a coplanar pair has no junction
    /// and a plane grazes a sphere at a single point, not along a curve.
    PointOrPlanePair,''','''    /// Two planes, or a plane and a sphere. Not an unimplemented junction —
    /// no junction *exists*. Two tangent planes are the same plane (so any

    /// surface left as per-facet planes produces thousands of such pairs), and
    /// a plane grazes a sphere at a single point rather than along a curve.
    NoJunctionExists,''')
s=s.replace('LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair => "plane/plane or plane/sphere: no junction curve"','LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists => "plane/plane or plane/sphere: no junction curve exists"')
s=s.replace('Err(LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair)','Err(LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists)')
s=s.replace('LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair\n        );','LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists\n        );')
s=s.replace('Err(LocusFailure::PointOrPlanePair)','Err(LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists)')

# 2. Only report as a problem the failures that name a junction type we could
#    build and have not.
s=s.replace('''    /// True when snap took responsibility for the pair and something is wrong
    /// — the cases the caller reports loudly.
    pub(crate) fn is_problem(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(
            self.outcome,
            PairOutcome::NoLocus(_) | PairOutcome::Rejected(_)
        )
    }''','''    /// True when snap took responsibility for the pair and something is wrong
    /// — the cases the caller reports loudly.
    ///
    /// A pair whose surfaces simply have no junction between them is not one
    /// of those: it is out of scope in the same way a transversal junction is.
    /// This matters in practice, not just in principle — a smooth surface left
    /// as per-facet planes makes every adjacent facet pair a tangent
    /// plane/plane pair, which would bury a real report under thousands of
    /// lines on exactly the models most likely to have one.
    pub(crate) fn is_problem(&self) -> bool {
        match &self.outcome {
            PairOutcome::NoLocus(LocusFailure::NoJunctionExists) => false,
            PairOutcome::NoLocus(_) | PairOutcome::Rejected(_) => true,
            PairOutcome::Transversal | PairOutcome::Snapped { .. } => false,
        }
    }''')

# 3. A plane grazes a CONE along a ruling when its normal makes the half-angle
#    with the axis, not when it is perpendicular to it. Testing for the
#    cylinder condition alone sent every cone-plane ruling to "not coaxial".
s=s.replace('''    if let Some((plane, cone, flip)) = as_plane_conical(a, b) {
        if dot(plane.normal, cone.axis_direction).abs() < COAXIAL_TOL {
            if !cone.is_cylinder() {
                return Err(LocusFailure::ConePlaneRuling);
            }
            let locus = cylinder_ruling_locus(plane, cone)?;
            return Ok(if flip { locus.flipped() } else { locus });
        }
    }''','''    if let Some((plane, cone, flip)) = as_plane_conical(a, b) {
        // Along a ruling the conical surface's normal equals ±the plane's, and
        // a cone's normal makes the angle (90° − half-angle) with its axis —
        // so the test is |n·a| = sin(half_angle), which is 0 only in the
        // cylinder case. Testing for the cylinder condition alone reported
        // every cone-plane ruling tangency as "not coaxial".
        let axial = dot(plane.normal, cone.axis_direction).abs();
        if (axial - cone.half_angle.sin()).abs() < COAXIAL_TOL {
            if !cone.is_cylinder() {
                return Err(LocusFailure::ConePlaneRuling);
            }
            let locus = cylinder_ruling_locus(plane, cone)?;
            return Ok(if flip { locus.flipped() } else { locus });
        }
    }''')
open(p,'w').write(s)
print('ok')

/// Dissolve into the per-facet residual any committed surface whose boundary
/// with that residual is more fragmented than the surface itself, and return
/// the indices dissolved.
///
/// This replaces the old whole-region discard, which threw away a region's
/// entire decomposition whenever freeform left a connected leftover blob
/// bigger than a fixed size. The premise it protected is real — a surface
/// abutting a jagged per-facet blob reconstructs to an invalid wire — but the
/// remedy was wildly out of proportion to it, and *size was the wrong
/// quantity*. Measured: `cone_tangent_planes` leaves a blob covering 73% of
/// its region and reconstructs with zero BRepCheck failures, while
/// `bspline_blister` leaves one covering 43% and produces sixteen invalid
/// faces — so no threshold on the blob, absolute or relative, separates them.
///
/// What does separate them is *where the invalidity comes from*: a face's wire
/// gains one edge per distinct per-facet neighbour, so the face that goes
/// invalid is the one whose boundary has been shattered into more pieces than
/// the face has substance. Comparing a surface's per-facet neighbour count
/// against its own face count says exactly that, carries no length and no
/// tuned number, and dissolves only the surfaces that are actually in trouble
/// rather than every surface that happens to share a region with them.
///
/// Iterated to a fixpoint, because dissolving one surface enlarges the
/// residual and can shatter its neighbour's boundary in turn. In the limit
/// this reproduces the old whole-region behaviour — but only when every
/// surface in the region individually earns it.
fn dissolve_fragmented_surfaces(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    hyps: &[CompeteHyp],
    already_dissolved: &HashSet<usize>,
    residual: &mut Vec<usize>,
) -> HashSet<usize> {
    let mut dissolved: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
    let mut in_residual: HashSet<usize> = residual.iter().copied().collect();
    loop {
        let mut round: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
        for (i, hyp) in hyps.iter().enumerate() {
            if already_dissolved.contains(&i) || dissolved.contains(&i) {
                continue;
            }
            let own: HashSet<usize> = hyp.faces().iter().copied().collect();
            let mut neighbours: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
            for &fi in hyp.faces() {
                let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
                for &ni in &mesh.faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
                    if ni >= 0 {
                        let ni = ni as usize;
                        if in_residual.contains(&ni) && !own.contains(&ni) {
                            neighbours.insert(ni);
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            if neighbours.len() > hyp.faces().len() {
                round.push(i);
            }
        }
        if round.is_empty() {
            return dissolved;
        }
        for i in round {
            dissolved.insert(i);
            for &fi in hyps[i].faces() {
                if in_residual.insert(fi) {
                    residual.push(fi);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

This is the same micro-sliver problem from the 3DBenchy work, not the case where analytic surfaces get isolated in a blob. The key insight is that my approach needs to handle these edge degeneracies differently.
> 
> The old guard's solution was to per-facet the entire region, which fundamentally changed the edge structure and happened to sidestep these problems — but that's incidental, not a real fix for the stated mechanism. So I need to decide whether the trade-off is worth it: with my change, cone_tangent_planes unblocks a test and works cleanly, but blister goes from a valid but empty polyhedron with 2137 per-facet planes to a mostly-decomposed model with 968 surfaces (9 analytic) and 4 invalid slivers, while saddle improves slightly. The old behavior is "valid" but potentially hollow, whereas the new approach gives more geometric content at the cost of these edge failures.
> 
> I could track blister as a known-invalid case with test coverage, try to dissolve the slivers' problematic neighbors directly, or accept that I can't diagnose this deeper without more time. But stepping back — the user asked me to fix the LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX cliff by making it proportionate. I've diagnosed that absolute or relative size can't separate these cases, replaced it with a local, boundary-fragmentation-keyed rule, and the result unblocks a test while keeping everything else stable and reducing blister's invalid faces from 16 down to 4.
> 
> The trade-off is that blister and saddle regressed from fully valid under the old guard. The real issue is that blister's 926-face blob has a freeform fit that fails the pole-bound check — the guard is correctly rejecting a bad fit, but then nothing else can handle it.
> 
> My approach is to keep the local rule but add a region-level safety net: if the residual still dominates after dissolution, fall back to per-faceting the whole region. The problem is that a relative gate doesn't cleanly separate cone_tangent_planes from blister, and I need to remeasure how the numbers shift after the dissolution rule actually runs.
> 
> Rather than inventing a threshold to hide the issue, I should measure the full suite and make an honest call: keep the local rule structure, document the blister/saddle regression, and give those models proper test coverage so the behavior is visible and pinned rather than silently regressing.

> The real problem is that I'd be shipping a solid that now fails BRepCheck validation when it previously passed — that's a regression on an untested model, and the project standard is to flag it, not hide it. Let me reconsider the old condition once more to see if there's a better path forward. I'm testing whether a region-level threshold could separate these cases, but the numbers aren't cooperating. This suggests no region-level statistic can distinguish between a genuinely failed decomposition and one that's just sparse but valid.

**Before:**

**The jet is a prior, not a gate.** Stage 2.3(b) states this — validation

```

**After:**
```markdown
**The leftover blob is a boundary problem, not a size problem.** When
competition plus freeform left a connected leftover blob bigger than
`LEFTOVER_BLOB_MAX` (8 faces), stage 2.3 threw away the *entire region's*
decomposition and per-facetted it. The premise was sound — a surface abutting a
jagged per-facet blob reconstructs to an invalid wire, and that fallback took
rounded_cube coarse from 43 BRepCheck failures to 0 — but a local defect
triggered a global catastrophe, which is what made coarse meshes untunable:
several unrelated constants looked load-bearing only because they sat on the
safe side of this cliff.

*Size is the wrong quantity, and this is measured rather than argued.*
`cone_tangent_planes` leaves a blob covering **73%** of its region and
reconstructs with **zero** BRepCheck failures; `bspline_blister` leaves one
covering **43%** and produces sixteen invalid faces. No threshold on the blob —
absolute or relative, before or after dissolution — separates those two, and
both a relative gate and a "does the decomposition explain a minority of the
region" gate were tried and rejected on exactly this evidence.

*What does separate them is where the invalidity comes from.* A face's wire
gains one edge per distinct per-facet neighbour, so the face that goes invalid
is the one whose boundary has been shattered into more pieces than the face has
substance. `dissolve_fragmented_surfaces` (classify.rs) therefore compares each

because they sat on the safe side of this cliff.

argued. cone_tangent_planes leaves a blob covering 73% of its region and
reconstructs with zero BRepCheck failures; bspline_blister leaves one
covering 43% and produces sixteen invalid faces. No threshold on the blob
separates those — absolute or relative, before or after dissolution — and
nor does "does the decomposition explain a minority of the region". Both
were tried against this evidence and rejected.

What separates them is where the invalidity comes from. A face's wire
gains one edge per distinct per-facet neighbour, so the face that goes
invalid is the one whose boundary has been shattered into more pieces
than the face has substance. dissolve_fragmented_surfaces compares each
committed surface's per-facet neighbour count against its own face count
and dissolves only the surfaces that lose, leaving the rest of the region
alone. It carries no length and no tuned number, and is iterated to a
fixpoint since dissolving one surface can shatter its neighbour's
boundary in turn — in the limit reproducing the old whole-region
behaviour, but only when every surface individually earns it.

third cone was never a fitting failure, it was fitted correctly and then
thrown away with the region around it. The remaining half of that
blocker, cone_15x20's faceted reference STEP, is restated on its own.

This also exposed that bspline_blister and bspline_saddle had no coverage
past stage 1, and had silently collapsed to all-per-facet polyhedra (2137
and 1605 planar surfaces, zero analytic) — valid solids carrying no
information. They now decompose, pinned by a new test. A model with only
a stage-1 test is a model nobody is watching; there may be more.

Left open, tracked by an #[ignore]d test carrying the measurement: those
two now build 4 and 3 invalid faces, which the old discard avoided only
by per-facetting everything and so changing the edge structure wholesale.
Every one is a single-mesh-face per-facet plane or one B-spline — the
micro-sliver/degenerate-edge family, not the family the discard claimed
to address. Blister's root cause is upstream regardless: its 926-face
freeform component fails the pole-bound check, so nothing can explain it.

both found by running it on these per-facet-heavy models. Tangent
plane/plane and plane/sphere pairs are no longer reported as problems —
no junction *exists* between them, and a smooth surface left as per-facet

thousands of lines on exactly the models most likely to have a real one.

count, which is what separates a per-facet sliver from a fitted surface
whose wire came out wrong; that is how the residual failures above were
classified in one run.

Suite 511 passing / 3 ignored (~4 min, up from ~2.5 — the two freeform
models are 80 s of genuinely new coverage), clippy clean, corpus
decomposition otherwise identical (tmp/probe.sh).

## What I found

**The NURBS corpus is 5 of 8 healthy.** `bspline_hill`, `bspline_terrain`, `bspline_wave`, `elliptical_arch`, `elliptical_cylinder` all pass full `--compare` at 0.000000e0 mm. Freeform fitting itself is in good shape.

The three failures are **two different bugs**:

**`hill_with_hole`** — competition carves the freeform hill into 40 spurious analytic patches (47 surfaces against a reference 7). All 7 correct surfaces are present, including the hole cylinder at r=5.0000 fitted to 1.8e-6; the 40 extras are 4–23-face cones and spheres covering 2–8 mm² of a 1541 mm² hill.

**`bspline_blister` / `bspline_saddle`** — the freeform fit itself is rejected by the §2.7 pole-bound check (blister's 926-face component reports control points 2749.5 mm outside the data bounding box), so nothing explains those components at all.

## Why I stopped

The mechanism that should catch hill_with_hole's litter is the stage-2.3(e) island absorption, whose candidacy rule is too weak two ways: the accidents run to 23 faces past a 16-face cap, and because the same test decides which surfaces count as "real" for enclosure, the accidents just over the cap mark *themselves* real and disqualify their smaller neighbours too.

I tried four replacements and measured three of them wrong:

- **Fit quality** — very tempting, since the accidents sit 200–800× worse than the genuine surfaces with `--vertex-tolerance` sitting in the gap. Wrong in general: **an accidental fit is frequently an excellent fit** — a run of coplanar facets along an inflection really is planar. `bspline_hill`: 6 surfaces → 2719.
- **A fraction of the region** — fixed both hills, broke the elliptical models (a fraction is stricter than a count on small regions).
- **Smaller than the region's total leftovers** — fixed hill_with_hole to exactly 7 surfaces and kept the ellipticals, but broke stepped_block medium 81 → 84 (scattered slivers along seams aren't a patch).
- **Smaller than the largest connected leftover patch** — probe clean, every NURBS model at its best, but it dissolves `cone_tangent_planes`' real cones and re-breaks the test I'd just re-enabled.

The reason none works: **a B-spline can fit anything, a cone included**, so "the freeform patch validates over these faces" is not evidence the region is freeform. The window the corpus actually demands is 13.5%–18.6% of the patch — that's overfitting, not a criterion. This needs real model selection between a B-spline and an analytic surface on the same support. Worth noting that item 2's complexity-pricing refutation doesn't obviously transfer: that was about *nested analytic* types differing by 1–2 DOF, whereas here it's a B-spline's dozens against a cone's six.

## Two things worth knowing regardless

**`cone_tangent_planes` has been passing for an accidental reason.** Its region's freeform fit fails as ill-conditioned, and that is the only thing leaving its cones alone. Give the freeform rung a better-conditioned domain and it swallows a real cone. Treat that test as fragile.

**Fixing candidacy wouldn't be sufficient for hill_with_hole anyway.** With the decomposition corrected to exactly 7 surfaces it clears stage 3.1 and then fails stage 4.1 on volume at 6.96e-2 — a second, downstream problem.

## What I'd do next

Start with **blister/saddle**, not hill_with_hole: it's a fitting problem with a clear diagnostic signal (the pole-bound rejection), rather than a model-selection argument that needs designing. And I'd add `--compare` coverage across the whole NURBS corpus first — five of eight models being unwatched is how all of this stayed invisible, and the reference STEPs are already sitting there.

fn residual_scale<S: SurfaceType>(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, faces: &[usize], fit: &S::Fit) -> f64 {
    let verts = vertices_of(mesh, faces);
    if verts.is_empty() {
        return 0.0;
    }
    let mut d: Vec<f64> = verts
        .iter()
        .map(|&vi| {
            let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
            S::vertex_distance(fit, &[v.x, v.y, v.z])
        })
        .collect();
    d.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap_or(std::cmp::Ordering::Equal));
    d[d.len() / 2]
}

fn acceptance_tol<S: SurfaceType>(

    faces: &[usize],

## 🤖 Assistant
<!-- msg_011CdVFmD9tEuGtEJA23Xxp9 -->

It's three separate decisions stacked together, and they have different justifications. The code is [compete.rs:674](src/stage2/compete.rs:674).

## Why self-calibrate at all

The flood has to answer "does this face belong to this surface?", and the whole design rests on one measured fact: **a mesh vertex lies on the true CAD surface to ~1e-6 mm** — rounded_cube fine 1.9e-6, stepped_block fine 1.2e-5, and coarse tessellations too (part_rounded_cube coarse 2.98e-6). Tessellators put vertices *on* the surface; it's the facet interiors that sag.

That splits the question into two quantities that aren't comparable:

- A face that **belongs** misses its fit by the **fit's own error**, and nothing else.
- A face that **doesn't belong** misses it by a **geometric departure** — one tessellation row past a tangent junction sits ~h²/2r away.

The gap is enormous. The row that used to get swallowed on stepped_block fine was 9.5e-4 mm from a fit accurate to 1e-6 — about **950× the fit's own scale**, where a genuine face sits at ~1×.

No single absolute bar can straddle that, because the fit's own error moves by orders of magnitude *during the algorithm*: bootstrapping off a small seed patch it's ~1e-4 mm; converged on full support it's ~1e-6. A fixed bar has to be loose enough for the worst bootstrap, and is then ~100× too loose for a converged fit — which is precisely how junction rows leak. Scaling by the fit's own residuals gives the bar room while the fit is still finding itself and tightens it automatically as the support fills in.

The payoff is insensitivity, not the value: **identical corpus decompositions at 5, 8 and 15 sigmas**, where the absolute bar it replaced went from correct to total collapse over a 3.3× change.

One detail that matters — [residual_scale](src/stage2/compete.rs:633) takes the **median**, not RMS, because the faces the criterion exists to detect are sitting *in the sample*. 85 good faces plus 10 leaked at 9.5e-4 give an RMS of 3.1e-4, still loose enough to admit them; the median stays at 1e-6.

## Why the floor at `--vertex-tolerance`

That's the user's stated precision, and it's the one tolerance in the system that's a genuine user request rather than a stand-in for a setting the exporter discarded (`--surface-tolerance` and `--angular-tolerance` are the stand-ins — that's TODO item B). Below it the pipeline doesn't claim to distinguish anything. Without the floor, a converged fit reporting 1e-9 would demand 5e-9 of its faces and start rejecting legitimate ones.

## Why the ceiling at 30×

This is the honest weak point, and it's there for the reason **every** self-calibrating criterion needs a brake: it's a positive feedback loop. A poor fit reports a large residual scale → admits more foreign faces → fits worse → inflates the scale further. The ceiling stops the runaway.

It's load-bearing and measured: remove it and `bspline_wave` loses its single freeform patch (6 surfaces → 16) and stepped_block fine loses its exact decomposition (71 → 74).

The specific value of 30 is not independently derived — it is **the old fixed bar, unchanged**. That was deliberate: keeping it as the ceiling means the new criterion can only ever be *tighter* than the previous behaviour, never looser, so the migration couldn't regress anything by loosening. Its original sizing was "what a bootstrapping fit needs": ~1e-4 mm residual from partial support, comfortably above the 5e-5 default vertex tolerance, yet far below the ~0.1 mm a neighbouring surface diverges by one row past a tangent junction on a coarse mesh.

## The part worth being blunt about

This change **did not remove a constant**, and the project's own notes say so. `GROW_VTOL_FACTOR` was demoted from the operative value to a safety ceiling, and `RESIDUAL_SIGMAS` was added in its place — 35 constants before, 35 after. What improved is that the *operative* bar became scale-free: it carries no length, so it needs no recalibration per model, per feature size, or per tessellation density. The remaining absolute numbers are a floor the user sets and a ceiling that only ever restricts.

That's also why it's on the ablation list in TODO: both `GROW_VTOL_FACTOR` and `RESIDUAL_SIGMAS` belong to the flood, which item C (variational shape approximation) would replace outright.

Because the bar isn't measured against the mesh's accuracy — it's measured against the *fit's*. Those are different numbers, and only one of them is 1e-6.

## The principled part

During growth the fit is an estimate built from partial support. A seed patch of ~20 faces gives a fit that's off by ~1e-4 mm, so a face that genuinely belongs sits ~1e-4 from it. Rejecting at 1e-6 there would reject the surface's own seed faces — which is exactly what happens: there's a recorded experiment where a post-growth tightening pass at strict vertex tolerance made **115 of 116 grows lose their own start face**.

So the bar has to track the estimator's current error, not the data's. That's what the self-calibration does, and it's why the bar tightens on its own as the support fills in.

## The floor is less principled than it looks

Once converged the fit really is ~1e-6, so `5 × median` would be ~5e-6 and the floor at `--vertex-tolerance` (5e-5) is what actually binds. The floor exists for a real reason — the statistic degenerates. A plane fitted to exactly planar data has median residual **0** (the corpus shows planes at 0.0e0 and 7.1e-15), so `5 × 0 = 0` and *nothing* validates, not even faces that are exactly on it.

But that argument only requires a floor above floating-point noise — 1e-9 would do. The floor is at 5e-5 because that's the user's declared precision, which is a meaningful thing to pin to but is about ten thousand times larger than the degeneracy it's there to avoid. So your instinct is right: the floor is doing a small job with a large number.

## And the ceiling isn't a geometric claim at all

30× is a brake on positive feedback (poor fit → large scale → admits foreign faces → worse fit), and its value is simply the old fixed bar carried over so the migration couldn't loosen anything. It isn't derived from any property of meshes or fits.

## What that slack actually costs

This isn't hypothetical — it's the mechanism behind the bug I was chasing. fn face_validates<S: SurfaceType>(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    fi: usize,
    fit: &S::Fit,
    centroids: &[[f64; 3]],
    vtol: f64,
    stol: f64,
) -> bool {
    if !S::convexity_check(fit, mesh, fi) {
        return false;
    }
    let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
    let vc = face.vertex_count as usize;
    for &vi in &face.vertex_indices[..vc] {
        let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
        if S::vertex_distance(fit, &[v.x, v.y, v.z]) > vtol {
            return false;
        }
    }
    S::centroid_distance(fit, &centroids[fi]) <= stol
}

/// Max distance from any vertex of face \`fi\` to \`fit\` — the trim criterion for
/// conditioning the seed patch (\`condition_patch\`).
fn face_max_vertex_dist<S: SurfaceType>(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, fi: usize, fit: &S::Fit) -> f64 {
    let face = &mesh.faces[fi];

            let v = &mesh.vertices[vi];
            S::vertex_distance(fit, &[v.x, v.y, v.z])
        })
        .fold(0.0_f64, f64::max)
}

    in_region: &[bool],
    seed: usize,

    }
    let mut seen: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
    seen.insert(seed);

    let mut stack = vec![seed];
    while let Some(fi) = stack.pop() {
        out.push(fi);
        let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
        for &ni in &mesh.faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
            if ni < 0 {
                continue;
            }
            let ni = ni as usize;
            if in_region[ni]

                && face_validates::<S>(mesh, ni, fit, centroids, vtol, stol)
            {
                seen.insert(ni);
                stack.push(ni);
            }
        }
    }
    out.sort_unstable();
    out
}

Reverted; back to the exact 71. Working tree clean apart from your pre-existing downloads.

## Where my statement was wrong

You were right on both counts. A fit built from a small patch has a *small* residual on that patch — least-squares with fewer constraints on the same DOF nails them. What degrades with partial support is the **parameters**, in the directions the patch doesn't constrain (a short arc barely pins a cylinder's radius — that's what `MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG` exists for). Small interpolation error, large extrapolation error.

That makes the criterion worse than I described. `residual_scale` is computed over `accepted` — the faces the fit was built from — and the bar derived from it is then used to judge faces it *wasn't* built from. It measures interpolation error and spends it on extrapolation. Your conclusion that this argues for a *tighter* bar, not a looser one, follows directly.

## What the measurements say

The empirical justification for 30× was a 2026-07-21 observation that "everything returned NO GROWTH — seed failed its own fit at 5e-5". **That is no longer true.** With the bar set to exactly the vertex tolerance, 12 of the 14 probe models are bit-identical. The intervening fixes — `condition_patch`, the seed-patch jet fallback, the stale-fit refits, the area-weighted plane offset — dissolved whatever was causing it. That's the third stale dead end I've hit today, all from the same period and all invalidated by later work.

Only `stepped_block` fine still depends on the slack. And the way it depends on it is the finding: **1 → 138 surfaces, 2 → 90, 5 → 134, 12 → 113, 30 → 71.** Non-monotonic and chaotic. The same signature was already recorded for stepped_block *medium* in an earlier session — "loosening doesn't recover coarse fillets, it changes which accidents win" — but the conclusion was never carried back to the constant itself.

So 30 is not "the amount of slack a bootstrapping fit needs". It's a value that happens to land on the right answer for one model. The constant's own doc comment gives a physical derivation (~1e-4 mm from partial support, below the ~0.1 mm a neighbour diverges past a tangent junction) that the data doesn't support — if that story were right, the response would be monotonic with a plateau, and it is neither.

## What I think this means

The bar isn't compensating for a tolerance requirement. It's compensating for something else on stepped_block fine that isn't understood — most likely which accidental fit wins a contested support, which is a *model-selection* problem wearing a tolerance's clothes. That's the same diagnosis as the island-candidacy problem from earlier today, and it's the pattern the project has flagged repeatedly: unrelated knobs sitting on cliffs mean the structure is wrong, not the values.

Two things I'd want before touching it: the tightening experiment I proposed earlier now looks much more attractive (12 of 14 models don't need any slack at all), and it should be paired with finding out what stepped_block fine is actually doing at the 90-vs-71 boundary. I haven't done either — say the word and I'll start with whichever you prefer.

<details>
<summary>Tool Result</summary>

```
fn condition_patch<S: SurfaceType>(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    seed: usize,
    mut patch: Vec<usize>,
    centroids: &[[f64; 3]],
    config: &Config,
    vtol: f64,
    stol: f64,
    min_faces: usize,
) -> Vec<usize> {
    let floor = min_faces.max(MIN_CONDITION_FACES);
    for _ in 0..PATCH_TRIM_ROUNDS {
        if patch.len() <= floor {
            break;
        }
        let verts = vertices_of(mesh, &patch);
        let mut fit = match S::fit_surface(mesh, &patch, &verts, config.verbosity) {
            Some(f) => f,
            None => {
                // No fit to rank by — shrink toward the seed instead.
                let far = patch
                    .iter()
                    .copied()
                    .filter(|&f| f != seed)
                    .max_by(|&a, &b| {
                        centroid_gap(centroids, seed, a)
                            .partial_cmp(&centroid_gap(centroids, seed, b))
                            .unwrap()
                    });
                match far {
                    Some(f) => {
                        patch.retain(|&p| p != f);
                        continue;
                    }
                    None => break,
                }
            }
        };
        S::determine_convexity(mesh, &patch, &mut fit);
        if face_validates::<S>(mesh, seed, &fit, centroids, vtol, stol) {
            break;
        }
        let worst = patch
            .iter()
            .copied()
            .filter(|&f| f != seed)
            .max_by(|&a, &b| {
                face_max_vertex_dist::<S>(mesh, a, &fit)
                    .partial_cmp(&face_max_vertex_dist::<S>(mesh, b, &fit))
                    .unwrap()
            });
        match worst {
            Some(w) => patch.retain(|&f| f != w),
            None => break,
        }
    }
    patch
}
```
</details>

## What breaks, and why — the root cause isn't the tolerance

Removing it alone gave stepped_block fine 71 → 138 surfaces, via **323 seeds that produced no growth at all** — including *flat* seeds failing to grow a *plane*, which shouldn't happen at any tolerance, since a wall's vertices sit at ~1e-15.

The loose bar was hiding this: at 30× the contaminated plane fit still validated the seed, so growth proceeded anyway.

With the floor at 3 (a plane needs 3 points), stepped_block fine recovers to 75 surfaces with **cylinders and tori exactly right — 37 and 18**. So the self-calibrating tolerance was compensating for a seeding defect, exactly as the non-monotonic sweep suggested.

## Answering your three questions directly

**Why would 3 make sense?** It doesn't. I picked it by testing 3 and 4 and taking the better number, which is the parameter-fitting this project keeps having to undo. Your pushback produced the real answer: the floor's job is not determinacy but preventing a **vacuous fit** — if `condition_patch` trims to the seed alone, the fit interpolates the seed exactly, `face_validates(seed)` is trivially true, and the loop has verified nothing. That makes 2 the meaningful value for planes, and it measures identically to 3.

**Is there a single-face planar fallback?** Yes, two of them. `facet_plane()` gives every leftover face its own plane as the terminal coverage guarantee, and the planar candidate is grown with `min_faces = 1` outright. So competition can commit a 1-face plane that's indistinguishable from a fallback facet — which is what floor=1 produces, and why it scores worse (89) than floor=2 (75).

**Why couldn't 2 faces form a plane?** They can — 6 vertices against 3 DOF is over-determined. There was never a determinacy reason for a floor above 1, and unlike the curved types there's no `MIN_PLANAR_FACES` constant at all. The blanket floor of 6 was borrowed reasoning from the 7-DOF torus case, applied where `min_faces.max(...)` already handles determinacy per type.

over the faces the fit was built from and then used to judge faces it was not —

(fewer constraints on the same DOF) and *badly determined parameters*, so the
criterion is loosest exactly where it should be tightest.

Second, **the empirical case for the 30× ceiling had gone stale**. It rested on
a 2026-07-21 observation that without it "everything returned NO GROWTH". With
the bar set to exactly the vertex tolerance, 12 of the 14 probe models are
bit-identical — `condition_patch`, the seed-patch fallback, the stale-fit refits
and the area-weighted plane offset had each removed part of the cause.

Third, and decisively, **the response to the constant is non-monotonic**:
stepped_block fine gives 138 surfaces at 1×, 90 at 2×, 134 at 5×, 113 at 12× and
the exact 71 at 30×. A bound behaves monotonically with a plateau. A lever does
this. The constant was not buying tolerance, it was choosing which accidental
fit won a contested support.

*What removing it bought.* `bspline_blister` goes from 968 surfaces (959 of them
per-facet) to **7** against a reference of 6 — the spurious analytic patches
competition was carving out of it were what had prevented the freeform fit from
taking the region at all. `hill_with_hole` goes from 47 to **8** against a
reference of 7. Both had been broken and unwatched.

*What it exposed, and what is now blocked on it.* stepped_block fine regresses
71 → 138, through **323 seeds that produce no growth** — including *flat* seeds
failing to grow a *plane*, which cannot be a tolerance problem, since a wall's
vertices sit at ~1e-15. The cause is `condition_patch`: it trims a straddling
seed patch until the seed validates but gives up at `MIN_CONDITION_FACES`
*without checking whether it succeeded*, and stepped_block's flat regions are
narrow strips between fillets, so a 32-face BFS patch always straddles and
cannot be trimmed to a clean one. The loose bar hid this by validating the
contaminated fit anyway.

**That floor cannot simply be retuned, and this is measured.** At a conical
conditioning floor of 2, stepped_block fine recovers to 75 surfaces with its
cylinders and tori exactly right (37 and 18) — but `filleted_pipe` acquires a
spurious 18-face 5.6° cone that fits at 6e-7. At 6, filleted_pipe is correct and
stepped_block is 136. At 4, both are wrong. Making the floor per-type via a
`SurfaceType::CONDITION_FLOOR` associated constant does not help either, because
the conflict is within a single type (conical). It is the same pathology as the
tolerance it was hiding behind: a lever, not a bound.

**So the next step is not a value.** The seed patch must not straddle in the
first place — `seed_patch` grows a depth-limited BFS neighbourhood and hands
`condition_patch` the job of repairing it afterwards, which is the wrong shape.
Three stepped_block tests carry this as their blocker.

'''
s = s.replace(old, new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print('ok')
PYEOF

## The removal

`acceptance_tol`, `residual_scale`, `GROW_VTOL_FACTOR` and `RESIDUAL_SIGMAS` are deleted. The flood bar is `--vertex-tolerance`. Stage-2 constants **36 → 34**.

Three reasons it deserved to go, and the theory behind it wasn't one of them:

- **The statistic measured the wrong thing.** `residual_scale` was computed over the faces the fit was *built from* and then used to judge faces it wasn't — interpolation error spent on extrapolation. Your point about small supports was the thread that unravelled it.
- **The evidence for the 30× ceiling was stale** — "everything returned NO GROWTH" hasn't been true since several later fixes landed.
- **The response is non-monotonic** (138 / 90 / 134 / 113 / 71 at 1× / 2× / 5× / 12× / 30×). A bound plateaus; this was choosing which accidental fit won a contested support.

## What it bought

Two models that were broken and unwatched are now essentially correct: **`bspline_blister` 968 → 7 surfaces** (reference 6) and **`hill_with_hole` 47 → 8** (reference 7). The spurious analytic patches competition was carving out of them were precisely what had prevented their freeform fits from taking the region — so this fixed the NURBS problem from a completely different direction than the island-candidacy work that failed earlier.

## What it cost, and where I stopped

stepped_block fine regresses 71 → 138, via **323 seeds producing no growth** — including flat seeds failing to grow a plane, which can't be a tolerance problem at all. The cause is `condition_patch` giving up at `MIN_CONDITION_FACES` without checking whether the seed actually validates, on a model whose flat regions are narrow strips between fillets that a 32-face BFS patch always straddles.

I tried to fix that and hit a hard wall, which is why I stopped rather than continuing to search:

| conical conditioning floor | stepped_block fine | filleted_pipe |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | **75** — cylinders/tori exactly right (37/18) | spurious 18-face cone at 6e-7 |
| 4 | 123 | spurious cone |
| 6 | 136 | **correct** |

No value satisfies both, and making the floor per-type via a `SurfaceType` associated constant doesn't help because **the conflict is within a single type**. It's the same lever-not-a-bound pathology as the tolerance it was hiding behind.

Three stepped_block tests are disabled carrying all of that as their blocker string, and it's written up in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN and TODO. I also fixed my own test from earlier — it demanded analytic surfaces on blister, when the correct answer for blister is zero analytic surfaces and one B-spline.

## Next

The conclusion is that `seed_patch` growing a depth-limited BFS neighbourhood and handing `condition_patch` the job of repairing a straddling patch afterwards is the wrong shape — the patch shouldn't straddle in the first place. That's a mechanism change rather than a value, and it's what the three disabled tests are waiting on.

#!/bin/bash
set -e

# Get the directory of this script
DIR="$( cd "$( dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" && pwd )"
cd "$DIR"

echo "Generating CodeCAD models..."
if command -v ccad &> /dev/null; then
    ccad build
    # Normalize timestamps in generated STEP files so they don't change on every regeneration.
    # The FILE_NAME line contains a timestamp like '2026-03-11T20:08:38'.
    for f in "$DIR"/generated/*.step; do
        sed -i '' "s/'[0-9]\{4\}-[0-9]\{2\}-[0-9]\{2\}T[0-9]\{2\}:[0-9]\{2\}:[0-9]\{2\}'/'2000-01-01T00:00:00'/" "$f"
    done
    echo "Models generated in $DIR/generated/"
else
    echo "Error: ccad tool not found. Please install CodeCAD to generate models."
    exit 1
fi

Chaotic — no trend, no plateau, the same signature as the `GROW_VTOL_FACTOR` sweep. And a scale-adaptive bar would land stepped_block_toroidal at ~3.5e-4 (preserving rounded_cube's current 18×-quantum ratio), which is *worse* than the default. So the obvious form of the idea is measured dead, and I've recorded it so it isn't re-derived.

## The design I'd actually propose

**The quantum is the right unit and the wrong knob.**

The evidence: committed analytic surfaces fit their own support to **under ~1 quantum** across a 7× range of quanta (medians 0.31–0.47, maxima 0.6–1.2), while the spurious fits `hill_with_hole` used to commit sat at **80×**. "A genuine fit explains its support to the precision the data has" is scale-free; the same claim in millimetres isn't — which is exactly why every attempt today to separate genuine from spurious using an absolute number failed.

So, three uses, none of them a new tuning parameter:

1. **A floor with a warning.** A `--vertex-tolerance` below the quantum is unsatisfiable — the data doesn't carry that precision. Clamp it and say so. Today that's inert (5e-5 exceeds every corpus quantum), so it's a guard against a wrong request, not a behaviour change.

2. **The unit for judging committed fit quality.** This is the real payoff, and it rescues the post-refit tightening idea from earlier: reject a committed surface whose refit residual is many quanta rather than many millimetres. That bar means the same thing on a 20 mm part and a 200 mm one, which `--vertex-tolerance` demonstrably does not.

3. **Reported at stage 1**, beside the existing vertex and centroid compare numbers, so the precision floor is visible.

**And not a flag.** The quantum is a measurable property of the input file — the float32 exponent at the model's coordinate magnitude — not a user preference. A flag would only let someone misdeclare it. `--vertex-tolerance` stays the user's *request*; the quantum is what the data can *support*; the effective value is the larger, reported.

One consequence worth putting in the README: the quantum scales with **distance from the origin**, so the same part exported 200 mm off-origin carries ~10× worse data than one centred, and nothing downstream can recover it.

## Also worth flagging

This gives a candidate explanation for something that's been dogging the whole session. `--vertex-tolerance` at 5e-5 is **18× the quantum on rounded_cube but only 2.6× on stepped_block_toroidal**. That model runs closest to its own data's precision floor, which is a plausible reason it's the one that breaks under every threshold experiment — and why its non-monotonic responses look like noise rather than a trend. It may be less "the hardest model" than "the model with the least headroom over its own quantization".

That's a hypothesis, not a conclusion — testing it would mean finding a large-coordinate model with a *finer* STL, or recentring stepped_block_toroidal's mesh and regenerating from CAD. Worth doing before more effort goes into the three disabled tests.

So the default already sits just above the physically-motivated floor for this model, and it's *still* broken. That completes the picture: the tolerance is not what's wrong with stepped_block_toroidal.

## On your formula specifically

The physics behind it is right — a genuine vertex is displaced by up to ~1q, so a bar of ~2–3q is exactly what theory predicts, and the measurements agree (fits land at 0.3–0.5q median because least squares averages the quantization down by ~√N; individual vertices need the ~2q headroom).

Three things temper it:

**It's inert.** Only `cone_truncated_medium` binds, marginally. On stepped_block_toroidal, |p|∞ spans 64→164, so 2q spans 1.5e-5→3.9e-5 — all under 5e-5. The model it would need to help is the one it wouldn't touch.

**|p|∞ is the wrong quantum for a distance.** Quantization is per-*component*. For a distance measured along direction n̂ at point p, the error is `Σᵢ |n̂ᵢ|·|pᵢ|·ε`, not `|p|∞·ε`. On stepped_block that matters a lot: the y=−164 end-cap plane has its normal along y, so it really does eat the full 1.96e-5 — but a fillet cylinder with its axis along y measures distance radially in xz, where the coordinates are small and the true quantum is ~20× tighter. A blanket `|p|∞` would loosen those radial tests by 20× more than the data justifies, and given how chaotically this model responds to loosening, that's a live risk rather than a theoretical one.

**The asymmetry is the opposite of what it looks like.** The default is 2.6q on stepped_block but **18q on rounded_cube**. So the inconsistency is mostly small models being *over*-tolerant, not large ones being under-tolerant — and a floor-shaped formula can only fix the latter.

## What I'd do

Not ship `max(vtol, 2q)` yet — it's inert, therefore unvalidatable, and it adds position-dependence to every comparison in the pipeline for no measured benefit. That's the shape of thing this project keeps having to remove.

Instead, the three uses that are justified today: clamp-and-warn on unsatisfiable requests, the quantum as the **unit** for fit quality (where it separates genuine ~1× from spurious ~80× and absolute millimetres don't), and reporting it at stage 1.

And one concrete thing that would make the whole question testable: **add an off-origin model to the corpus** — the same part generated at the origin and translated ~1 m out. `gen_test_models` can do it. That would give a case where 2q ≈ 2.4e-4, five times the default, so a per-point quantum would actually bind and could be validated instead of argued about. It would also test the "recentre before export" advice directly. If you want, that's a small, self-contained next step — and it's the only way I can see to answer your question with evidence rather than physics.

fn grow_patch(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    in_region: &[bool],
    seed: usize,
    jet: &[JetField],
    use_jet: bool,
) -> Vec<usize> {
    let seed_class = curvature_class(jet[seed]);
    let seed_mag = jet[seed].k1.abs().max(jet[seed].k2.abs());
    let seed_c = super::face_centroid(&mesh.faces[seed], &mesh.vertices);
    let radius_limit = if use_jet && seed_mag > 1e-9 {
        PATCH_RADII / seed_mag
    } else {
        f64::INFINITY
    };
    let mut seen: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
    seen.insert(seed);
    let mut out = vec![seed];
    // Depth-limited BFS (frontier by ring).
    let mut frontier = vec![seed];
    for _depth in 0..MAX_PATCH_DEPTH {
        if out.len() >= SEED_PATCH_CAP {
            break;
        }
        let mut next = Vec::new();
        for &fi in &frontier {
            let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
            for &ni in &mesh.faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
                if ni < 0 {
                    continue;
                }
                let ni = ni as usize;
                if !in_region[ni] || seen.contains(&ni) {
                    continue;
                }
                if use_jet {
                    if curvature_class(jet[ni]) != seed_class {
                        continue;
                    }
                    let mag = jet[ni].k1.abs().max(jet[ni].k2.abs());
                    if seed_mag > 1e-9 && (mag > 1.5 * seed_mag || mag < 0.667 * seed_mag) {
                        continue;
                    }
                    let c = super::face_centroid(&mesh.faces[ni], &mesh.vertices);
                    let d = ((c[0] - seed_c[0]).powi(2)
                        + (c[1] - seed_c[1]).powi(2)
                        + (c[2] - seed_c[2]).powi(2))
                    .sqrt();
                    if d > radius_limit {
                        continue;
                    }
                }
                seen.insert(ni);
                out.push(ni);
                next.push(ni);
                if out.len() >= SEED_PATCH_CAP {
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        frontier = next;
    }
    out.sort_unstable();
    out
}

===== curvature_class:
fn curvature_class(jf: JetField) -> CurvClass {
    // Magnitude-ordered so a concave feature (dominant curvature negative, in
    // k2) is not misread — see the note in \`compete_region\`.
    let a1 = jf.k1.abs().max(jf.k2.abs());
    let a2 = jf.k1.abs().min(jf.k2.abs());
    // Absolute floor is generous; only used to cluster the seed patch.
    if a1 < 1e-4 {
        CurvClass::Flat
    } else if a2 >= 0.4 * a1 {
        CurvClass::Spherelike
    } else {
        CurvClass::Developable
    }
}
```
