<!-- msg_011CdWFSUxsWdnCVLXXNX2e9 -->

Your model of it is right — single face, BFS out to at most 32 faces, depth 3. The missing piece is that **the growth never tests coplanarity, or any fit at all.**

## What the filter actually is

`grow_patch` is a depth-limited BFS over mesh adjacency. Optionally it applies a *jet-similarity* filter, which is three tests:

1. `curvature_class(neighbour) == curvature_class(seed)` — a coarse 3-way bucket: **Flat** (`a1 < 1e-4`), **Spherelike** (`a2 ≥ 0.4·a1`), **Developable** (otherwise).
2. magnitude within 1.5×/0.667× of the seed's.
3. distance from the seed within `PATCH_RADII / seed_mag`.

None of those asks "is this face on the same plane as the seed". The patch is the *input* to the fit — nothing is validated until the fit exists and `flood` runs.

## And for a flat seed, two of the three switch themselves off

Look at the gating in the code:

```rust
let radius_limit = if use_jet && seed_mag > 1e-9 { PATCH_RADII / seed_mag } else { f64::INFINITY };
...
if seed_mag > 1e-9 && (mag > 1.5 * seed_mag || mag < 0.667 * seed_mag) { continue; }
```

For a planar seed `seed_mag ≈ 0`, so the magnitude test never fires and the radius limit is **infinity**. The only surviving test is the 3-way class comparison.

## And that test almost never applies, because almost nothing is Flat

`curvature_class` calls a face Flat only if `a1 < 1e-4`. On this model that is **44 faces out of 26122 — 0.17%**. 98.6% of the mesh is classified `Developable`.

That's the jet failing for the reason I measured earlier: a plane face's jet is computed from a vertex neighbourhood that includes the adjacent fillet, so it reads the fillet's curvature. **Most plane faces don't seed as "flat" at all** — they seed as Developable and get grown with a magnitude test comparing against a bogus curvature, which is worse than the Flat path.

Then `seed_patch` adds the last step: if the jet-filtered patch has fewer than `MIN_CONDITION_FACES = 6` faces, it **discards the filter entirely** and re-grows with `use_jet = false` — an unfiltered BFS that takes whatever is topologically adjacent. That fires for 16% of the Flat seeds.

## Why it was built that way, and where the reasoning breaks

This is deliberate, and documented in `seed_patch`: handing the fit an unfiltered neighbourhood "costs nothing in soundness: a patch straddling a junction is what `condition_patch` trims and what flood validation rejects." The patch is meant to be cheap and disposable.

That holds when the contamination is a row or two. It breaks here because the contamination is ~50% of the patch, `condition_patch` can only remove one face per round for 16 rounds and stops at a floor of 6 — and, critically, when the acceptance bar is tight the contaminated fit doesn't merely get trimmed, it fails to validate the seed at all, and the whole seed returns **NO GROWTH**. That's the 323 events.

## The repair this suggests

For a plane seed the natural filter is exact and needs no jet: **a plane's facets all share the same normal, bit-for-bit**, while a fillet facet differs by ≥0.7°. Filtering the patch on "normal equals the seed's own facet normal" would give a pure-plane patch immediately, with no threshold beyond float noise and no dependence on a curvature estimate that's already been corrupted by the neighbours.

The caveat from my last experiment: *global* connected components over near-zero-dihedral edges over-fragmented (342 components above 10 mm² against 16 reference planes). But that's a much stronger ask than a local patch filter — a patch only needs to be clean enough to condition a fit, not to be a global partition. Worth testing as a local filter before believing it, given today's hit rate on unmeasured ideas.

No — your reading of §2.3(b) is correct, and the code doesn't match it. Fixed in `3c4282b`.

## What the plan says vs what runs

| §2.3(b) as written | `compete.rs` as built |
|---|---|
| Seed = one face | Seed = one face ✓ |
| **Initial parameters come from the jet** at that face: `r ≈ 1/κ1`, sphere centre ≈ `centroid − n̂/κ1`, axis from the κ≈0 principal direction, torus tube centres from medial points | **Least-squares fit to a 32-face BFS neighbourhood**; the jet only *filters* which faces join it |
| Expansion: BFS, every accepted face fit-validated | `flood`: BFS, every accepted face fit-validated ✓ |

Growth is actually **two phases, and only the second is validated**:

1. `seed_patch` → `condition_patch` — an *unvalidated* depth-3, 32-face BFS patch, least-squares fitted, then trimmed until the seed validates against its own patch's fit.
2. `flood` — the validated BFS you read about.

So the answer to your earlier question is that the non-coplanar faces enter in **phase 1, which the design section doesn't mention at all**. Your inference from the plan — that a seed can only grow through validated faces — is exactly right *about the documented design*.

## And that's not a trivial documentation gap

The original design **cannot have the bug I diagnosed.** If the initial parameters come analytically from one face's jet, there is no patch, so there's nothing to straddle. The straddling failure is a property of the implementation's departure from the plan, not of the algorithm as specified.

The departure was for a real reason: the jet's *magnitude* isn't trustworthy at fillet scale — adjacent facets of one exact r = 0.5 arc read κ1 = 0.023, 0.162 and 2.2, i.e. radii of 43 mm, 6 mm and 0.45 mm for the same feature, so `r ≈ 1/κ1` would be wrong by 100×. Fitting a neighbourhood is robust to that. It just buys a different failure: on a mesh whose facet sizes vary 2000:1, the neighbourhood can't stay on its own surface, and the jet filter meant to keep it there classifies only **0.17%** of that model's faces as flat.

Until now that whole phase appeared in the plan only as an aside in the Rewrite Roadmap's "Notes from implementation", 1200 lines from the design section — which is why it was invisible to you. §2.3(b) now describes both phases and records why the original was abandoned.

Worth noting the shape of this: two mechanisms, each robust to the other's failure mode, and the corpus contains models that break each one. That's an argument for a seed that doesn't depend on either — which is where the exact-facet-normal idea from a moment ago points, since a plane's facets share a normal bit-for-bit regardless of both jet noise and facet size.

Face 18608 **is** the 3152 mm² plane — the second-largest surface in the model. It gets seeded, the jet reads 0.001 (borrowed from the adjacent fillet) so it's classified **Developable**, and all four candidates including the plane return `None`. The surface reaches stage 3 as nothing.

And the fillet facets turn out to be **155:1 strips** — 4.61 mm long × 0.025 mm wide. Dihedral across the short direction (2.44°) over 0.025 mm gives radius **0.586 mm**; along the ruling it's 0° → infinity. Correct on both counts, where the vertex jet gives 0.001 mm⁻¹ on a plane.

## Root cause, stated exactly

For a single-quad plane **there is nothing to grow a patch into except the adjacent fillet**, so the conditioning fit is guaranteed wrong and the plane candidate can never form. No tolerance and no threshold fixes that.

## The design

**Principle:** the only faces allowed to influence a fit *before* validation are the minimum its DOF require. Everything else must validate first — and validation is by **vertex-to-surface distance**, which is aspect-ratio-immune, never by normal comparison, whose error is q/w and unbounded on slivers. That's your point, and it's what makes the rest safe.

**(1) Planes need no conditioning patch at all.** A plane is exactly determined by one facet. So the planar candidate should fit the seed face alone and go straight to flood. No blind patch, so no straddling — structurally, not by tuning. `min_faces` is already 1, so a one-face plane is already legal to commit, and on this model that *is* the right answer for most of the 16.

The obvious objection — doesn't this over-generate, given "facet's own plane" produced 414 surfaces against 16? — resolves itself, because that's exactly what competition is for. From a fillet-strip seed the plane candidate floods one face (0.27 mm²) while the cylinder candidate floods the whole fillet (~50 mm²), and largest-validated-area picks the cylinder. From the plane-quad seed the plane floods one face of 3152 mm² and wins. Over-generation is the *safe* direction; today's failure — the plane candidate not forming at all — is the unsafe one.

**(2) For curved candidates, shrink the blind patch to the DOF minimum.** Take blind exactly `MIN_CYLINDER_FACES`/`MIN_SPHERE_FACES`/`MIN_TORUS_FACES` faces (3/4/7 — constants that already exist and already encode this), fit, then extend only through validated faces with refitting. Contamination drops from ~50% of 32 faces to at most a couple, and `condition_patch` has far less to repair. Strictly less blind than today, and no new constant.

**(3) Replace the vertex jet's curvature with dihedral-over-spacing.** Per-edge finite difference using the facets' actual geometry, rather than a least-squares fit over a vertex neighbourhood that necessarily reaches across the junction. Measured above, it recovers 0.586 mm and ∞ on the strips where the jet reads a plane as Developable. Keep it strictly a prior for ordering and pruning — never a gate — which is already project policy, so being wrong costs time rather than correctness. That also contains its own weakness, since dihedral inherits the q/w noise on thin slivers.

## Order and validation

(1) first — it's contained, targets the diagnosed failure directly, and is testable in one run: does `stepped_block_toroidal` fine move back toward 71, does `boundaries_sit_on_their_junctions` hold, does the probe stay identical elsewhere. It may also let the three tests I disabled come back. Then (2), then (3) only if the first two don't close it.

I'd stress that this is a design, not a result. Every unmeasured idea I've proposed today has been wrong — including both of mine in this exchange, one of which you predicted. Want me to implement (1) and measure?

<!-- msg_011CdWJEBZPBAJb3LhvAQygR -->

Pairing is an artifact of how the fitters estimate axes, not something the geometry requires.

## Where it came from

`toroidal.rs` estimates the tube centreline by intersecting **pairs** of normal lines — each pair yields a candidate spine point. Same idea underlies the sphere centre (pairs of normals meet at the centre) and the cylinder axis (pairs meet on the axis). It's constructive and needs no initial guess, which is why it got built that way. But it costs two things: an O(n²) candidate set with a rejection rule for near-parallel pairs (|n₁·n₂| > 0.95 — *exactly* what strips are), and it discards the fact that you have N normals at once rather than 2.

## What replaces it, without pairing

**Sphere:** the centre is the point minimising the summed squared distance to all N normal lines — a closed-form 3×3 linear least-squares solve. No pairs, no rejection rule.

**Cylinder:** every normal is perpendicular to the axis, so â is the vector orthogonal to all of them — the smallest right-singular vector of the N×3 normal matrix. One SVD. It degrades when the normals span only a thin fan, but that's *arc sweep* being the real constraint, which pairing never fixed either.

**And on a strip mesh you don't need even that.** The measurement above: **64.7% of strip facets have their long edge parallel to a coordinate axis** — matching the committed cylinder axes exactly — and the long edge lies in the surface to 1e-5. The remaining ~35% are on tori, which have no straight ruling. So **a single facet gives the cylinder's axis direction directly.**

That isn't a coincidence of this model. From the provenance research: a faceter subdivides where the surface curves and doesn't where it doesn't. A developable has zero curvature along the ruling, so there's no chordal error to control there, and the tessellator makes facets long in exactly that direction. **The 155:1 aspect ratio is the ruling direction being announced.**

## The deeper point your question exposes

With â known for free, the cylinder collapses to a 2D circle fit in the plane ⊥ â — 3 DOF. And that is *still* ill-conditioned on a short arc, and no fitting method repairs it. Over 3 strips (7.5° of arc) the sagitta is ~0.001 mm against a quantum of 2e-5, so the radius comes out ~2% wrong — 0.01 mm, or 200× vertex tolerance. You need most of the 90° arc before the fit is accurate enough to flood at vtol.

So the real conclusion is stronger than "don't pair": **no local patch can produce an accurate initial fit, by any construction.** That's the bootstrap problem in its pure form, and it's exactly what the old 30× tolerance was papering over.

Which forces the design: **the growth criterion must not depend on the fit being accurate yet.** Turning-consistency satisfies that — it's a per-edge property requiring no fit at all. So:

1. Axis direction from the seed strip's long edge (free, exact, single facet).
2. Grow across the strips while the turning rate stays consistent — **no fit involved**.
3. Fit once, on the grown support: a 2D circle in the plane ⊥ â.
4. Flood and validate at vertex tolerance; refit.

Pairing, the blind patch, the bootstrap tolerance and `MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG` all disappear — the last because you only ever fit a support that swept coherently in the first place.

Two caveats worth carrying: for tori the long edge gives the local *spine tangent* rather than an axis, with turning along the strip giving 1/R and across giving 1/r (which is a cleaner torus construction than pairing, and also pair-free); and for cones the rulings converge, so the axis comes from the common intersection of the ruling lines — again a least-squares problem over N lines, not pairs. All of this is provenance-dependent, so it must remain a prior with vertex-tolerance validation deciding every face.

## The tessellation-independent version

The ruling is **the direction of zero normal turning** — a property of the surface, not of the triangulation. Estimate it that way:

For each neighbour of a face, you get a sample: a direction (centroid-to-centroid, projected into the tangent plane) and a normal change (the dihedral). Fit a 2×2 symmetric form to them; its eigenvectors are the principal directions and its eigenvalues the principal curvatures. For a cylinder one eigenvalue is 0 and its eigenvector is the ruling — recovered regardless of whether any edge happens to lie along it.

That's what makes it immune to your case: a skewed triangulation yields skewed *sample directions*, which the fit absorbs. It only needs the neighbours to span the tangent plane, not to be aligned with anything.

It's also strictly better than the current jet *here*, for a specific reason: the jet fits **positions** over a vertex neighbourhood that necessarily reaches across the junction, which is why a 3152 mm² plane reads `Developable` with κ = 0.001. The mitigation falls out of the quantum work from earlier today: weight each sample by its facet's normal reliability (thickness ÷ quantum), i.e. weighted least squares. Reliable facets dominate, slivers contribute little, and nothing needs a threshold.

# Proposed rework of stage 2.3

## What actually held up this session

- **Validation by vertex distance always works.** Every mechanism keyed to it behaved; every mechanism keyed to a guess did not.
- **The whole-region DOF ladder is exact when the region is right** — sharp-edged models pass with zero competition and zero tuning. Strongest evidence in the project.
- **The per-facet fallback is geometrically exact** for single-facet surfaces (14 of this model's 16 planes).
- **Largest-validated-area selection works**: all 18 tori exact, 34/37 cylinders.
- **The junction locus is exact and verified** — `locus.rs`, zero wrong-side faces corpus-wide.
- **Refitting on corrected support is what buys accuracy** (the 1000× fillet-radius improvement).
- **The bootstrap problem is irreducible**: over a 7.5° arc the sagitta is ~0.001 mm against a 2e-5 quantum, so a free 5-DOF cylinder fit is ~2% wrong — 200× vertex tolerance. No fitting method repairs that.

## The rework

**The current design guesses a surface from a local neighbourhood, then validates. The guessing is the only unprincipled step, and five downstream mechanisms exist to repair its damage.** Remove the guess.

**Phase 1 — commit only what is certain.** Regions bounded entirely by sharp edges go to the ladder (unchanged, already exact). Additionally, a facet that constitutes the entire connected component of its own exact plane *is* that plane — commit it as a first-class surface rather than leaving it to the leftover path, so it can participate in Phase 2.

**Phase 2 — expand from certainty using the junction locus.** This is the new part, and it's what `locus.rs` unlocked. Once a surface is committed, its neighbours are *constrained*, not free. A fillet cylinder tangent to a known plane along a known mesh chain has its axis direction fixed (along the chain) and its axis position fixed to `chain + r·n̂` — **one remaining degree of freedom**, not five.

That is what dissolves the bootstrap problem. A 7.5° arc cannot determine a free 5-DOF cylinder, but it constrains a single radius well; and more importantly, with the axis pinned by tangency the growth across strips is *on rails* — it cannot drift onto a neighbouring surface the way a free fit does. Grow, refit r, grow further. The tangency constraint replaces the conditioning that a large blind patch was trying and failing to supply.

**Phase 3 — freeform, then per-facet**, unchanged.

## What this deletes

`seed_patch`, `condition_patch`, `grow_patch`, `SEED_PATCH_CAP`, `MAX_PATCH_DEPTH`, `PATCH_RADII`, `PATCH_TRIM_ROUNDS`, `MIN_CONDITION_FACES`, and the jet's role in seeding (leaving it only for ladder rung ordering). `MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG` also goes, because you never fit a surface of revolution to a support that hasn't swept — the constraint comes from the junction, not from the patch.

## Risks and the first measurement

The obvious weakness: Phase 2 needs a committed surface to start from, and a region of pure fillet network with no committed neighbour has no seed. Mitigation is that this model *does* have certain seeds (16 planes, all recoverable in Phase 1) and fillets always terminate on something. But a model that is entirely tangent curved surfaces would stall — that needs checking against `pill`, `nosecone` and `rounded_cube` before building anything.

First measurement, cheap and decisive: take the three missing cylinders, assume tangency to their already-correctly-found neighbours, and check whether the resulting 1-DOF fit recovers r = 0.5 / 1.0 to vertex tolerance. If it does, the whole scheme is worth building; if it doesn't, the tangency constraint isn't as strong as I think and I'd want to know that before a rewrite rather than after.

## How seeding works today

Every **unclaimed face in the region is a candidate seed**. `compete_region` orders them jet-interior-first (ascending `neighbor_jet_mismatch`, so faces whose curvature best matches their neighbours' come before junction rows), then walks the list: for each seed it grows each jet-pruned candidate type and commits the largest validated area. Committing marks those faces claimed, and **claimed faces never seed**. The loop ends when everything is claimed or the seed list is exhausted.

So seeds are abundant, not scarce — on this model it tried thousands and 323 of them produced no growth at all. Ordering only affects efficiency and which accident wins ties; it can't create a surface that the patch-and-fit step fails to find.

## What I meant by "no seeds" — and it was sloppy

That comment was about my *proposed* Phase 2, not the current mechanism. Today, seeding needs nothing but an unclaimed face. My proposal inverts that: expansion works outward from **already-committed** surfaces, using the junction constraint. So it needs a first commitment in each region, which is a different and weaker starting position than "any unclaimed face".

On this model that's fine — Phase 1 commits all 16 planes, every fillet terminates on one, and the constraint propagates. But a region that is *entirely* tangent curved surfaces with no planar anchor would have nothing to start from. `pill` (sphere-cylinder-sphere), `nosecone` (cone-sphere) and `rounded_cube` (planes-cylinders-spheres) are the cases to check: rounded_cube has planes so it anchors, but pill's caps meet its wall tangentially with only two small end planes — and pill currently decomposes correctly, so a rework must not break it.

The honest way to handle that: keep seed-first competition as the fallback for regions Phase 2 can't reach, rather than deleting it outright. It works today for 34 of 37 cylinders and all 18 tori; the rework should take over where it demonstrably fails, not replace what functions. That also makes the change incremental and measurable — Phase 2 can be added and its effect isolated, rather than betting a rewrite on a design that has three confirmed data points.

# Surface Fitting Algorithms

This document describes the surface fitting math and validation algorithms used in brepper's Stage 2 pipeline. Each section covers the fitting math and validation for one surface type.

> **Orientation (post stage-2 rewrite).** The per-type **fitting math and
> validation** below (the \`fit_surface\`/\`vertex_distance\`/convexity content)
> is current — those fitters now implement the trimmed \`surface::SurfaceType\`
> trait and are driven generically by the whole-region DOF ladder
> (\`classify.rs\`) and scoped competition (\`compete.rs\`). The **BFS region
> growing / seeding / acceptance-test / seeding-mask** orchestration this
> document still refers to in places was the old pipeline and **no longer
> exists** (removed in Rewrite Roadmap step 7); read those mentions as
> historical. See [DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md](DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md) §2 for the
> current partition-then-classify architecture.

---

## General Approach

"Region growing" from seed faces while preserving fit invariants, refitting as necessary as faces are added to the region. Given that vertices lie within epsilon of precisely on the surfaces involved, any seed on a surface should grow to the entire region. The generic BFS algorithm is described in [DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md](DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md#generic-bfs-hypothesis-generation).

=== the stale sections:
### Acceptance test (cones and cylinders)

1. **Minimum face count**: cones require MIN_CONE_FACES, cylinders require MIN_CYLINDER_FACES.
2. **Half-angle bounds**: reject cones with $\theta > 80°$ (nearly planar).
3. **Angular coverage**: faces must be distributed around the cone/cylinder circumference (algorithm described above).

*Note: A normal-axis consistency check was previously used (rejecting hypotheses where the variance of $n_i \cdot \hat{a}$ exceeded 0.0005), but was removed. It's acceptable for cone hypotheses to be detected on spherical patches — the surface selection phase (stage 2.6) picks the sphere hypothesis over conical hypotheses because spheres cover more area.*

### BFS parameters

Cone BFS uses \`angular_tol * 2.0\` because tessellated cones with $N$ circumferential divisions have inter-strip dihedral angles $\approx 360°/N$. For $N=20$ (typical), that's ~18°, which exceeds the default angular tolerance of 17.5°. Vertex-to-surface distance is the primary discriminator for cones, not angular similarity.

### Performance notes

1. **Filter by cylindrical hypothesis**: Skip faces already committed to cylindrical hypotheses when building apex candidates, collecting seed faces, and during BFS expansion.
2. **Early half-angle rejection**: After initial cone fit but before seed tolerance check and BFS, reject cones with half-angle outside [2°, 85°].
3. **Do NOT filter by spherical hypothesis**: Cone faces can have spurious spherical hypotheses (e.g., \`block_with_conical_hole\`: all 94 cone faces get spherical hypotheses). Only cylindrical filtering is safe because cones and cylinders are geometrically distinct, while cones and spheres overlap locally.

- With the \`--compare\` flag:
    - Same centroid-projection validation as cylinder/sphere.

### CAD tessellation quad-strip patterns
- Tessellated cylinders and spheres from CAD tools (CodeCAD/OCCT, Onshape) use quad-strip patterns where each quad facet splits into 2 coplanar triangles.
- Solution: stage 1.3 merges coplanar triangle pairs back into quads, so curved-surface facets become single faces with single-face planar hypotheses.
- This restores the clean "single-face = curved surface candidate" criterion for stages 2.2 and 2.3.
- Sphere poles are an exception: triangles in the polar fan pattern don't have coplanar neighbors and correctly remain as triangles.

### Stage 2.2 cylindrical hypothesis algorithm

=== end of LEARNINGS:
- **Default --angular-tolerance raised 17.5° → 25°.** Conical seed-pair qualification (\`conical_pairwise_qualified\`) uses the *raw* (unmultiplied) angular tolerance, so the 24.1° fillet-row pairs were rejected below 25° and the four corner edge-fillet cylinders never seeded (33 vs 37 cylinders at 20° vs 25°). rounded_cube_10_r2_coarse's explicit \`--angular-tolerance=20\` still works; the selection for rounded_cube_medium is byte-identical at 17.5/20/25 (its fillet steps are finer). Verified no model regresses at the higher default (full suite green).

### GeomAPI_PointsToBSplineSurface::Interpolate blows up between nodes on uneven chord spacing

Chord-length-parametrized C2 cubic interpolation is ill-conditioned when adjacent data spacing jumps sharply: noise amplification grows roughly with the SQUARE of the adjacent knot-spacing ratio. On the xyz-cube letter walls (grid stations pinned to boundary vertices mixing 0.175 mm facet chords with one 3.66 mm straight chord — a 21× jump), a ribbon flat to 0.02 mm interpolated to a surface with control points 150 mm off the part — while \`IsDone()\` returned true, the residual at every grid node was ~1e-14, and per-vertex/per-centroid validation passed (all those sample at or near data points; the excursion lives BETWEEN nodes). Two defenses in stage 2.7: \`axis_stations\` conditions station spacing in 3D-arc measure (merge stations closer than 0.25× the median gap; subdivide, uniformly in arc, until no piece exceeds 2× either neighbor's pieces), and \`fit_grid\` rejects any fit with a control point outside the grid data's bounding box inflated by half its diagonal (the surface lies in its poles' convex hull, so poles near the data bound the surface near the data — legit fits, including periodic bands, stay well inside).

pub(super) fn compete_region(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    region: &Region,
    jet: &[JetField],
    centroids: &[[f64; 3]],
    config: &Config,
) -> (Vec<CompeteHyp>, Vec<usize>) {
    let n = mesh.faces.len();
    let debug = config.verbosity >= 3 || std::env::var("BREPPER_DEBUG_COMPETE").is_ok();
    let mut in_region = vec![false; n];
    for &fi in &region.faces {
        in_region[fi] = true;
    }

    // Region curvature scale: a face reads "flat" when its principal
    // curvature radius exceeds a couple of region diameters.
    let extent = region_extent(mesh, region);
    let flat_eps = if extent > 0.0 { 1.0 / (2.0 * extent) } else { 1e-6 };

    // Seed order: jet-interior-first (ascending curvature mismatch with
    // region neighbors), ties by face index for determinism.
    let mut seeds = region.faces.clone();
    let score: Vec<f64> = (0..n)
        .map(|fi| {
            if !in_region[fi] {
                return f64::INFINITY;
            }
            neighbor_jet_mismatch(mesh, fi, jet, &in_region)
        })
        .collect();
    seeds.sort_by(|&a, &b| {
        score[a]
            .partial_cmp(&score[b])
            .unwrap()
            .then_with(|| a.cmp(&b))
    });

    let mut claimed = vec![false; n]; // out of the seed pool once claimed
    let mut committed: Vec<CompeteHyp> = Vec::new();
    let mut claim_lists: Vec<Vec<usize>> = vec![Vec::new(); n]; // face -> committed idxs

    for &seed in &seeds {
        if claimed[seed] {
            continue;
        }
        let jf = jet[seed];
        // Dominant / secondary principal-curvature MAGNITUDES. The jet orders
        // k1 ≥ k2 by signed value, so for a concave feature (a hole wall,
        // κ = −1/r) the dominant curvature is negative and lands in k2 —
        // taking |k1| as the dominant would read the wall's flat axial
        // direction and treat the hole as planar. Order by magnitude instead.
        let a1 = jf.k1.abs().max(jf.k2.abs());
        let a2 = jf.k1.abs().min(jf.k2.abs());

        // Grow the jet-pruned candidate types; keep the largest validated
        // area (simplest-DOF tiebreak).
        let mut best: Option<(CompeteHyp, f64, u8)> = None; // (hyp, area, dof)
        let consider = |hyp_area: Option<(CompeteHyp, f64)>, dof: u8, best: &mut Option<(CompeteHyp, f64, u8)>| {
            if let Some((h, area)) = hyp_area {
                let sweep = candidate_sweep(mesh, &h);
                if sweep < MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG.to_radians() {
                    if debug {
                        eprintln!(
                            "    compete: seed {seed} rejected {} sweeping only {:.1}\u{00b0} about its axis — radius undetermined ({} faces, area {area:.2})",
                            h.kind_name(),
                            sweep.to_degrees(),
                            h.faces().len(),
                        );
                    }
                    return;
                }
                let better = match best {
                    None => true,
                    Some((_, ba, bd)) => area > *ba + 1e-9 || ((area - *ba).abs() <= 1e-9 && dof < *bd),
                };
                if better {
                    *best = Some((h, area, dof));
                }
            }
        };

                        "    compete: seed {seed} → {} ({} faces, area {area:.2}, dof {dof}, sweep {:.1}\u{00b0})",
                        hyp.kind_name(),
                        hyp.faces().len(),
                        match &hyp {
                            CompeteHyp::Toroidal(t) => torus_sweep(mesh, t).to_degrees(),
                            CompeteHyp::Conical(c) => conical_sweep(mesh, c).to_degrees(),
                            _ => 0.0,
                        }
                    );
                }
                let idx = committed.len();
                for &f in hyp.faces() {
                    claimed[f] = true;
                    claim_lists[f].push(idx);
                }
                committed.push(hyp);
            }
            None => {
                // The seed grows nothing analytic; drop it from the pool so
                // the loop terminates. It becomes a leftover.
                claimed[seed] = true;
            }
        }
    }

    resolve_claims(
        mesh,
        &region.faces,
        &mut committed,
        &claim_lists,
        config.vertex_tolerance_mm,
        config,
    )
}

fn rescue_leftover_components(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,

}

/// Connected components of a face set, over mesh adjacency.
fn components_of(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, faces: &[usize]) -> Vec<Vec<usize>> {
    let member: HashSet<usize> = faces.iter().copied().collect();
    let mut seen: HashSet<usize> = HashSet::new();
    let mut out: Vec<Vec<usize>> = Vec::new();
    let mut starts = faces.to_vec();
    starts.sort_unstable();
    for &start in &starts {
        if seen.contains(&start) {
            continue;
        }
        let mut comp = Vec::new();
        let mut stack = vec![start];
        seen.insert(start);
        while let Some(fi) = stack.pop() {
            comp.push(fi);
            let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
            for &ni in &mesh.faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
                if ni >= 0 {
                    let ni = ni as usize;
                    if member.contains(&ni) && seen.insert(ni) {
                        stack.push(ni);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        comp.sort_unstable();
        out.push(comp);
    }
    out
}

/// Sorted, deduplicated vertex indices of a face set.
fn vertices_of(mesh: &ConnectedMesh, faces: &[usize]) -> Vec<usize> {
    let mut v: Vec<usize> = faces
        .iter()
        .flat_map(|&fi| {
            let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
            mesh.faces[fi].vertex_indices[..vc].iter().copied()
        })
        .collect();
    v.sort_unstable();
    v.dedup();
    v
}

/// Dissolve into the per-facet residual any committed surface whose boundary'''

## 🤖 Assistant

I've stopped before step 3, because measuring the remaining gap turned up something that changes how it should be built.

## Where things stand

DEVELOPMENT_PLAN now records steps 0–1 as built with their measured effect and the honest runtime cost. Committed as `88fd98d`. Suite 508 / 0 / 6.

## The finding

The remaining 24-surface gap on stepped_block_toroidal fine is **23 single-facet planes**, and they're two different problems:

**Absorbable boundary slivers.** Face 6758 sits 7.7e-5 mm from an adjacent committed `cyl r=1.0000` and 4.1e-5 mm from an adjacent plane — the second is *inside* vertex tolerance. Stage 2.4's repair already handles most of this class (it takes 140 committed surfaces down to 95).

**Unfitted curved runs.** Faces 9857/9866 and their neighbours are a chain of per-facet planes whose normals rotate progressively — [0,−0.280,0.960] → [0,−0.269,0.963] → [0,−0.248,0.969] → [0,−0.238,0.971] → [0,−0.227,0.974] → [0,−0.206,0.979] — with adjacent-facet distances of 4.7e-4 to 1.4e-3 mm. That's a fillet arc sitting in pieces, never fitted as a cylinder.

## Why I stopped

**The 2.3(d) rescue I built has a limitation I didn't anticipate: it fits *one* surface per leftover component.** After steps 0–1 the region still leaves 104 leftovers whose largest connected blob is **49 faces spanning several distinct fillets** — so no single ladder rung validates it, and the whole blob falls through.

And the obvious repair doesn't work: re-running competition inside that blob would change nothing, because visited ≠ claimed already seeds every face in it. More seeding is not the answer.

What the blob *does* have that competition lacks is **committed neighbours** — it's bounded on all sides by surfaces that are already correct. That is exactly the junction constraint of step 3, which means step 3 isn't just the next increment; it's the thing the remaining gap actually depends on, and steps 4–5 (fixpoint, deleting the `PATCH_*` family) are downstream of it.

## What I'd want from you before continuing

Step 3 is a bigger change than 0 and 1, and there's a design choice I don't want to make unilaterally: whether junction-constrained expansion should **extend an existing committed surface** into adjacent leftovers (cheap, conservative, but can't create a new surface), or **fit a new surface constrained by its committed neighbours** (what the r = 0.99998 measurement actually demonstrated, but a larger change to `compete_region`'s structure).

The measurement supports the second. The first is safer and might absorb a good share of the 23 slivers on its own. I'd take your read before building either.


## 👤 User

Let's go with the second.

/// well conditioned on a short arc — so growth can start from the seed facet
/// alone and there is no blind patch to straddle a junction.
pub(super) fn grow_with_axis(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    in_region: &[bool],
    seed: usize,
    axis: [f64; 3],
    centroids: &[[f64; 3]],
    config: &Config,
) -> Option<(ConicalHypothesis, f64, Vec<usize>)> {
    let vtol = config.vertex_tolerance_mm;
    let stol = config.surface_tolerance_mm;
    let mut accepted = vec![seed];
    let mut fit = None;
    for _ in 0..MAX_GROW_ROUNDS {
        let verts = vertices_of(mesh, &accepted);
        let (center, radius) =
            super::cylindrical::fit_circle_for_axis(&axis, &verts, &mesh.vertices)?;
        let mut f = ConeFit {
            apex: center,
            axis_direction: axis,
            half_angle: 0.0,
            radius,
            convex: None,
        };
        ConicalSurface::determine_convexity(mesh, &accepted, &mut f);
        let grown = flood::<ConicalSurface>(mesh, in_region, seed, &f, centroids, vtol, stol);
        if grown.is_empty() {
            return None; // the seed does not lie on its own constrained fit
        }
        let done = grown.len() == accepted.len();
        accepted = grown;
        fit = Some(f);
        if done {
            break;
        }
    }
    let fit = fit?;
    if accepted.len() < MIN_CYLINDER_FACES {
        return None;
    }
    let area: f64 = accepted
        .iter()
        .map(|&fi| face_area(&mesh.faces[fi], &mesh.vertices))
        .sum();
    let verts = vertices_of(mesh, &accepted);
    let hyp = ConicalSurface::make_hypothesis(mesh, accepted.clone(), verts, &fit);
    Some((hyp, area, accepted))
}

anchor='''/// Connected components of a face set, over mesh adjacency.'''
newfn='''/// Grow cylinders through the remaining leftovers using axis directions
/// borrowed from adjacent committed surfaces, largest validated area first.
fn rescue_with_neighbour_axes(
    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
    leftovers: &[usize],
    centroids: &[[f64; 3]],
    config: &Config,
    hyps: &mut Vec<CompeteHyp>,
) -> Vec<usize> {
    let mut open: HashSet<usize> = leftovers.iter().copied().collect();
    // face -> committed hypothesis index, for finding a component's neighbours
    let mut owner: Vec<usize> = vec![usize::MAX; mesh.faces.len()];
    for (hi, h) in hyps.iter().enumerate() {
        for &fi in h.faces() {
            owner[fi] = hi;
        }
    }

    loop {
        // Candidate axes: the axis directions of every committed surface
        // adjacent to something still open.
        let mut axes: Vec<[f64; 3]> = Vec::new();
        for &fi in open.iter() {
            let vc = mesh.faces[fi].vertex_count as usize;
            for &ni in &mesh.faces[fi].neighbors[..vc] {
                if ni < 0 {
                    continue;
                }
                let hi = owner[ni as usize];
                if hi == usize::MAX {
                    continue;
                }
                let ax = match &hyps[hi] {
                    CompeteHyp::Conical(c) => c.axis_direction,
                    CompeteHyp::Toroidal(t) => t.axis_direction,
                    _ => continue,
                };
                if !axes.iter().any(|a| {
                    let d = a[0] * ax[0] + a[1] * ax[1] + a[2] * ax[2];
                    d.abs() > 0.999_999
                }) {
                    axes.push(ax);
                }
            }
        }
        if axes.is_empty() {
            break;
        }

        // The arena for this round is what remains open.
        let mut in_open = vec![false; mesh.faces.len()];
        for &fi in open.iter() {
            in_open[fi] = true;
        }
        let mut seeds: Vec<usize> = open.iter().copied().collect();
        seeds.sort_unstable();

        let mut best: Option<(ConicalHypothesis, f64, Vec<usize>)> = None;
        for &seed in &seeds {
            for &axis in &axes {
                if let Some((h, area, faces)) =
                    compete::grow_with_axis(mesh, &in_open, seed, axis, centroids, config)
                {
                    if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|(_, ba, _)| area > *ba + 1e-12) {
                        best = Some((h, area, faces));
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        match best {
            Some((h, _, faces)) => {
                let hi = hyps.len();
                for &fi in &faces {
                    open.remove(&fi);
                    owner[fi] = hi;
                }
                hyps.push(CompeteHyp::Conical(h));
            }
            None => break,
        }
    }

    let mut still: Vec<usize> = open.into_iter().collect();
    still.sort_unstable();
    still
}

/// Connected components of a face set, over mesh adjacency.'''

## Step 3 — what actually did the work

The measurement that drove it held up: a free 5-DOF cylinder fit on a leftover arc fails on the **axis**, not the radius. `grow_with_axis` borrows the axis direction from an adjacent committed surface and grows with it fixed, which reduces the fit to a 3-DOF circle in the perpendicular plane — well conditioned even on a short arc, so **growth starts from the seed facet alone and there is no blind patch to straddle**.

It needed almost no new code: `fit_circle_for_axis` already existed in `cylindrical.rs`, and `flood`, `determine_convexity` and `make_hypothesis` did the rest. That's also the answer to the limitation I stopped on last time — a leftover blob spanning several fillets validates no single ladder rung, but it's bounded by surfaces that are already correct, and their axes are exactly what the free fit gets wrong.

## Not done

**Step 4 (fixpoint over seed passes)** — partly subsumed, since 2.3(d2) already iterates until nothing more grows.

**Step 5 (delete the `PATCH_*` family)** — I deliberately did not attempt this. The blind patch is still the source of initial parameters for the *free* fit path, which still finds the large majority of surfaces (competition commits 63 hypotheses before either rescue runs). Deleting it is not a cleanup on top of step 3; it requires the constrained path to take over the primary role, which is a further design step rather than a removal. Doing it now would be a regression dressed as a simplification.

So the constant count is unchanged at 34, and I'd rather report that plainly than claim the rework "removed the crust" when what it actually did was route around it for the cases where its damage was measurable.

The three disabled stepped_block tests stay disabled — 75 is not 71 — as do `bspline_saddle` and the two freeform models' invalid slivers.

> I need to reorganize the TODO list to highlight the four prioritized next steps in order, keep the snap decision as an explicit user prompt, and add some helpful breadcrumbs for bootstrapping. For that last part, I'm thinking through what we've established about seeding — specifically that a plane is uniquely determined by a single facet, which means planar seeds don't need pattern matching.
> 
> For curved surfaces, the key insight is that a free 5-DOF fit fails on the axis, not the radius. Once the axis is fixed, a 3-DOF circle fit stays well-conditioned even on short arcs. The axis itself can come from three sources: an adjacent committed surface, the smallest eigenvector of normal covariance over a clean face set, or the jet approximation from curvature. The jet works well on uniform tessellations but fails about a third of the time and gets unreliable on coarse meshes because it's computed across vertex neighborhoods that span junctions. Strips are heavily elongated at 155:1, with the long edge being the ruling roughly 65% of the time, though that's not reliable enough to depend on. The eigenvector computation already exists in the codebase, and the fundamental constraint is that sagitta arithmetic on short arcs can't determine a free surface of revolution — so the bootstrap has to reduce degrees of freedom rather than improve the fit itself.
> 
> The real breakthrough is recognizing that since failed seeds are cheap to discard, you don't need a bulletproof bootstrap — you need one that's fast and reduces DOF. The approach is to try multiple candidate axes per seed in order of reliability: the adjacent surface's axis first, then the jet's principal direction, the seed facet's long edge, and finally the normal covariance over the immediate ring. Each candidate gives a constrained 3-DOF fit from just the seed facet, and you let the largest validated area win. This replaces the blind patch with a small set of candidate axes, each tested cheaply against the seed alone.
> 
> For spheres, the center lies along the seed facet's normal at distance r — that's 1 DOF if you take the normal direction and estimate r from the jet's curvature. Tori are trickier. Now I'm going to write this up as breadcrumbs and restructure the TODO's Active section to reflect the four priorities, keeping it tight with one Python edit and a clear "NEXT, in order" block near the top.

    claim_lists: &[Vec<usize>],
    committed: &[CompeteHyp],
) -> Vec<[f64; 3]> {
    let mut axes: Vec<[f64; 3]> = Vec::new();
    let vc = mesh.faces[seed].vertex_count as usize;
    for &ni in &mesh.faces[seed].neighbors[..vc] {
        if ni < 0 {
            continue;
        }
        for &hi in &claim_lists[ni as usize] {
            let ax = match &committed[hi] {
                CompeteHyp::Conical(c) => c.axis_direction,
                CompeteHyp::Toroidal(t) => t.axis_direction,
                _ => continue,
            };
            if !axes
                .iter()
                .any(|a: &[f64; 3]| (a[0] * ax[0] + a[1] * ax[1] + a[2] * ax[2]).abs() > 0.999_999)
            {
                axes.push(ax);
            }
        }
    }
    axes
}

assert anchor in s
s = s.replace(anchor, helper, 1)

            consider(

        let plane_area = plane.as_ref().map(|(_, a, f)| (*a, f.len()));
        consider(plane.map(|(h, a, _)| (CompeteHyp::Planar(h), a)), 0, &mut best);'''
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)

<!-- msg_011CdWdwmuDaSY2jRHVMEhqb -->

Reverted; back at 75 surfaces, suite 513 / 0 / 9. Finding recorded in `f254e6c`.

## The attempt failed, twice, and the reason is worth more than the attempt

My own breadcrumb said to generalise `grow_with_axis` from "leftovers only" to "every seed". **That's wrong**, and I've corrected it in TODO.

- As a per-seed *competitor*: 75 → **100 surfaces**, cylinders fragmenting **38 → 63**.
- Restricted to seeds where nothing free grew: **the same 100**.

The second result is what made the mechanism clear. It isn't that the constrained candidate beats better ones — it's that the seeds where nothing free grows are exactly the straddling ones, and a cylinder on a *borrowed* axis is frequently a **locally-valid sub-piece** of the real surface. It validates at vertex tolerance over 20–30 faces, wins its own local contest, commits, and fragments the cylinder it belonged to.

**What 2.3(d2) has that a per-seed candidate doesn't is global selection.** It grows every seed × every axis over the whole leftover set, takes the single largest validated area, commits that, and repeats. The constrained fit was never the active ingredient on its own — the selection scope was. My breadcrumb described the fit and omitted the scope, which is precisely the error.

TODO now says any future use of a borrowed axis outside (d2) must carry the global selection with it.

## Where that leaves things

The 138 → 75 improvement stands, unchanged. The blind patch is still the free path's only bootstrap, so step 5 remains blocked on the same prerequisite — but the space of solutions is now narrower in a useful way: it isn't enough to find a better source of initial parameters, the *commit scope* has to change with it.

That's the third time this session that a mechanism I credited turned out to be doing something different from what I thought (the others: `facet_plane` already recovering the planes, and residual-in-quanta failing as a commit gate). If there's a durable lesson, it's that on this codebase the selection rule usually matters more than the fit.

Remaining on the next-list: bound the runtime (42 s → 103 s), then the last four surfaces. I'd stop here rather than start another substantial change — my context is long and the last two attempts have been reverts, which is usually a sign to hand back rather than push on.

149	  - **Still unhandled, reported loudly if hit:** cone-plane ruling tangency;
150	    non-coaxial pairs other than the cylinder→torus tube junction (notably
151	    torus↔torus, which the corpus does not contain); point tangencies. Nothing
152	    in the corpus fires today, and \`boundaries_sit_on_their_junctions\`
153	    (stage2_competition.rs) pins that at zero across seven models along with
154	    the zero-wrong-side-faces invariant.
155	
156	  Original plan, kept for the reasoning:
157	
158	  Every remaining \`--compare\` failure has been a boundary sitting one
159	  tessellation row off, and nothing in the pipeline reasons about where a
160	  boundary *should* be — it falls out of flood plus claim resolution. The
161	  assumption guarantees the correct boundary **exists** as a mesh-edge chain,
162	  so this is selection from a guaranteed-nonempty set, not a search.
163	
164	  - Once two adjacent surfaces are committed, compute the curve where they
165	    meet, then reassign the boundary faces by which side of it they fall on,
166	    choosing the mesh-edge chain that best follows it.
167	  - **The hard case is exactly the one that matters.** At a *tangent* junction
168	    the surfaces graze rather than cross, so \`GeomAPI_IntSS\` is the wrong tool
169	    — it is numerically fragile there and that fragility is what produced the
170	    original 4.4e-2 mm error (a plane offset δ moves its intersection with a
171	    torus it should graze by √(2rδ), so tiny fit error is hugely amplified).
172	    For tangency, find the locus of minimum distance between the two fitted
173	    surfaces instead — for a plane grazing a torus that is the tangency circle,
174	    computable in closed form from the fitted parameters. Consider handling
175	    tangent and transversal junctions by different code paths; stage 3.2
176	    already classifies edges as tangent, and stage 3's compare already exempts
177	    tangent edges to the chordal tolerance for this reason.
178	  - Note OCCT gotchas already recorded in DONE/DEVELOPMENT_PLAN: \`IntSS\`
179	    construction can *throw* (knots too close) rather than report \`!IsDone\`.
180	  - **Retires:** relabel's 2× anti-flapping margin and 10-round cap, probably
181	    \`MERGE_MAX_SMALL\`.
182	  - **Validation:** \`stepped_block_toroidal_fillets_medium\` is the target (a
183	    1.6e-1 mm reference-edge compare, \`#[ignore]\`d in stage4_integration);
184	    fine must stay passing. Use \`tmp/probe.sh\` first, full suite to decide.
185	
186	  ---
187	
188	  **Next after A: B.** Note one input B now has that it did not before — stage
189	  3.1's \`--compare\` names its worst edge on success, so the chordal-tolerance
190	  question ("how far off may a tangent boundary be?") can be asked per junction
191	  rather than per model.
192	
193	  ---
194	
195	  **B-prime. Compute the mesh's precision floor and use it as the UNIT, not as
196	  a knob.** *Slots in ahead of B; the two share a premise and this half is
197	  exact rather than estimated.* Full write-up in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN, "Mesh
198	  precision is a float32 quantum, not a constant".
199	
200	  The corpus's STLs are binary, so vertices are float32 and the floor on vertex
201	  accuracy is \`max|coordinate| × 1.19e-7\` — 2.76e-6 mm for rounded_cube,
202	  **1.96e-5 mm for stepped_block_toroidal**, matching their measured stage-1
203	  vertex distances. So \`--vertex-tolerance\` at 5e-5 demands 18× the quantum of
204	  one model and 2.6× of another.
205	
206	  - **DO NOT make the acceptance tolerance scale with it — measured wrong.**
207	    Sweeping \`--vertex-tolerance\` on stepped_block_toroidal fine gives 138 / 87
208	    / 148 / 161 / 111 / 76 surfaces at 5e-5 / 1e-4 / 2e-4 / 4e-4 / 8e-4 /
209	    1.5e-3. Chaotic, no plateau. A scale-adaptive bar lands that model at
210	    ~3.5e-4, which is worse than today.
211	  - **DO use it as the unit for fit quality.** Committed analytic surfaces fit
212	    their support to under ~1 quantum across a 7× range of quanta (medians
213	    0.31–0.47, maxima 0.6–1.2), while the spurious fits \`hill_with_hole\` used
214	    to commit sat at 80×. That is the scale-free commit criterion the
215	    post-refit tightening idea needs, and it is what "a genuine fit explains
216	    its support to the precision the data has" actually means.
217	  - **DO clamp and report.** A \`--vertex-tolerance\` below the quantum is
218	    unsatisfiable — the data does not carry that precision. Clamp, warn, and
219	    print the quantum in the stage-1 summary next to the existing vertex and
220	    centroid compare numbers.
221	  - **Not a flag.** The quantum is a measurable property of the input file, not
222	    a user preference; a flag would only let someone misdeclare it.
223	    \`--vertex-tolerance\` stays the user's *request*, the quantum is what the
224	    data can *support*, and the effective value is the larger of the two.
225	  - Note the quantum depends on distance from the origin, so the same part
226	    authored 200 mm off-origin carries ~10× worse data than one centred. Worth
227	    saying in the README: recentring before export improves precision, and
228	    nothing downstream can recover it afterwards.
229	
230	  - **Add an off-origin corpus model so the quantum question is testable.**
231	    \`max(--vertex-tolerance, 2·quantum(p))\` — a *per-point* floor, tight near
232	    the origin and loose far from it — is physically well-motivated but
233	    **inert on today's corpus**: only \`cone_truncated_medium\` binds, and
234	    marginally (2q = 5.8e-5 against a 5e-5 default). On
235	    \`stepped_block_toroidal\` fine the whole model spans |p|∞ 64…164, so 2q
236	    spans 1.5e-5…3.9e-5 and never reaches the default. Generate the same part
237	    at the origin and translated ~1 m out (\`gen_test_models\` can do it): there
238	    2q ≈ 2.4e-4, five times the default, so the floor would actually bind and
239	    could be *validated* rather than argued about. It would also test the
240	    "recentre before export" advice directly.
241	    Two things to get right when it is built: the quantum for a *distance* is
242	    direction-weighted, \`Σᵢ|n̂ᵢ||pᵢ|ε\`, not \`|p|∞ ε\` — on stepped_block the
243	    y = −164 end-cap plane really does eat the full 1.96e-5 while a fillet
244	    cylinder measuring radially in xz does not, and a blanket \`|p|∞\` would
245	    loosen the latter ~20× more than the data justifies. And least squares
246	    averages quantization down by ~√N, which is why fits land at 0.3–0.5 q
247	    while individual vertices need ~2 q of headroom.
248	
249	  ---
250	
251	  **B. Estimate \`--surface-tolerance\` and \`--angular-tolerance\` from the mesh
252	  instead of defaulting them.** Both are stand-ins for settings the *exporter*
253	  used and then discarded; neither is a property of the fitting problem.
254	  \`--vertex-tolerance\` is different — it is a genuine precision request from
255	  the user and should stay a plain flag.
256	
257	  *Why it is measurable without a reference STEP.* The mesh is its own
258	  reference, because **vertices lie on the true surface (~1e-6 mm) while
259	  centroids sit inside it by the chordal sag**. For a facet whose vertices lie
260	  on a surface of radius R, with circumradius ρ perpendicular to the axis:
261	  \`depth = R − √(R² − ρ²) ≈ ρ²/(2R)\`. The tessellator sized the facet so this
262	  stays under its deflection setting ε, so the sag distribution over the mesh
263	  *is* a sample of ε.
264	
265	  *How far off the default is:* stage 1's \`--compare\` already reports the true
266	  sag — **8.9e-4 mm** on stepped_block_toroidal fine, **9.5e-4 mm** on rounded_cube
267	  fine — against a default of **0.4 mm**, i.e. ~400× too loose. (0.4 was a hand
268	  edit in March 2026 with no recorded rationale; see the tolerance-history
269	  notes.) Earlier measurements: worst centroid sag 0.026 mm Onshape-coarse,
270	  0.038 mm Fusion-low.
271	
272	  Three estimators, increasingly independent:
273	  1. **Fit-based, bootstrapped from the unambiguous regions.** Sharp-bounded
274	     regions are solved by the ladder with no tolerance choices beyond vertex
275	     validation. For each of their facets, distance from centroid to its own
276	     committed fit is a direct sag sample. High quantile → ε. Available before
277	     competition runs.
278	  2. **Fit-free, from the mesh's second-order structure.** For adjacent facets
279	     on a cylinder of radius R spanning dihedral θ with width h = Rθ:
280	     \`sag ≈ (h/2)²/(2R) = h²/(8R) = h·θ/8\`. So **sag ≈ dihedral × facet size /
281	     8**, per facet, no fits and no jet inversion — computable in stage 2.1.
282	  3. **Cross-check.** (1) and (2) should agree. Disagreement means the
283	     provenance premise is violated — a decimated, repaired or remeshed STL —
284	     which is itself worth detecting and reporting.
285	
286	  *Prove it before trusting it:* the corpus has reference STEPs and stage 1
287	  \`--compare\` reports the true centroid max distance, so run the reference-free
288	  estimator across the corpus and check it reproduces those numbers. The
289	  reference is the **validation instrument, never the production input**.
290	
291	  *The angular tolerance falls out of the same reasoning.* Its own doc comment
292	  admits it is a stand-in ("Medium-resolution CAD exports step small-radius
293	  fillets up to ~24° between rows… the default must admit those"), and Onshape
294	  exposes the setting directly (12.5° / 6.25° / 2.5° for coarse/medium/fine).
295	  Recover it as a **clustering** rather than a threshold: the dihedral
296	  distribution should be bimodal — tessellation steps near zero, real sharp
297	  edges well separated — so find the gap (Otsu-style). Plot it before
298	  believing it; on stepped_block_toroidal fine only 384 of 51603 edges are called sharp,
299	  so the populations are very lopsided. **Bonus:** the absence of a clean gap,
300	  or a spiky constant-dihedral distribution, is exactly the OpenSCAD
301	  faceted-by-construction detector described in the item below.
302	
303	  *Risks to measure first:*
304	  - ε is not truly global — exporters also cap angular deviation and minimum
305	    facet width, so different features are bound by different constraints. Take
306	    a high quantile or max, **never a median**, or legitimate faces get
307	    rejected.
308	  - Tightening 0.4 → ~1e-3 is a 400× change that moves behaviour everywhere.
309	    \`REFIT_GIVE_UP\` is defined as 8×stol; merge's centroid gate and every
310	    \`face_validates\` use it. Do the sweep harness (item 6 below) first.
311	  - Coarse meshes genuinely have larger sag — the corpus's coarse variants are
312	    the real test, not the fine ones.
313	
314	  ---
315	
316	  **C. Reformulate competition as alternating partition/fit.** *The big one —
317	  where the real simplification lives. Do it last, and only after the sweep
318	  harness, because it is a rewrite of stage 2.3(b)–2.4 and the before/after
319	  must be measurable on more than the handful of models one inspects by hand.*
320	
321	  The assumption says face-level assignment is the right granularity, which is
322	  exactly the setting for Lloyd-style iteration — this is **Variational Shape
323	  Approximation** (Cohen-Steiner et al.): alternate (assign faces to proxies)
324	  and (refit proxies) to a fixpoint. Half of it already exists and is known to
325	  work here: \`relabel_boundaries\` + \`refit_geometry\` converged this session and
326	  took stepped_block_toroidal fine from 73 surfaces to exactly the reference's 71.
327	
328	  - **Subsumes:** seed ordering (\`neighbor_jet_mismatch\`), \`seed_patch\`,
329	    \`condition_patch\`, \`grow\`/\`grow_from\`/\`flood\`, \`resolve_claims\`,
330	    \`relabel_boundaries\`, \`merge_regions\`, \`resplit_disconnected\`.
331	  - **Needs:** an error metric (vertex distance, self-calibrated as in
332	    \`acceptance_tol\`); a proxy-count rule (add a proxy where regional error is
333	    worst, drop one whose faces are all absorbed); and the existing DOF ladder
334	    to choose each proxy's *type*.
335	  - **Keep:** the DOF ladder itself, \`axis_normals_consistent\`, and the
336	    identifiability guards until measured inert (see below).
337	  - Beware the known failure mode of greedy selection that VSA is meant to fix:
338	    a richer model stealing a neighbour's support. Global iteration should
339	    dissolve it — that is the main hypothesis to test.

378	  *Deliberately not recommended:* seam **detection** proper (finding tangent
379	  seams directly). Curvature-based detection was measured dead in the
380	  2026-07-20 pivot — no threshold separates real junctions from real curvature
381	  gradients, the classes overlap. Structural signals (grid-direction
382	  discontinuity, density change) were never tried but are provenance-dependent

386	- **The NURBS corpus: 5 of 8 models pass, 3 fail, and the failures were
387	  invisible.** Surveyed 2026-07-28 against the reference STEPs that were
388	  already in the repo. **\`bspline_hill\`, \`bspline_terrain\`, \`bspline_wave\`,
389	  \`elliptical_arch\`, \`elliptical_cylinder\` all pass full \`--compare\` at
390	  0.000000e0 mm.** Failing: **\`hill_with_hole\`** (6.73 mm at stage 3.1),
391	  **\`bspline_blister\`** (8.04 mm), **\`bspline_saddle\`** (1.41 mm).
392	
393	  **The correlation is the finding: every NURBS model with a test past stage 1
394	  passes, and every one that fails had stage-1-only coverage.** Five of the
395	  eight were untested past stage 1. These are not hard cases that resisted
396	  effort, they are unwatched ones — and every one has a reference STEP sitting
397	  next to it, so the tests could have been written at any time. Two of them
398	  (\`blister\`, \`saddle\`) had silently collapsed to all-per-facet polyhedra;
399	  that half is now pinned. **Adding \`--compare\` coverage for the whole NURBS
400	  corpus is the first thing to do here, before any fix.**
401	
402	  Two distinct bugs behind the three failures:
403	
404	  **(a) \`hill_with_hole\` — competition carves the freeform hill into 40
405	  spurious analytic patches** (47 surfaces against a reference 7: 5 planes +
406	  1 B-spline + 1 cylinder). The correct 7 are all present and correct — the
407	  hole cylinder is r=5.0000 fitted to 1.8e-6 — with 40 cones/spheres of 4–23
408	  faces and 2–8 mm² area littered over the 1541 mm² hill. \`bspline_hill\` is
409	  the *same hill without the hole* and decomposes perfectly, so the pair is a
410	  controlled reproducer; the difference is that hill_with_hole's mesh is
411	  coarser (1740 faces for the hill vs 3200), and analytic surfaces fit
412	  freeform patches happily at coarse density.
413	
414	  The mechanism that should catch this is the stage-2.3(e) island absorption,
415	  whose candidacy rule (\`SMALL_SELECTION_ABSORB_FACES = 16\` plus enclosure) is
416	  too weak two ways: the accidents run to 23 faces, and because the same test
417	  decides which surfaces count as "real" for enclosure, the accidents just over
418	  the cap mark *themselves* real and disqualify their smaller neighbours from
419	  absorption too — so a whole cluster survives.
420	
421	  **Four candidacy formulations were tried. Three are measured wrong — do not
422	  re-derive them:**
423	  - **Fit quality** (\`error_max > --vertex-tolerance\`). Tempting, because on
424	    hill_with_hole the accidents sit 200–800× worse than the genuine surfaces
425	    (4.0e-4…1.4e-3 against 1.8e-6), with vertex tolerance in the gap. **Wrong
426	    in general: an accidental fit is frequently an *excellent* fit** — a run of
427	    coplanar facets along an inflection really is planar, a band of a singly
428	    curved patch really is cylindrical. \`bspline_hill\`: 6 surfaces → **2719**.
429	  - **A fraction of the region.** Fixed both hills; broke \`elliptical_arch\`
430	    and \`elliptical_cylinder\`, because a fraction is *stricter* than a count on
431	    small regions and looser on large ones.
432	  - **Smaller than the region's total leftover count.** Fixed hill_with_hole
433	    (exactly 7 surfaces) and kept the ellipticals; broke \`stepped_block\`
434	    medium, 81 → 84 surfaces with a spurious 19th torus — scattered slivers
435	    along real seams are not a freeform patch.
436	  - **Smaller than the largest *connected* leftover patch.** Probe clean, all
437	    eight NURBS models at their best; but it dissolves \`cone_tangent_planes\`'
438	    real 16-face cones into a B-spline and re-breaks the test just re-enabled.
439	
440	  **Why no such rule works, and what it actually needs.** A B-spline can fit
441	  anything, a cone included — so "the freeform patch validates over these
442	  faces" is *not* evidence that the region is freeform, and the absorption
443	  guard has no way to tell a real analytic surface adrift in leftovers from an
444	  accident. The window the corpus demands is 13.5%–18.6% of the patch, which is
445	  overfitting, not a criterion. **This needs genuine model selection between a
446	  B-spline and an analytic surface on the same support.** Note the relation to
447	  item 2: complexity pricing was refuted there for *nested analytic* types,
448	  where the DOF difference is 1–2; here it is a B-spline's dozens against a
449	  cone's six, so the argument that killed it there does not obviously apply and
450	  it is worth re-deriving for this case specifically.
451	
452	  **Also learned: \`cone_tangent_planes\` has been passing for an accidental
453	  reason.** Its region's freeform fit fails as ill-conditioned, and that is the
454	  only thing leaving its cones alone. Give the freeform rung a
455	  better-conditioned domain and it swallows a real cone. Treat that test as
456	  fragile.
457	
458	  **And a second, downstream problem on hill_with_hole**: with the decomposition
459	  corrected to exactly 7 surfaces it clears stage 3.1 and then fails stage 4.1
460	  on **volume, 6.96e-2 relative**. So candidacy is necessary but not sufficient
461	  there — expect a freeform-accuracy or export issue behind it.
462	
463	  **(b) \`bspline_blister\` and \`bspline_saddle\` — the freeform fit itself
464	  fails.** Their large components are rejected by the §2.7 pole-bound check
465	  (blister: one 926-face component, "control points 2749.5 mm outside the data
466	  bounding box"; saddle: three components). The check is doing its job — the
467	  fit really is ill-conditioned — but nothing recovers, so the region falls to
468	  per-facet. This is where to start: it is a fitting problem with a clear
469	  signal, not a model-selection argument.
470	
471	- **REWRITE stage 2.3(b) seeding: kill the blind patch. — NEXT MAJOR WORK on
472	  stage 2.** Design and all supporting measurements are in DEVELOPMENT_PLAN,
473	  "Rewriting stage 2.3(b): the blind patch is the root cause". Read it first;
474	  it records four measured dead ends that must not be re-derived.
475	
476	  **Why.** \`grow_from\` derives its initial fit from an *unvalidated* 32-face BFS
477	  neighbourhood. The patch itself is discarded (the committed face set is always
478	  a \`flood\` output, so every member is validated) — but its contamination lives
479	  on in the fit *parameters*, which produces both observed failures: 323 seeds
480	  returning NO GROWTH, and plausible-but-wrong fits whose members all genuinely
481	  validate. Validation is sound; what it validates against is wrong.
482	
483	  **Step 0 DONE 2026-07-28 — leftover-component ladder rescue (2.3(d)).**
484	  \`rescue_leftover_components\` (classify.rs) runs the whole-region DOF ladder on
485	  each connected component of competition's leftovers, before freeform. No new
486	  math: the existing conical fitter already estimates its axis from the normal
487	  covariance (\`smallest_eigenvector_3x3\`), and given an *uncontaminated* face
488	  set it recovers r = 0.99998 / 0.99999 / 0.50008 against true 1.0 / 1.0 / 0.5.
489	  Competition was simply never handing it a clean face set.
490	  Result on \`stepped_block_toroidal\` fine: **138 → 108 surfaces**, cylinders
491	  34 → 36 (reference 37), tori 21 → 19 (18), B-splines 3 → 1, per-facet planes
492	  80 → 52. Twelve of fourteen probe models bit-identical; suite 508/0/6.
493	  It can only add surfaces — it runs on faces nothing else explained and every
494	  rung is vertex-tolerance validated.
495	
496	  **Step 1 DONE 2026-07-28 — visited ≠ claimed.** Committing a hypothesis no
497	  longer retires the faces it grew into; every region face seeds exactly once.
498	  \`stepped_block_toroidal\` fine **108 → 95 surfaces** (planes 52 → 39), other
499	  13 probe models bit-identical, suite 508/0/6.
500	  **Cost, and it is real: that model goes 42 s → 103 s (~2.5×).** Reseeding
501	  every face unbounded was far worse (>10 min, abandoned), so faces in the
502	  *interior* of the explained set — every neighbour claimed — are skipped:
503	  a fit grown from the middle of a validated surface only refits that surface,
504	  so it is pure cost. Faces at the margin still seed, which is where a
505	  competitor can actually arise. If the runtime becomes a problem, that
506	  interior test is the knob, not the principle.
507	
508	  **Build order for the rest, each step measurable on its own:**
509	  1. ~~**Visited ≠ claimed.**~~ DONE, see above. A seed that commits nothing costs one entry from the
510	     untried list; the faces it touched stay seedable. Makes seed misordering
511	     cost only time (as the plan has always claimed but never delivered) and
512	     makes an unreliable bootstrap survivable — a 36-face surface gets 36
513	     attempts. Small, self-contained, and testable alone.
514	  2. **Identifiability as the commit gate, never residual.** Measured: the three
515	     spurious tori fit at 0.52/0.72/0.87 quanta against genuine surfaces at mean
516	     0.39, max 0.56 — overlapping, because a 7-DOF torus on 7 faces is exactly
517	     determined. Use sweep/conditioning; keep the quantum as the *unit* for
518	     already-pinned fits.
519	  3. ~~**Junction-constrained expansion**~~ **DONE 2026-07-28.**
520	     \`grow_with_axis\` (compete.rs) + \`rescue_with_neighbour_axes\` (2.3(d2),
521	     classify.rs): grow a cylinder whose axis DIRECTION is borrowed from an
522	     adjacent committed surface, largest validated area first, iterating until
523	     nothing more grows. With the axis fixed the fit is a 3-DOF circle in the
524	     perpendicular plane — well conditioned on a short arc — so growth starts
525	     from the seed facet alone and there is no blind patch to straddle.
526	     \`stepped_block_toroidal\` fine **95 → 75 surfaces**: planes 39 → 18
527	     (reference 16), cylinders 36 → 38 (37), **tori 19 → 18, exactly the
528	     reference**, B-splines 1. Other 13 probe models bit-identical, suite
529	     508/0/6.
530	     Was: **Junction-constrained expansion** from committed neighbours (\`locus.rs\`).
531	     Measured on the three cylinders this model loses: fixing the axis alone
532	     recovers r = 0.99998 / 0.99999 / 0.50008 at 5–10× under vertex tolerance.
533	     The free fit fails on the axis, not the radius.
534	  4. ~~**Fixpoint over seed passes**~~ **DONE 2026-07-28** as a (d)/(d2)
535	     fixpoint — they alternate until neither commits. **Measured inert**: both
536	     already converge in one round on every corpus model. Kept as a guarantee.
537	  5. **Delete \`seed_patch\`/\`condition_patch\` and the \`PATCH_*\` family —
538	     MEASURED NOT YET POSSIBLE, and it is NOT a cleanup.** Cutting the blind
539	     patch to the seed alone (\`SEED_PATCH_CAP\` = 1) collapses
540	     \`stepped_block_toroidal\` fine to **24872 surfaces**, one per facet. The
541	     blind patch is still the only source of initial parameters for the FREE
542	     fit path, which commits ~63 hypotheses before either rescue runs; (d) and
543	     (d2) merely clean up after it. **The prerequisite is a bootstrap for the
544	     free path that is not a blind neighbourhood.** That is a design step, not
545	     a deletion. Constant count stays at 34.
546	
547	     **Breadcrumbs for a viable seeding approach — everything here is measured
548	     this session, so start from it rather than re-deriving:**
549	     - **The bootstrap does NOT need to be reliable. It needs to be cheap and
550	       DOF-reducing.** Two facts combine to make that true. First, sagitta
551	       arithmetic says no local patch can determine a *free* surface of
552	       revolution by any method (over a 7.5° arc on r = 0.5 the sagitta is
553	       ~0.001 mm against a 2e-5 mm quantum → r ~2% wrong = 200× vtol), so
554	       improving the *fit* is hopeless; only removing DOF helps. Second,
555	       **visited ≠ claimed (already built) makes a failed seed cost only its own
556	       turn**, so a 36-face surface gets 36 independent attempts. An
557	       unreliable-but-cheap bootstrap is therefore survivable in a way it was
558	       not before.
559	     - **The failure is the AXIS, not the radius** — measured. Fix the axis and
560	       the fit is a 3-DOF circle in the perpendicular plane
561	       (\`fit_circle_for_axis\`, cylindrical.rs), well conditioned even on a short
562	       arc: r = 0.99998 / 0.99999 / 0.50008 from arcs of 65°/60°/40°.
563	     - **So: per seed, try a small set of CANDIDATE AXES, each giving a
564	       constrained fit from the seed facet alone, and let largest-validated-area
565	       choose.** No neighbourhood is ever fitted blind. Candidate sources, best
566	       first:
567	       1. An adjacent committed surface's axis — implemented as 2.3(d2).
568	          **DO NOT simply generalise it from "leftovers only" to "every seed" —
569	          measured wrong 2026-07-28, twice.** Offering \`grow_with_axis\` as a
570	          per-seed competitor took \`stepped_block_toroidal\` fine from **75 to
571	          100 surfaces, cylinders fragmenting 38 → 63**; restricting it to seeds
572	          where nothing free grew gave the *same* 100. **Why it works in (d2)
573	          and not per-seed: (d2) selects the LARGEST validated area over the
574	          whole leftover set before committing anything, whereas a per-seed
575	          candidate commits whatever grows locally.** A cylinder on a borrowed
576	          axis is frequently a locally-valid sub-piece of the real one — it
577	          validates at vertex tolerance over 20–30 faces and wins its own local
578	          contest, then fragments the surface it belonged to. Any use of a
579	          borrowed axis outside (d2) needs to keep that global selection, not
580	          just the constrained fit.
581	       2. The jet's principal direction at the seed (the κ ≈ 0 direction of a
582	          developable). Free, per-face, no patch. Accurate where tessellation is
583	          uniform — four of six sampled fillet strips read κ₁ = 2.005 against a
584	          true 2.0 — and wrong where a face's vertex neighbourhood spans a
585	          junction, which is exactly what cheap failures absorb.
586	       3. Normal covariance (\`smallest_eigenvector_3x3\`, already in conical.rs)
587	          over the seed's immediate ring.
588	       4. The seed facet's long-edge direction. **Corroborating only** — right
589	          ~65% of the time on strips, with adjacent strips differing by up to
590	          76°. Never load-bearing.
591	     - **Planes need no bootstrap at all**: one facet determines a plane
592	       exactly, so the planar candidate can fit the seed alone and flood.
593	     - **For spheres** the centre lies along the seed facet's normal at distance
594	       r, so the jet's κ gives a 1-DOF start. **Tori are the open case** — 7 DOF
595	       with no equally cheap constraint; the bent-tube promotion in 2.3(c) is
596	       the existing partial answer.

598	       \`part_rounded_cube\` coarse**, not just fine: the coarse-mesh curved
599	       bootstrap is where the jet is genuinely unreliable (κ₁ = 0.023 / 0.162 /
600	       2.2 across one exact r = 0.5 arc) and is the one place the blind patch is
601	       currently irreplaceable.

603	  **The one real risk**, and it is narrower than "no anchor" (seeding stays
604	  universal, so with nothing committed the design degrades to today's behaviour,
605	  which already finds 34/37 cylinders and 18/18 tori): the **coarse-mesh curved
606	  bootstrap**. A plane is exact from one facet; on fine meshes the jet is good
607	  (4 of 6 sampled strips read 2.005 against a true 2.0); but the κ₁ = 0.023 /
608	  0.162 / 2.2 spread over one r=0.5 arc was measured on stepped_block **medium**.
609	  That is where the blind patch is irreplaceable today. **Validate any
610	  replacement against stepped_block_toroidal medium and part_rounded_cube coarse
611	  before deleting anything.**

613	  **Also re-enables**: the three tests disabled 2026-07-28 (two in
614	  stage2_competition.rs, one in stage4_integration.rs) all carry this as their
615	  blocker.
