231	### Surface Seed Requirements
232	
233	A surface is discovered by growing a **seed set** — a set of facets that is the
234	entire initial fit support — under validation, refitting as it grows. There is no
235	separate unvalidated "patch": the seed set is what the first fit sees.
236	
237	A **facet chain** is a set of facets forming a path in the dual graph: each facet
238	shares an edge with the next, and each has at most two neighbours within the set.
239	(This section previously called it a "non-contiguous facet chain", which
240	contradicted its own definition — a set whose members share edges is contiguous.)
241	
242	* **Plane:** any facet of the surface. *Measured: 99.9% of plane facets have a
243	  working seed; 98.7% of plane faces have one for every facet.*
244	* **Cylinder:** a facet chain of at most 4 facets with **exactly 6 distinct
245	  vertices**. Measured, exactly three shapes reach 6 — two quads, four triangles,
246	  or two triangles and a quad — and the rule works: **94.1%** of cylinder facets
247	  have a working seed. Two quads on a cylinder give 6 vertices against 5 DOF, so
248	  there is one redundant constraint, which is what pins the right root.
249	* **Cone:** the same chain, or three triangular facets sharing one vertex (the
250	  candidate apex). The apex alternative earns its place — it is the *least*
251	  working rule for 21% of cone facets, cases the chain cannot reach. But the cone
252	  is the weak type: **49.4%** of cone facets have a working seed under these
253	  rules, and 22% have none at any support size up to 48 facets. The cause is the
254	  fitter, not the rule — see Surface Identification.
255	* **Sphere:** the seed facet plus every facet sharing an edge with it (and the
256	  same ring taken about each of its neighbours). *Measured: **100.0%** of sphere
257	  facets and **100.0%** of sphere faces. This rule is exactly right as written.*
258	* **Torus:** the closed ring of facets about one vertex — its **vertex star** —
259	  grown outward while the seed set's own fit does not yet validate the whole seed
260	  set. Typically 4–12 facets, occasionally up to 32.
261	* **NURBS:** fallback for the connected leftovers nothing analytic explains.
262	
263	**Why a torus needs a star rather than a chain.** A torus's normal lines cross the
264	axis at a point that *slides with the tube angle*, so a seed confined to one tube
265	angle cannot pin the axis — and two quads along the major direction is exactly
266	that, which is why a 6-vertex chain is under-determined for a torus. A vertex
267	star wraps a grid node, so it spans both parametric directions by construction.
268	Measured, the least support that works per torus facet: bare star 40%, the union
269	of the anchor's own vertex stars a further 25%, and the rest need 8–48 facets,
270	with 0.8% never working. Requiring the ring to **close** matters: complete stars
271	win 40% of facets, boundary-cut ones 4%.
272	
273	**The "no more than three coplanar" clause is deleted.** It was aimed at a real
274	degeneracy — a fan of facets sharing a vertex, which on a cylinder leaves the apex
275	free along a line — but as a detector it is useless and as a filter it is
276	destructive. Measured over 27 984 six-vertex chains: it rejects **85.3%** of the
277	chains that produce a good axis while catching only 39.8% of those that produce a
278	bad one. Worse, a fused quad is coplanar *by construction* — that is why it was
279	fused — so the clause rejects, by definition, every seed containing one: 99.7% of
280	2-quad chains and 92.4% of 2-triangle-plus-quad chains. And four vertices spanning
281	two rulings of a cylinder lie on two parallel lines, hence in a plane, so it also
282	bites the ruling-aligned triangle strips that Phase 1.0 measured as the *good*
283	ones. Excluding only the wholly-coplanar chains changes the worst axis error not
284	at all (90° either way).
285	
286	**The "not effectively planar" clause is deleted.** A large-radius cylinder that
287	validates every vertex is a valid explanation of the data; preferring the plane is
288	a matter of ladder order, which stage 2.3 already has (simplest DOF first), not of
289	a radius threshold.
290	
291	**Seed admissibility, replacing the combinatorial clauses.** A seed set is valid
292	for type T iff:
293	
294	1. \`fit_T(seed)\` exists, and
295	2. every facet of the seed set validates that fit at vertex tolerance.
296	
297	Nothing about connectivity, vertex counts, or coplanarity. Measured over 87 510
298	seed sets: seeds failing this grow to the right surface **0.4%** of the time;
299	seeds passing it, **84.6%**. It is the fixpoint condition of growth itself,
300	evaluated at round 0 — \`S ⊆ flood(fit(S))\` is the round-0 case of
301	\`F = flood(fit(F))\` — so admission and termination are one predicate at two
302	scales, and it introduces no new constant.
303	
304	**Seed sets need not be connected**, and requiring it would make things worse:
305	measured, disconnected seeds stall on 0.67% of attempts against 2.46% for
306	connected ones, and the best-performing shape was two small balls at the two most
307	distant points of the surface — which is also the well-conditioned shape for an
308	axis (Phase 1.0's amplification law). The chain rules above are stated as chains
309	because that is what the corpus supplies, not because connectivity is required.
310	
311	### Surface Identification
312	
313	For every analytic surface in the reference, growth from some admissible seed
314	finds that surface — **subject to an identifiability precondition**, which is the
315	part this section previously left out.
316	
317	**A wrong type frequently explains a true support exactly, and the residual does
318	not discriminate.** Measured on the true facet set of each reference face:
319	
320	| true type | a wrong type also validates at vtol |
321	|---|---|
322	| cylinder | sphere on **496 of 652**; torus on 307 |
323	| cone | sphere on 64 of 91; torus on 32 |
324	| plane | sphere on 322 of 1261; cyl/cone on 126 |
325	
326	The impostor residuals sit at 0.2–0.5 float32 quanta — the same order as the
327	correct type's. **The tie-break this section used to propose is refuted, and
328	points the wrong way:** on **393 of 397** true cylinders the impostor sphere fits
329	the cylinder's own facets *better* than the cylinder does, median 0.555× the
330	residual. \`simple_cylinder\` shows why in one line: its 32-quad band has vertices
331	on exactly two circles, and two circles lie exactly on a sphere — residual
332	2.07e-7 mm, machine precision. This is identifiability, not model selection, and
333	the distinction is the one already drawn in stage 2.3.
334	
335	So type discrimination stays structural: ladder order (simplest DOF first),
336	largest validated area, and identifiability guards such as
337	\`MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG\`. Never a comparison of residuals between types.
338	
339	**The cone is the type where identification currently fails**, and the cause is
340	the fitter rather than the information. On \`simple_cone\`, a two-quad seed whose six
341	vertices determine the cone to **0.0001°** (two rings of three spanning 31.3°;
342	circumcircle radii to 0.1–0.2× vtol) produces a \`fit_cone\` half-angle of **2.54°**
343	against a true 9.4623°. \`axis_normals_consistent\` correctly refuses that, and the
344	fallback cylinder then misses its own seed vertices by 222.7× vtol. Of the cone
345	rung's refusals, 42% are the axis-normal check, 27% a half-angle outside
346	[2°, 85°], 12% an apex 429–2128 mm from a 41 mm model. The guards are right; the
347	initialization is not. Options are catalogued in SURFACE_FITTING.md, "Cone
348	initialization: the options not yet built".
349	
350	**One genuinely non-identifiable case exists** and is worth knowing: on one
351	\`simple_cone\` seed the fitter returned a half-angle 72.85° cone with its apex 10.8
352	patch-extents away that explains the six vertices to 6.7e-16 mm — *better* than
353	the true cone manages against a float32 mesh. Six points admit more than one right
354	circular cone. It is the exception (8 of 9 cone failures are convergence, not
355	identifiability), but it bounds what any optimizer can be asked to do.
356	
357	Because a NURBS surface can have sub-surfaces that fit other types (a cylindrical
358	strip around an ellipsoid's equator), NURBS identification is left out of these
359	invariants.
360	
361	### Surface Seed Independence
362	
363	Stated existentially, which is the right quantifier for an algorithm that gets to
364	*choose* its seeds:
365	
366	> **For every facet of a surface there is at least one admissible seed set
367	> containing that facet whose growth covers the surface.**
368	
369	Not "every admissible seed set works" — that is a much stronger claim and it is
370	false (34.9% of surfaces under the current seeding, 80.6% under the clean
371	operator). Measured with the section's own seed rules, growth limited only by
372	validation:
373	
374	| type | facets with a working seed | faces where every facet has one |
375	|---|---|---|
376	| sphere | **100.0%** | **100.0%** |
377	| plane | 99.9% | 98.7% |
378	| cylinder | 94.1% | 86.4% |
379	| cone | 49.4% | 26.8% |
380	| torus (star only) | 65.4% | 22.4% |
381	| torus (star, grown) | **99.2%** | **99.2%** |
382	| **all** | **89.7%** | |
383	
384	### Growth Independence
385	
386	Two halves, and only the second is empirical.
387	
388	**The flood is order-independent by construction.** Given a fixed fit, the grown
389	set is *defined* as the connected component of \`{facets validating the fit}\`
390	containing the seed — a set, not a traversal. Confirmed at **0 differences over
391	18 429 seeds** with the neighbour iteration reversed. This half is a theorem and
392	should be stated as one.
393	
394	**The refit fixpoint is start-dependent.** Growth is the iteration
395	\`F ← flood(fit(F))\`, which is neither monotone nor a contraction. Starting it from
396	the whole true face set instead of a seed reproduces the truth on 83.0% of faces,
397	and 648 of 1285 faces disagree between the two starts. Where the invariant needs
398	defending, this is where.
399	
400	### Coverage and boundary invariants
401	
402	Two invariants the earlier version of this section omitted, both of which the
403	per-surface clauses above permit violating:
404	
405	* **Partition.** Every mesh facet belongs to exactly one committed surface, and
406	  every surface is mesh-connected. Already enforced by \`assert_invariants\` in
407	  stage 2.4, and stated here because the per-surface clauses do not imply it.
408	* **Boundary.** Growth may **overshoot** — cover the surface and a collar beyond
409	  it — and every overshoot facet must belong to an adjacent surface that explains
410	  it strictly better. Measured, this holds identically: **100%** of overshoot
411	  facets land in a reference-adjacent face and **100%** of the scorable ones are
412	  closer to their true owner than to the fit that claimed them. Overshoot is
413	  small everywhere except fillet tori (median |result|/|truth| 1.000 for plane,
414	  cylinder, cone and sphere; torus median 1.019, p95 1.117).
415	
416	  This is why the growth invariant must be stated as *covers*, not *equals*.
417	  Scored per reference face over admissible seeds, requiring equality reads
418	  **80.6%** and requiring coverage **88.9%** — and the torus is essentially the
419	  whole difference, 16.8% against 60.8%. The boundary decision then belongs to a
420	  comparison between two surfaces, which is what \`resolve_claims\` already is, and
421	  it is handed exactly the information the clause promises.
422	
423	### Measuring these (\`--invariant-report\`, \`--viz-seeds\`)
424	
425	\`src/stage2/invariants.rs\`, diagnostics only — nothing downstream reads it. Runs
426	after stage 2.2, where the jet and the smooth regions exist and the mesh is still
427	untouched, so it works on models whose decomposition crashes or times out.
428	
429	- \`--invariant-report --compare ref.step\` scores the five families above, one TSV
430	  row per reference face on stdout plus a per-model summary on stderr.
431	  \`tools/invariants.sh\` sweeps the corpus (sharing \`sweep.sh\`'s model/reference
432	  pairing so the two instruments cover the same models); \`tools/inv_analyze.py\`
433	  aggregates.
434	- \`--viz-seeds\` walks anchor facets interactively and stops on those where *every*
435	  conforming seed set fails: seed green, covered blue, overshoot red, the true
436	  facets that blocked growth orange, missed yellow, anchor white. The status line
437	  names the failing clause.
438	- Env-gated probes: \`BREPPER_INV_FITDUMP=1\` prints the reference's own parameters
439	  beside the fitted ones for any seed that fails admission, with a
440	  NOT-IDENTIFIABLE / CONVERGENCE verdict from their sum-squared residuals;
441	  \`BREPPER_INV_BASIN=1\` sweeps the clean operator's basin of attraction;
442	  \`BREPPER_INV_PATCHSIZE=1\` measures fit accuracy against support size.
443	
444	**One reporting trap worth recording.** \`face_validates\` is a conjunction of
445	*three* tests — vertex distance, centroid distance, orientation coherence — and a
446	diagnosis naming only the first is actively misleading: 7% of seeds refused by
447	their own fit pass the vertex test and die on centroid or orientation. Every
448	verdict names its clause for that reason.
449	
450	### Open questions
451	
452	Answered by measurement:
453	
454	- *Do we need quad fusion?* Not for the invariants to hold, but it matters for
455	  conditioning: quad fusion is a 23× discriminator for ruling alignment (2.7% of
456	  fused quads straddle against 62.3% of triangles), and the edge-midpoint bound
457	  needs a quad's diagonals to be sound.
458	- *How do we test these without exponential search?* Seed independence is
459	  existential and per-facet, so the space is \`facets × conforming seeds per
460	  facet\` — polynomial, and sampled deterministically at a fixed stride. Growth
461	  independence needs no search at all for the flood half (it is a theorem) and
462	  randomised round-orders for the rest.
463	- *How well do they hold at finite precision?* The tables above. The short answer
464	  is that plane, cylinder and sphere hold well, the torus holds once its seed is
465	  allowed to grow, and the cone does not hold — for a reason that is a fitter
466	  defect rather than an invariant that needs weakening.
467	
468	Still open:
469	
470	- **Whether the sharp partition belongs in the growth invariant at all.** Growth
471	  confined to a smooth region cannot cover a surface the partition has cut, and
472	  stage 2.1 cuts 68 true surfaces on 350 edges (see 2.1(a)). Unconfined growth
473	  covers those but runs across tangent junctions instead. Neither bound is right
474	  as stated.
475	- **A cone seed rule that works**, which needs the fitter fixed first.
476	- **NURBS**, deliberately excluded above.
477

625	
626	**Status (2026-07-20): fit-driven pivot — the SECOND revision of the

664	**Pipeline:** sharp-edge classification + jet prior (2.1) → smooth-region
665	extraction (2.2) → per-region surface discovery: whole-region ladder, then
666	scoped fit competition with model promotion (2.3) → resolution & repair
667	(2.4) → emit selected surfaces (2.5).
668	
669	**The division of labor** (the load-bearing rule, Design Principle #4):
670	the jet prior allocates effort — seed order, rung order, initial
671	parameters, refit triggers — and **never decides membership or
672	boundaries**; vertex-tolerance fit validation decides all geometry. Every
673	jet error therefore converts to wasted or saved time, never to wrong
674	output.

679	#### 2.1 Sharp edges + jet curvature prior
680	
681	Two products, both deterministic, both cheap (O(N·ring), single pass —
682	the classification fixpoint is gone; nothing iterates on classification
683	anymore).
684	
685	**(a) Sharp-edge classification — the only *decision* this stage makes.**
686	A manifold edge is BOUNDARY when its dihedral angle exceeds
687	\`--angular-tolerance\`; everything else is INTERIOR. The default 25° stays
688	above the tessellator's maximum dihedral step on smooth surfaces (coarse
689	fillets step ~24°/row). This rule is measured-exact on the corpus: every
690	sharp-edged analytic model segments perfectly by it alone (cube 6,
691	block_with_hole 7, pipe 4, two_holes 8, spherical_pocket 7,
692	chamfered_cube 26, cone_15x20 2, simple_cone 3 — one pass, no knobs
693	beyond the user-facing tolerance). The fit-free *curvature-jump* rule
694	that used to accompany it is retired (evidence in the Retrospective's
695	Resolution; autopsy in Abandoned Approaches): tangent junctions are found
696	by stage 2.3's fit competition instead.
697	
698	**But "measured-exact" is exact only in the direction that was measured**
699	(2026-08-06, \`--invariant-report\`). Sharp edges never *miss* a true face
700	boundary — that is the seam assumption, and it holds. They do introduce
701	boundaries that are not there: this rule calls **350 edges sharp strictly
702	inside 68 reference faces**, cutting those true surfaces in two before any
703	fitting happens. The largest clusters are coarse exports whose angular step
704	exceeds the default — Fusion's "Low" preset is 30° against a 25° tolerance, so
705	every coarse Fusion cylinder is cut into 12 pieces — and small fillet tori
706	(\`filleted_pipe\`'s two big tori take 11 sharp interior edges each, at an
707	interior dihedral of 31.4°). Stage 2.4's repair sews most of them back, which is
708	why the corpus looks fine and why the effect was invisible until something
709	measured per-face coverage. Consequences: \`--angular-tolerance\` must exceed the
710	exporter's own angular setting (the stage-1 dihedral p95 recovers it on
711	curvature-dominated meshes), and a growth invariant that confines growth to a
712	smooth region cannot cover a surface this rule has cut — see **Invariants**,
713	"Open questions".
714	
715	**(b) The jet curvature prior — data for 2.3, never a decision.** Each
716	face carries the differential summary of an **anchored osculating jet**
717	(Cazals & Pouget SGP 2005 — the standard robust curvature estimator for
718	irregular meshes): a quadratic height field \`z = Q(u,w)\` fitted to vertex
719	*positions* over a PCA tangent frame of the face's own + 1-ring vertex
720	neighborhood. Three properties make it robust to how CAD models are
721	actually triangulated (each was forced by a measured corpus failure):
722	
723	- **It uses vertex positions** — exact f32 mesh data — not normals. A long
724	  skinny strip/sliver triangle's plane is a chord whose normal can sit
725	  several degrees off the true tangent, so normal-based estimators inherit
726	  that error; positions are ground truth. The fit is tessellation-layout
727	  agnostic (aspect-ratio slivers, staggered rows, pole fans, strip meshes).
728	- **The tangent frame comes from a PCA of own + 1-ring vertices, not the
729	  facet normal** — the smallest-variance direction of the neighborhood IS
730	  the local normal and stays accurate on strips. Own vertices dominate the
731	  frame (weight \`OWN_WEIGHT\`).
732	- **The face's own vertices anchor the fit** (weight \`OWN_WEIGHT = 50\`).
733	  Tessellators never straddle a B-rep boundary with a triangle, so a face's
734	  own corners always lie on its own surface. There is **no outlier
735	  rejection** (rejection forces arbitrary one-side reads that vary face to
736	  face — measured); sharp-crease neighbors are excluded from the point set,
737	  and tangent-junction mixing is allowed — junction rows read intermediate
738	  values, which is fine because no decision ever keys on them.
739	
740	*Estimator history, for context:* per-edge κ = θ/d failed on irregular
741	tessellation (the centroid distance doesn't measure arc length in the
742	rotation direction — the 65:1 sliver fillet of rounded_cube_10_r2_fine
743	read ~100× low and fragmented ~50×). The neighbor-normal tensor fixed
744	strips and slivers but deadlocked on balanced-mix junction rings
745	(stepped_block's blend zones). The jet subsumes both — as a *measurement*;
746	as a junction *detector* the whole family is dead (see Resolution).
747	
748	**Per-face prior contents** (\`JetField\`, on \`Segmentation\`):
749	- \`(κ1, κ2)\` — signed principal curvatures (jet Hessian eigenvalues;
750	  positive convex). Few-% accurate on region interiors; contaminated on
751	  junction rows (by design — the anchor mixes).
752	- Principal directions — the Hessian's eigenvectors lifted to 3D in the
753	  PCA frame. The κ≈0 direction is a cylinder/cone ruling; the κ1
754	  direction wraps a tube.
755	- The PCA normal, and the **medial point** \`centroid + n̂/κ1\` (defined when
756	  \`|κ1|\` clears the noise floor) — a curvature-center / tube-center
757	  estimate feeding torus initialization and bent-tube promotion.
758	
759	**Type signatures the prior predicts** (used ONLY to order and prune work
760	in 2.3): plane (0,0); cylinder (κ,0), κ locally constant; cone (κ,0), κ
761	drifting along the ruling; sphere (κ,κ); torus (κ1 constant around the
762	tube, κ2 varying, sign change past the inner equator); anything else →
763	freeform-ish.
764	
765	Output: \`EdgeClassification\` (sharp classes + counts) and \`JetField\`,
766	both on \`Segmentation\`, consumed by 2.3 and by diagnostics/viz.
767	
768	#### 2.2 Smooth-region extraction
769	
770	Connected components of the face graph over INTERIOR (non-sharp) edges
771	(union-find; deterministic numbering by smallest member face index). A
772	**smooth region** is a maximal set of faces reachable without crossing a
773	sharp edge. On sharp-edged models it IS the final segmentation; on models
774	with tangency it is a *chain of tangentially-joined surfaces* that 2.3
775	decomposes — e.g. the capsule is ONE smooth region (both caps tangent to
776	the wall), a rounded cube's entire outer shell is ONE smooth region, the
777	nosecone is TWO (the cone+sphere tangent chain; the base disk), and the
778	pipe elbow's tube surface is ONE (torus bend tangent to both straight
779	pipes).
780	
781	Output (in \`Stage2Output.segmentation\`):
782	- \`face_region: Vec<usize>\` — exactly one region per face (total coverage
783	  by construction).
784	- \`regions: Vec<Region>\` — member faces + member vertices.
785	
786	Regions are connected by construction. There is no minimum size: a single
787	facet is a valid region.
788	
789	**Diagnostics** (report-only at this stage): with \`--compare\`, sample
790	midpoints of sharp BOUNDARY edges and check distance to the nearest
791	reference STEP *edge* (within \`--surface-tolerance\`); report region counts
792	vs reference face counts. Smooth-region counts are NOT expected to match
793	reference face counts on tangent models — that match is 2.3/2.4's job.
794	
795	#### 2.3 Per-region surface discovery
796	
797	Decompose each smooth region into its true surfaces. Two mechanisms, in
798	order; both decide membership exclusively by fit validation.
799	
800	**Validation (used everywhere, decisive by Design Principle #1):**
801	- Every claimed vertex within \`--vertex-tolerance\` of the surface.
802	- Every claimed face centroid within \`--surface-tolerance\` (chordal
803	  sagitta ≈ h²/8R stays well inside for real tessellations).
804	- Orientation coherence: every face normal agrees in sign with the surface
805	  normal at its centroid — this determines the hypothesis \`convex\` flag and
806	  replaces the old per-face BFS convexity checks.
807	- Numeric-validity guards retained from the fitters (fit-domain
808	  constraints, not selection heuristics): cone half-angle in [2°, 85°],
809	  torus \`0 < r ≤ R\`, sphere radius ≤ 1000× bounding-box diagonal.
810	- **Sub-tolerance features**: when the fitted curvature radius is below
811	  \`--surface-tolerance\` (3DBenchy has r=0.2mm cylinders against the 0.4mm
812	  default), centroid checks are vacuous at that scale; validate by vertex
813	  tolerance alone and mark the region (stage 3's chain validation shares
814	  the blind spot — see TODO, face-5841 family).
815	
816	**(a) Whole-region ladder.** Try to explain the ENTIRE region with one
817	surface, ascending DOF; the first fit that validates wins. Simplest-first
818	resolves degeneracy (any plane also lies on an infinite-radius cylinder; a
819	single facet is exactly a plane) without coverage heuristics.
820	
821	| Rung | Surface | DOF | Fit (see SURFACE_FITTING.md) |
822	|------|---------|-----|------------------------------|
823	| 1 | Plane | 3 | Area-weighted normal average |
824	| 2 | Sphere | 4 | Algebraic LSQ + Gauss-Newton |
825	| 3 | Cylinder | 5 | Normal-covariance axis + 2D circle fit + LM |
826	| 4 | Cone | 6 | Two-path (pointed/truncated) + LM; the existing code fits cylinder and cone together and this rung keeps that dual-fit internally, preferring the cylinder when both validate |
827	| 5 | Torus | 7 | Medial-axis tube-center + SOR axis + LM |
828	
829	The **jet signature orders and prunes the rungs** (a (κ,κ) region tries
830	sphere first; (0,0) tries plane; a failed prediction falls through to the
831	remaining rungs — a misprediction costs one cheap failed fit, never a
832	wrong region). Fits see the whole region — maximal support, which keeps
833	the strip problem dead for any region that IS one surface. For large
834	regions, fit on a deterministic vertex subsample, validate against all
835	vertices, refit augmented with the worst offenders on a near-miss
836	(bounded retries). Most regions of most models end here.
837	
838	**(b) Scoped fit competition** — for regions the ladder cannot explain
839	(tangent chains). Seed-first multi-type competition, run INSIDE the smooth
840	region; the sharp boundary cordons the arena, so competition cost is
841	bounded and cross-region accidents are impossible.
842	
843	- **Seeds**: faces not yet claimed by any committed hypothesis, in
844	  jet-interior-first order (faces whose (κ1,κ2) best match their
845	  neighbors' — the descendant of curvature-guided seed ordering;
846	  misordering costs only time). Claimed faces never seed.
847	- **Per seed**: run the surface types' fit-and-expand from that same seed
848	  (jet-pruned rung set, as in (a)) and commit the hypothesis with the
849	  **largest validated area** (simplest-DOF tiebreak — a plane ties an
850	  infinite-radius cylinder).
851	- **Growth is two phases, and only the second is validated.** *This is the
852	  as-built shape and it differs from the original design; the difference
853	  matters, so it is spelled out here rather than left to the roadmap notes.*
854	  1. **Conditioning patch** (\`seed_patch\` → \`condition_patch\`): an
855	     **unvalidated** depth-limited BFS neighbourhood of the seed —
856	     \`MAX_PATCH_DEPTH\` 3 hops, \`SEED_PATCH_CAP\` 32 faces — optionally
857	     filtered by *jet similarity* (same coarse curvature class; magnitude
858	     within 1.5×; within \`PATCH_RADII\` = 4 curvature radii of the seed).
859	     The initial fit is a least-squares fit to that patch. \`condition_patch\`
860	     then trims fit-outlier faces until the seed validates against its own
861	     patch's fit, bottoming out at a size floor.
862	  2. **Flood**: BFS from the seed accepting a face only when the current fit
863	     validates it (vertex tolerance + centroid tolerance + orientation

2055	### Goal and thesis
2056

2058	CAD-derived meshes**, not score on the current corpus. Fragility is

2066	retires them in dependency order:

2069	   three NURBS models rotted silently because nothing watched them. You cannot

2088	### Phase 1 design: earned patches (replaces the blind patch)
2089	
2090	Replace grab-then-repair with **grow-under-validation**: BFS from the seed,
2091	admitting a frontier face only if it validates against the current fit at
2092	vertex tolerance; when a face fails, attempt **promotion** up the ladder
2093	(plane → cylinder/cone or sphere → torus), refitting accepted+candidate and
2094	requiring *every already-accepted face* to still validate; if no type
2095	validates, the face is across a seam — exclude it and record it as a
2096	**frontier face** (Phase 2 consumes these). The patch can never straddle a
2097	junction by construction, which is the exact property the blind patch lacks.
2098	Commit semantics do not change: the earned (type, params, patch) goes to the
2099	unchanged \`grow_from\` flood/refit path, and every existing commit gate
2100	(\`MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG\`, torus ratio, \`MIN_*_FACES\`, \`resolve_claims\`) keeps
2101	its meaning.
2102	
2103	What makes promotion workable at tiny support — where a free least-squares fit
2104	is hopeless (sagitta arithmetic: over a 7.5° arc on r = 0.5 the sag is
2105	~0.001 mm against a 2e-5 mm quantum, so a free radius is ~2% ≈ 200× vtol
2106	wrong) — is that **facet normals are exact** and give closed-form,
2107	DOF-reducing initializers:
2108	
2109	- **Cylinder — axis = n₁ × n₂.** A planar facet spanning two rulings of a
2110	  cylinder has its normal exactly perpendicular to the axis, at any coarseness,
2111	  so two facets with non-parallel normals give the axis exactly on
2112	  strip/quad-tessellated surfaces. Radius+origin then come from
2113	  \`fit_circle_for_axis\` (cylindrical.rs), measured well-conditioned on short
2114	  arcs (r = 0.99998 / 0.99999 / 0.50008 from 65°/60°/40° arcs). **Provenance
2115	  caveat:** a general Delaunay triangle's normal is *not* exactly
2116	  perpendicular to the axis; measure axis error per provenance (Phase 0's OCCT
2117	  meshes), and degrade to the normal-covariance axis over the earned patch
2118	  where needed — still clean, still not blind.
2119	- **Sphere — concurrent normal lines.** For any planar facet inscribed in a
2120	  sphere, the line through the facet's **circumcenter** along its normal
2121	  passes exactly through the sphere centre (equidistance). Two facets → centre
2122	  at the near-intersection (common-perpendicular midpoint), radius = distance.
2123	- **Cone** — the existing normal-covariance axis (\`smallest_eigenvector_3x3\`)
2124	  over the earned patch, guarded by \`axis_normals_consistent\`, both existing.
2125	- **Torus — meridian coplanarity, the "open case" closed.** Every torus
2126	  normal line lies in the meridian plane through its point, which contains
2127	  the axis — so each facet contributes one coplanarity constraint
2128	  \`(pᵢ − a) · (nᵢ × d) = 0\` on the axis (point a, direction d; 4 DOF; the
2129	  system is bilinear — solve by alternation or pairwise elimination). Four
2130	  facets pin the axis; then (R, r) is a 2-D circle fit in (ρ, z) profile
2131	  coordinates — \`fit_circle_2d\` already exists (toroidal.rs). **Caveats:**
2132	  rank-deficient by construction on sphere data (any axis through the centre
2133	  satisfies it) and consistent-but-degenerate on cylinder data, so ladder
2134	  order and a conditioning floor must precede it; grid-aligned quads give
2135	  near-exact meridian normals, Delaunay triangles do not. **Time-boxed**: unit
2136	  test to ~1e-9 on synthetic tori before integrating; if conditioning does not
2137	  pan out, skip it — direct torus seeding stays as today and Phase 1 is not
2138	  blocked.
2139	
2140	Two behaviours need more than validation failure:
2141	
2142	- **Ambiguity → branch, don't choose.** Two same-height faces of a cylinder
2143	  validate as a sphere centred on the axis (the hole→sphere trap at patch
2144	  scale). Grow both branches; the false one should die within a face or two
2145	  (the next face at a different height is off the sphere by ≈ Δ²/2R ≫ vtol).
2146	  Instrument branch lifetime; persistent branches mean validation is less
2147	  sharp than believed — stop and ask.
2148	- **Bent tube → drift-triggered promotion.** A bend is locally a valid
2149	  cylinder (sag of the bend over a 2 mm patch at R = 14 is ~3.6e-5 mm), so
2150	  admission never fails and promotion never triggers on residual. The signal
2151	  is **systematic fit drift**: along a straight tube successive refits are
2152	  stationary; along a bend the fitted axis precesses with a consistent sign as
2153	  support accumulates. Test drift as sign-consistency of successive axis
2154	  deltas, *not* magnitude (a magnitude bar would be a new tuned constant —
2155	  stop and ask if one seems needed). Success retires \`promote_bend\` and the
2156	  \`BEND_*\` constants; failure keeps them, and that is fine.

2164	### Reference labeling, and what it settled (Phase 1.0, 2026-07-30)
2165	
2166	\`src/reference.rs\` (\`--reference-report\`) labels every mesh face with the
2167	reference face it came from and scores the mesh against that ground truth.
2168	Step-by-step numbers are in TODO.md 1.0; what belongs here is why it exists,
2169	why it is nearly free, and the four results that change later phases.
2170	
2171	**It is a read-back, not a new computation.** Stage 1's \`--compare\` already runs
2172	\`BRepExtrema_DistShapeShape\` from every mesh face centroid to a compound of the
2173	reference's faces. That call already determines which reference face won and at
2174	what (u,v); \`min_distance_to_shape\` was returning only the distance and dropping
2175	both. \`SupportOnShape2\` hands the winner back, so ground-truth labeling of the
2176	entire mesh costs one accessor call per face that was already being computed.
2177	The alternative that was on the table — a standalone probe — would have cost far
2178	more than that and measured the wrong object: it reads raw STL triangles, where
2179	the pipeline's mesh has been repaired and quad-fused, which is why
2180	\`step_measure_tolerance\` needed a \`--quad\` flag bolted on. **The general lesson
2181	is that a measurement belongs where the computation already happens**, and the
2182	same investigation found the cost of ignoring it: \`step_measure_tolerance\` still
2183	measures against the reference *solid*, so it silently reports exactly 0 for any
2184	deviation over OCCT's hard-coded 1 µm classifier tolerance (\`aTolerance = 0.001\`
2185	in \`BRepExtrema_DistShapeShape\`'s \`SolidTreatment\`) and is correct below it —
2186	exact where the answer does not matter, zero where it does. That is the same
2187	"never measure a distance against a solid" defect fixed in the pipeline on
2188	2026-07-29, in the one place the fix did not reach. It also refines that entry:
2189	the old stage-1 centroid check was not vacuous on all convex geometry, only
2190	above 1 µm, which is exactly why correct models looked right and nobody noticed.
2191	
2192	**1. The closed-form axis error is \`perpendicularity error / |n₁ × n₂|\`.**
2193	Verified to 0.1% on \`pipe_elbow_10\` Parasolid medium: a perpendicularity max of
2194	0.0280° over a conditioning p50 of 0.0271 predicts 1.033°, and the measured
2195	error is 1.0342°, identical across all 348 pairs. One relation explains every
2196	cylinder outlier in the sweep, and it separates two causes that a raw error
2197	number confounds — normals that are not perpendicular, and perfect normals
2198	amplified by an ill-conditioned cross product.
2199	
2200	**2. The Delaunay caveat did not reproduce, and the reason is architectural.**
2201	The Phase 1 design warned that "a general Delaunay triangle's normal is not
2202	exactly perpendicular to the axis" and told 1.4 to degrade that provenance to a
2203	covariance axis. Measured, OCCT's re-meshes read perpendicularity p50 = p95 =
2204	**0.0000°** and axis error **0.0000°** at every density on five of six models.
2205	The reason is already recorded under "Mesh provenance and the seam assumption":
2206	OCCT's Delaunay is *constrained* by the pre-discretized face boundaries, so a
2207	cylinder's triangles still span two rulings and their normals are still exactly
2208	perpendicular. The provenance fallback is not needed. The single genuine
2209	non-perpendicular case corpus-wide is \`l_bracket_simple\` Fusion medium
2210	(perpendicularity p50 0.2740°), a small hole carrying 96 facets over 75 mm².
2211	
2212	**3. Adjacent facets are the worst possible pairing, and finer meshes are
2213	worse.** \`|n₁ × n₂|\` for an adjacent pair is \`sin(angular step)\` — measured p50
2214	0.0432 on stepped_block fine, which is sin(2.48°) and independently recovers
2215	Onshape's 2.5° setting. So the amplification in (1) is ~23× on a fine mesh and
2216	grows as the mesh refines. This inverts the natural assumption that a denser
2217	mesh gives a better closed-form fit, and it is a design constraint on Phase 1.2
2218	rather than a property of any exporter: **pair the seed with the angularly most
2219	distant admitted facet**, where the factor is 1 and the axis error falls to the
2220	perpendicularity error itself (under 0.032° everywhere in the corpus). A 90°
2221	reading, which is the max on three rows, is the fully degenerate pair of two
2222	facets on one ruling strip — no information rather than a wrong answer.
2223	
2224	**4. The torus initializer should not be skipped.** Phase 1.1 time-boxes it on
2225	the suspicion that the meridian-coplanarity system is too ill-conditioned to
2226	solve. Its residual — the quantity the solve drives to zero — measures p50
2227	**2.354e-5 mm** over 23 863 torus facets on stepped_block fine, which is the
2228	mesh's own float32 quantum. The constraint is satisfied to the limit of what the
2229	mesh can express.
2230	
2231	**The seam assumption now has a direct measurement, and it holds.** Phase 0.5b
2232	measured only half of Design Principle #2 — that mesh *vertices* lie on the
2233	reference surfaces. The other half, that a *facet* never straddles a face
2234	boundary, is what the earned patch depends on and had never been measured.
2235	Labeling gives it for free: 51 of 157 483 facets across 79 meshes disagree about
2236	their own label across their own interior, **0.032%**. The number is an estimate
2237	rather than a bound in either direction — it over-reports where a neighbouring
2238	face curves back within reach of a sample point, and under-reports a straddle
2239	confined to a facet's rim, since the samples cover the middle of a facet — but
2240	both error terms are bounded by something this small, so the conclusion survives
2241	the imprecision even though the count does not. The only recurring cluster is
2242	exactly 12 facets on \`stepped_block_toroidal\` under OCCT coarse/medium and
2243	Fusion medium/fine, absent under Parasolid and under OCCT fine; consistent with
2244	coarse facets spanning that model's known narrow flat regions, and not chased.
2245	
2246	**Segmentation scoring closes the over-segmentation hole**, which this document
2247	recorded as needing its own step. Two area-weighted, threshold-free numbers from
2248	the same labels: \`ref coverage\` = \`Σ_R max_S area(R,S) / Σ area\` is 1.0 when no
2249	reference face was split across several of our surfaces, and \`surf purity\` =
2250	\`Σ_S max_R area(S,R) / Σ area\` is 1.0 when none of our surfaces spans several
2251	reference faces. They separate the two failure directions that "over-segmented"
2252	was being used for loosely. On the case that motivated it — \`rand_filleted_box_0\`,
2253	9 surfaces against a reference 26, passing every existing gate at 6.7e-3
2254	relative volume — they read **1.0000 and 0.2201**, correctly diagnosing merging
2255	rather than splitting, where a correct model reads 1.0000/1.0000. This satisfies
2256	the standing rule about metrics: asked what it returns for a grossly wrong
2257	input, it returns something unmistakably different from a right one.
2258	
2259	**Freeform reference faces, and the property that actually governs facet-normal
2260	exactness.** The normal report initially covered only analytic reference faces,
2261	which is 32–66% of a NURBS model's area — the rest was announced as unmeasured
2262	by the \`analytic area\` figure but not scored. Extending it needed only the
2263	footpoint (u,v) that \`ParOnFaceS2\` already reports from the same distance query,
2264	plus \`GeomLProp_SLProps\` (which arrived in the bindings on 2026-07-30).
2265	\`SLProps\` is used rather than a raw \`D1U × D1V\` because it answers
2266	\`IsNormalDefined\`, and a B-spline face has poles and seams where the normal
2267	genuinely does not exist; those facets are excluded rather than scored as an
2268	error of some size. Over the 8-model NURBS corpus every freeform facet evaluated
2269	and none landed on a pole.
2270	
2271	The result is not the obvious one. Freeform facet normals are 2–3 orders of
2272	magnitude less exact than analytic ones — \`bspline_terrain\` p50 0.9396°,
2273	\`hill_with_hole\` 0.9014°, against 0.0000° for planes — but that comparison is
2274	confounded, because the corpus's freeform models are ~100× coarser per facet.
2275	Ruledness separates them better: **\`bspline_wave\`'s *extrusion* faces read p50
2276	0.0507° at 16.7 mm² per facet, while \`bspline_terrain\`'s B-spline faces read
2277	0.9396° at 0.53 mm² per facet — the 30× coarser surface is 19× more exact.**
2278	
2279	**But ruledness is necessary, not sufficient — the real condition is that the
2280	tessellation be ruling-ALIGNED.** (Raised by the user, then measured; an earlier
2281	version of this section claimed ruledness governs, which is wrong.) The exact
2282	statement: a facet on a cylinder has its normal perpendicular to the axis **iff
2283	two of its vertices share a ruling**. Parametrize the cylinder and project the
2284	vertices along the axis; they land on a circle, the facet's plane is parallel to
2285	the axis iff those projections are collinear, and three points on a circle are
2286	collinear only when two coincide. A tessellator that lays triangles *across* the
2287	ruling family therefore produces skewed normals on a geometrically perfect
2288	cylinder.
2289	
2290	Measured over the 12 cylinder-bearing models, 12 275 cylinder facets: facets
2291	with an edge on a ruling are perpendicular to a worst case of **0.0006°**, while
2292	the **25.6%** that straddle three or more rulings reach **1.0528°**. Every
2293	non-zero perpendicularity in the corpus comes from a straddling facet, so
2294	alignment is the whole story — though straddling is necessary rather than
2295	sufficient for a *large* error, since the tilt grows with a facet's angular
2296	spread and shrinks with its axial one. That also explains the extrusion number
2297	above: 0.0507° rather than 0.0000° is itself evidence that those facets are not
2298	aligned, because alignment would force exactness.
2299	
2300	Where alignment comes from: quad fusion is a **23× discriminator but not a
2301	guarantee** — 2.7% of fused quads straddle against 62.3% of triangles (a
2302	coplanar quad on a cylinder *usually* spans two rulings, but four points on an
2303	elliptical section are coplanar too). Simple geometry gets alignment for free —
2304	a plain cylinder under OCCT is 120 quads / 0 triangles, 100% aligned, which is
2305	the real reason result (2)'s OCCT re-meshes read 0.0000°, sharper than "the
2306	rulings survive as face boundaries". Straddling concentrates where a tessellator
2307	cannot lay a clean strip: \`stepped_block_toroidal\` straddles 49–53% at every
2308	OCCT density, and its narrow flat regions between fillets are exactly its known
2309	pathology.
2310	
2311	This is *better* news for Phase 1.2 than the aggregate suggested, because the
2312	test needs no ground truth. Given a candidate axis, the minimum angular gap
2313	between a facet's vertices says whether that facet's normal can be trusted, so
2314	the earn loop can **select** the facets it initializes from rather than hoping.

> I'm getting a clearer sense of the project structure now. I should review the stage-2 code to see how compete.rs and classify.rs are implemented, and check the section about the blind patch issue since it's directly relevant to understanding the problem. The key thing I'm trying to pin down is the user's approach: starting with a single seed face and progressively expanding it while promoting the fitting strategy from plane to cylinder to cone to sphere as more faces get added.
> 
> The user's idea is to use the simplest fit that stays within tolerances, which echoes an earlier Phase 1.2 design that was attempted but never shipped. That earlier approach ran into several documented failure modes — validated-only growth creating a chicken-and-egg problem, breadth-first collection being wrong for developables, spread-first collection straddling junctions, curvature similarity being insufficient, and validation needing to trim rather than filter. The crucial difference here is that instead of using type-specific fitters locked into a decision ladder, the user is proposing a general quadric fitter or a hierarchy of fits where promotion happens continuously — defaulting to the simplest surface that fits when there isn't enough support to pin down a more complex one.
> 
> This partially addresses that first failure mode: a general quadric fitter with regularization could always produce some fit at any support size, whereas the ladder can't (you can't fit a cone from two facets, but a regularized quadric could return the plane or cylinder that actually fits, and growth doesn't need to decide the type upfront). The real question becomes whether there's fitting math where the model space is continuous and nested, so promotion isn't a discrete re-decision but a natural sharpening of parameters as support grows. The literature offers several approaches — Taubin's method, Pratt's method, gradient-one fitting, and Andrews & Séquin's type-constrained direct fitting of quadric surfaces. Quadrics cover planes, spheres, cylinders, cones, ellipsoids, paraboloids, and hyperboloids, though not tori.
> 
> But tori are quartic surfaces, specifically Dupin cyclides, which actually form a unified fitting space that includes tori, cones, cylinders, spheres, and planes as special cases. There's classical work on cyclide fitting in Lie-sphere and Laguerre geometry frameworks where cyclides can be represented linearly, plus applied work on direct fitting and recognition from surface meshes. A unified cyclide fitter would elegantly handle all these analytic surface types in a single continuous model space, sidestepping the question of whether to upgrade to quartics or use specialized torus fitting. Dupin cyclides form a 9-parameter family (roughly 3 shape parameters plus 6 pose), far more tractable than general quartics with their 34 degrees of freedom and poor conditioning. There's likely an even more elegant approach emerging here. So the meridian coplanarity condition in the initialize.rs code is actually the linear complex constraint from kinematic fitting — the axis of rotation emerges directly from that linear line congruence. This unified framework classifies surfaces by their velocity field: pure rotation gives surfaces of revolution, translation gives extrusions, helical motion gives helical surfaces. Planes, cylinders, cones, spheres, and tori all fit this scheme, though some have degenerate cases like the sphere's three-parameter family of rotation axes.
> 
> Now I'm working through the null space dimensions to understand the symmetry groups: a cylinder's normal lines all pass through and stay perpendicular to its axis, giving a 2D null space for rotation about that axis plus translation along it. For a plane, the normal lines are all parallel, so the velocity field can be any translation in the plane's tangent directions or rotation about any axis parallel to the normal.
> 
> This reveals something elegant: the null-space dimension of the kinematic system directly classifies surface types. Planes and spheres both have 3D null spaces (though they're distinguished by whether normals are parallel or concurrent), cylinders have 2D, cones and tori have 1D, and generic surfaces have 0D.
> 
> What's powerful is that this is entirely linear and incrementally computable—just a rank-1 update to a 6×6 Gram matrix as each face is added, where each row stacks position and normal vectors together. The framework handles the measured bias in facet normals—they're O(Δθ²/8) approximations, so they seed least-squares fitting rather than provide final answers. The kinematic null space guides type selection and initialization, then type-specific vertex-based LSQ refines the result, which aligns with the project's principle of taking directions from normals but magnitudes from vertices. The user's alternative—a general algebraic quadric fitter with 10 coefficients—runs into practical constraints: it needs at least 9 points, and the ill-conditioning from adjacent facets compounds the problem.
> 
> Beyond the data requirements, the quadric family itself is mismatched to CAD geometry. It covers ellipsoids, paraboloids, hyperboloids, and hyperbolic paraboloids—shapes rarely used in CAD—while completely excluding the torus, which appears in every fillet. This creates a double failure: spurious fits where a general quadric through cylinder points could be any elliptic cylinder or hyperboloid, destroying identifiability, while missing the surfaces that actually matter in practice.
> 
> The eigenvalue-based type extraction from a fitted quadric has no exactness guarantee, and the repeated eigenvalue constraint isn't even linear or quadratic. Algebraic distance bias compounds the problem—Taubin normalization helps but doesn't eliminate it—and when fitting to nearly-degenerate data like a small patch on a large cylinder, the null space becomes multi-dimensional, forcing an arbitrary projection onto a subspace.
> 
> A proper solution would need a regularization hierarchy that prefers planes over spheres over cylinders, but that's essentially rebuilding the algebraic solver's logic with worse conditioning and unit scaling problems (quadratic terms carry different dimensional powers than linear ones, a scaling issue already noted for Plücker systems and worse for quadrics). The torus-as-quartic approach is even more problematic: 35 coefficients means 34 degrees of freedom, requiring at least 34 points with atrocious conditioning from moment matrices of degree 8.
> 
> In practice, torus fitting uses established routes instead: the SOR/kinematic approach (fit axis first, then profile circle), the medial/tube-center method, or the Dupin cyclide route via Lie-sphere geometry, where cyclides fit linearly in the sphere space by mapping each surface point and normal to a contact element on the Lie quadric.
> 
> Canal surfaces—envelopes of sphere families—provide another framework: in the cyclographic/Laguerre model, an oriented sphere becomes a point in R^4 (center plus signed radius), so a canal surface's sphere family traces a curve in that space, and for a Dupin cyclide that curve is a conic lying on a specific locus. There's a whole body of work on this—Peternell and Pottmann on canal surface reconstruction, Krasauskas and Mäurer on cyclides. The key insight is that each mesh vertex with its normal defines a one-parameter family of tangent spheres (a line in R^4), and the spine-sphere curve of a canal surface must pass through all of them. But the practical reverse-engineering literature—Lukács, Martin, Marshall, and others—actually uses specialized fitters for each surface type rather than trying to unify everything under one algebraic framework.
> 
> The field really converged on per-type geometric fitting with shared machinery for estimating axes. And there's a direct precedent for the user's "simplest fit that fits" idea: Besl and Jain's 1988 work on segmentation through variable-order surface fitting, which does exactly that—region growing where the polynomial order escalates (planar to biquadratic to bicubic to biquartic) as needed, always choosing the lowest order that stays within tolerance. That's the classic formulation, and it's been extended by others like Leonardis, Gupta, and Bajcsy using model selection criteria like MDL.
> 
> More recent work has tackled this from different angles—Attene and colleagues use bottom-up merging with primitive fitters that pick the best-fitting shape per cluster, which is conceptually close but inverts the direction. There's also the variational shape approximation approach with Lloyd iteration and proxy-based methods that can handle spheres and cylinders, which the project apparently has in reserve already. Based on the search results, here's information about the Besl and Jain segmentation research:

"Segmentation through Variable-Order Surface Fitting" is a paper by Paul J. Besl and Ramesh C. Jain published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence in 1988.

**Overview:**
The work uses a piecewise-smooth surface model for image data that possesses surface coherence properties to develop an algorithm that simultaneously segments a large class of images into regions of arbitrary shape and approximates image data with bivariate functions.

**Two-Stage Approach:**
Besl and Jain introduced a two-step initial algorithm: (1) coarse segmentation, in which seed pixels are selected based on the mean and Gaussian curvature of each point and its sign; and (2) region growing, in which interactive region growing is used to refine the result based on a variable order bivariate surface fitting.

**Methodology:**
Surface curvature sign labeling provides an initial coarse image segmentation, which is refined by an iterative region-growing method based on variable-order surface fitting.

This seminal work has been influential in image segmentation and continues to be cited in contemporary research on point cloud segmentation and surface analysis.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Bénière's work on reverse engineering CAD meshes:

## Overview

Bénière's work presents a comprehensive method to reconstruct a B-Rep model composed of planes, spheres, cylinders and cones from a 3D mesh whose vertex coordinates are considered exact.

## Method and Approach

The detection method uses curvature features to recover each primitive type, with segmentation based on the curvature feature computed for each vertex. Simple primitives like planes, spheres, cones and cylinders have specific curvature characteristics: planes have zero curvature at each point, spheres have equal curvature at all points, while cone and cylinder points are defined by one principal curvature equal to 0 with the other principal curvature equal to the inverse of the radius.

## Process Steps

The approach comprises three sequential steps: primitive extraction, wire construction, and solid creation. Initially, the matching geometric primitive (such as a plane, sphere, cylinder, or cone) corresponding locally to the 3D mesh of interest is determined by analyzing differential geometry operators.

## Application Context

In reverse engineering, the aim is to reconstruct a continuous model of an object (a B-Rep model for example) from a discretized representation (as a 3D mesh).

# Summary: Type-Constrained Direct Fitting of Quadric Surfaces

## (1) Kinematic Surface Fitting as First Step

The authors employ kinematic fitting to establish an initial linear system for quadric surface recovery. The unknowns include parameters representing rigid motions (rotation, translation) and scaling/dilation operations. Each equation row is constructed from either point constraints or normal vector constraints at sampled surface locations.

For points, the constraint comes from the intersection conditions; for normals, gradient-based information provides directional constraints. The method accommodates several field types including rotations (SO(3)), translations (R³), central dilations (scalar scaling), and helical motions (screw parameters).

## (2) Solution Space Dimension to Quadric Type Mapping

The dimensionality of the solution space directly correlates with quadric classification. Lower-dimensional solution spaces indicate more constrained geometric types (spheres, cylinders), while higher-dimensional spaces correspond to general quadrics. This relationship allows the authors to infer surface type from fitting rank.

## (3) Constraining to Specific Quadric Types

For specialized types like circular cones and cylinders, the authors impose additional algebraic constraints beyond the basic kinematic framework. These constraints reduce the degrees of freedom to match the geometric requirements of each surface class, forcing the fitted solution toward these restricted families.

## (4) Degenerate Cases and Linear Limitations

The paper acknowledges that "no linear method exists for cones and cylinders from points alone." Degenerate cases arise when fitting data cannot uniquely determine surface parameters; the authors address this through constraint-based disambiguation rather than purely algebraic approaches.

## (5) Torus Fitting

The document does not substantially address torus fitting methodology within the presented framework.

Probe 3 censuses strip-band ambiguity across the corpus to find what fraction of cylinders are single-centroid-height strips where the sphere interpretation stays viable in both views, sizing how much structural gates still matter. All three reuse the existing invariants machinery.

## TL;DR

Your instinct — one nested fitter, promote only when the data forces it, default to the simplest surface that fits — is sound and has a 40-year literature trail (Besl & Jain 1988 onward). But the **general algebraic quadric is the wrong nested family** for this codebase, for reasons your own measurements already pin down. The right family is hiding in plain sight: the **generalized kinematic system** — one linear solve from facet positions+normals whose *null-space dimension* is exactly the "simplest surface that fits" ladder, and whose four corners you have already built separately in `initialize.rs` without naming the whole. Tori then need **neither a quartic nor only a torus-specific fitter**: the kinematic solve pins the axis, and in (ρ,z) profile coordinates the torus is just a circle — a linear 2-DOF fit, with sphere/cylinder/cone as the circle's own degenerate cases.

A crucial framing first: this proposal is Phase 1.2's earn loop with the missing piece supplied. The earn loop died on a chicken-and-egg — "a cone cannot be fitted from the two facets a validated loop has when it must first decide, so it never grows." A rank-adaptive fitter dissolves exactly that: **the type is an output of the fit, never a precondition for it**. Whether that actually removes the need for the blind patch is a hypothesis to measure, not a fact — but it targets the specific mechanism that forced Phase 1.2 back onto `seed_patch`+`condition_patch`.

## Option A — the generalized kinematic ladder (recommended backbone)

Fit an instantaneous similarity velocity field `v(p) = γp + c×p + c̄` (7 unknowns: scaling γ, rotation c, translation c̄) tangent to the surface. Each facet contributes one linear row:

```
γ·(pᵢ·nᵢ) + c·(pᵢ×nᵢ) + c̄·nᵢ = 0
```

This is Pottmann's kinematic surface fitting as generalized by [Andrews & Séquin](http://graphics.berkeley.edu/papers/Andrews-GBI-2013-03/index.html) ([type-constrained companion paper](https://www.cad-journal.net/files/vol_11/CAD_11(1)_2014_107-119.pdf)) — both already in SURFACE_FITTING.md's sources. What the papers don't emphasize, and what makes it the answer to your question, is the **null-space dimension ladder**. For exact data:

| surface | tangent fields | null dim |
|---|---|---|
| plane | 2 in-plane translations, rotation ⊥, scaling about an in-plane point | **4** |
| sphere | rotations about center | **3** |
| cylinder | rotation about + translation along axis | **2** |
| cone | rotation about axis + dilation from apex (γ≠0) | **2** |
| torus / SOR / extrusion / helix | one field | **1** |
| freeform | none | **0** |

The dimension order *is* your simplicity order, and "insufficient support to pin down the result" becomes a *rank statement instead of a residual statement*: one facet gives rank 1 (everything fits → plane), and as faces accrue the null space contracts until the surviving generators name the type. Your sphere example resolves itself — plane at one facet, sphere as soon as three facet-normal lines are concurrent in 2D spread — and the cone never appears as an intermediate because sphere data never produces γ-structure. **The promotion chain is emergent; you never enumerate plane→cylinder→cone→sphere transitions.**

Three facts make this nearly free to try:

1. **You already built all four corners.** The torus meridian solve `qᵢ·d + nᵢ·m = 0` is the rigid sub-block (γ=0); cone Option A `γ(p·n) + a·n = 0` is the scaling sub-block (c=0); `cylinder()`'s `n₁×n₂` and `sphere()`'s concurrent normal lines are 2-row closed forms of the same structure. The unification is a 7×7 Gram matrix that *reads which structure is present* instead of assuming one per solve.
2. **It's incremental.** One rank-1 update of a 7×7 symmetric matrix per admitted face, one tiny eigensolve per promotion check. Your per-type LM fitters can't do that; this can, so the check can run at every face admission.
3. **Your measured lessons transfer verbatim**: normalize rows to patch centroid/extent (the meridian solve's recorded scale-mismatch lesson); take the result as a *seed* for the exact vertex-based fitters, never as the answer (chord-plane lean, O(Δθ²/8) ≈ 200× vtol); select initializer rows by ruling alignment (`min_ruling_gap_rad` exists) while collection stays validation-gated — which is precisely the similarity-vs-spread separation Phase 1.2 discovered the hard way.

One warning from your own record: **don't threshold the spectrum to decide rank** — that's the "detector needs just one threshold" trap, and the measured sphere-vs-torus conditioning gap (2.06e-6 vs 9.2e-4, only 450×, data-dependent) says the separation isn't there. Use the spectrum to *order* candidate interpretations; let vertex-tolerance validation decide, exactly as the jet prior works today.

And one honest limit: the normals channel kills the measured sphere-impostor pathology (393/397 cylinders) only when the support spans ≥2 distinct facet-centroid heights. A single-strip band — vertices on two rings, all centroids at one height — is genuinely sphere-ambiguous in *both* the vertex and normal views. There the load stays on structural gates (`MIN_AXIAL_SWEEP_DEG`, solid-angle coverage) and on Phase 1's branch-don't-choose. No fitting math dissolves a true ambiguity.

## Option B — the literal general quadric (your stated option)

Fit `x^TAx + b^Tx + c = 0` (Taubin/Pratt), watch A's eigenvalues for degeneracy, project onto the nearest constrained type. Assessment against your own measurements:

- **No torus** — the family omits the one surface every fillet needs, while *including* ellipsoids, paraboloids, hyperboloids that CAD essentially never uses. On support that barely pins a circular cylinder, the best algebraic quadric is generically some elliptic cylinder or hyperboloid — the impostor problem, made systematic.
- Your Invariants section measured that vertex-only algebra *cannot* discriminate types (impostor residuals at 0.2–0.5 quanta, sphere beating cylinder on its own support). A points-only quadric fitter inherits that blindness in full; the kinematic rows add the normal information that (partially) escapes it.
- The type-projection step is not sound: a circular cone needs a repeated eigenvalue, a condition [Andrews & Séquin](http://graphics.berkeley.edu/papers/Andrews-TCD-2013-06/index.html) note can't be imposed linearly or quadratically — this is already recorded as Option B's weakness in SURFACE_FITTING.md, with its ≥9-point cost and algebraic-distance bias.

Verdict: fine as a *triage* signal (analytic-vs-freeform, initializer of last resort), wrong as the backbone. "Upgrade to quartic" for tori is strictly worse: 34 DOF, ≥34 points, a degree-8 moment matrix whose conditioning is hopeless on patches, and an even larger zoo of irrelevant surfaces. Nobody in the reverse-engineering literature fits tori that way.

## Option C — per-type fitters with degeneracy-safe parameterizations

The conservative version: keep the exact per-type fitters and adopt the [Lukács–Martin–Marshall](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/BFb0055697) (ECCV 1998) parameterizations, which were designed for exactly your property: *"as the principal curvatures decrease, the results naturally become closer to the surfaces of simpler type, unlike other methods which may diverge."* Curvature-space parameters (k = 1/r, taper = tan α) put the simpler surface at a regular interior point of the parameter space instead of at infinity — the move your cone taper parameterization and the bent-tube k = 1/R already made independently. Promotion machinery is then the only new code, and the 2026-08-06 torus fix (candidate pool + select-best + validate) already established the house pattern for it. This is the smallest step, but it leaves the four hand-built initializers un-unified and keeps promotion as hand-enumerated edges.

## Option D — Dupin cyclides (the exotic one, for completeness)

The mathematically "right" single family containing exactly {plane, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus} plus ring cyclides is the [Dupin cyclides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dupin_cyclide): in the space of oriented spheres a cyclide's generating family is a conic, so there is a genuinely unified linear-ish fitting theory ([Druoton/Garnier/Langevin line of work](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00006-014-0453-5)). But that literature is construction/blend-oriented; robust fitting from meshes is thin; the Minkowski–Lorentz machinery is heavy; and the extra coverage (general cyclides) is a liability in a pipeline whose discipline is "simplest surface that validates." Not worth it now — worth remembering if variable-geometry blends ever become a target.

## How the torus question resolves

Under Option A the torus needs no special family at all: the 1-dim rotational null space hands you the axis, and in (ρ,z) profile coordinates the SOR family becomes 2D curve fitting — line ρ=R (cylinder), sloped line (cone), circle centered on axis (sphere), offset circle (torus) — all linear, all trivially nested, which is the "Unified SOR Framework" section SURFACE_FITTING.md already sketches. Keep the existing torus LM (and the tube-center method) as the vertex-based refiner; the measured meridian-solve residual (p50 at the float32 quantum) says the axis half already works.

## What the fitting math does *not* solve

Carrying over from the measured record, unchanged by any option: **plane starvation of the B-spline rung** (a single-facet plane always validates, so freeform regions would tile into analytic confetti — the NURBS-collapse measurement; the leftover-coherence policy must survive); **branching at genuine ambiguity** (ring pairs); **trim-not-filter** at promotion failure (excluded face → frontier, keep the patch); boundary placement stays with flood + `resolve_claims`; and single-seed growth makes seed choice matter, which is exactly what the S/G invariant families instrument.

## What I'd measure first

House style says instrument before mechanism, and all three probes fit the `--invariant-report` harness:

1. **Rank-ladder read on truth**: accumulate the normalized 7×7 on each reference face's own facets at increasing support; measure at what support, eigengap, and straddling fraction the null-dim reads the true type. (~150 lines, diagnostics only.)
2. **Junction contamination race**: same read on supports deliberately grown across tangent junctions — does the rank signal move before or after vertex validation fails?
3. **Strip-band census**: what fraction of corpus cylinders are single-centroid-height strips (where sphere stays live in both views) — this sizes the permanent role of the structural gates.

## Literature map

- [Besl & Jain 1988, *Segmentation through Variable-Order Surface Fitting*](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/3881/) — the direct precedent for seed-and-promote region growing (curvature-sign seeds, lowest order that fits, escalate on demand).
- [Lukács, Martin, Marshall, ECCV 1998](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/BFb0055697) (+ [journal version](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2400512_Geometric_Least-Squares_Fitting_of_Spheres_Cylinders_Cones_and_Tori)) — graceful-degeneration parameterizations for sphere/cylinder/cone/torus.
- [Andrews & Séquin, *Generalized, Basis-Independent Kinematic Surface Fitting*](http://graphics.berkeley.edu/papers/Andrews-GBI-2013-03/index.html) and [*Type-Constrained Direct Fitting of Quadric Surfaces*](https://www.cad-journal.net/files/vol_11/CAD_11(1)_2014_107-119.pdf) — the Option A machinery.
- [Leonardis et al., recover-and-select](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-57956-7_35) — grow many, keep the simplest description; use its orchestration, not its MDL scoring (your 2026-07-28 measurement refuted complexity pricing in this regime).
- [Wu & Kobbelt 2005, hybrid VSA](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2005.00852.x), [quadric-proxy VSA](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/Quadric-Surface-Extraction-by-Variational-Shape-Approximation.pdf), and [VSA + model selection](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01577.x) — the global-competition alternative already in your reserve list.
- [Bénière et al.](https://perso.liris.cnrs.fr/gilles.gesquiere/Publications/2011_SPIE_EI_Beniere.pdf) ([CAD 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0010448513001012)) — the only sustained prior work in your exact regime (exact-vertex CAD meshes → B-rep); notably stops at plane/sphere/cylinder/cone, no torus.
- [Split-and-fit, SIGGRAPH 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.05261) — representative of the current learned/partition line; doesn't meet the exactness/determinism bar but useful as a survey of the field's framing.

My recommendation: **Option A as the backbone, with Option C's parameterization discipline in the refiners**, quadrics demoted to triage, cyclides declined. If you want, I can record this survey in SURFACE_FITTING.md alongside the cone-options section (it's the same genre), or go straight to building probe 1.

2361	    if v.is_empty() {
2362	        return f64::NAN;
2363	    }
2364	    v.sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap());
2365	    let i = ((v.len() - 1) as f64 * q).round() as usize;
2366	    v[i]
2367	}

2515	/// Jaccard index of two sorted face sets.
2516	fn jaccard(a: &[usize], b: &HashSet<usize>) -> f64 {
2517	    if a.is_empty() && b.is_empty() {
2518	        return 1.0;
2519	    }
2520	    let inter = a.iter().filter(|f| b.contains(f)).count();
2521	    let union = a.len() + b.len() - inter;
2522	    if union == 0 {
2523	        1.0
2524	    } else {
2525	        inter as f64 / union as f64
2526	    }
2527	}

1	//! Closed-form initializers (Phase 1.1): a surface's parameters from a handful
2	//! of facets, exactly, with no iteration and no seed patch.
3	//!
4	//! Phase 1's earned patch grows face by face under validation, which means it
5	//! must fit a surface to *tiny* support — where a free least-squares fit is
6	//! hopeless. The sagitta arithmetic: over a 7.5° arc on r = 0.5 the sag is
7	//! ~0.001 mm against a 2e-5 mm mesh quantum, so a free radius comes out ~2%
8	//! wrong, about 200× the vertex tolerance. What rescues it is that **facet
9	//! normals carry exact information**, which turns each surface type into a
10	//! small linear problem rather than an optimization.
11	//!
12	//! Nothing here iterates and nothing here is tuned. Every constant is a
13	//! numeric-conditioning floor — it decides whether a quantity is *defined*,
14	//! never whether a fit is *good* — and each is documented as such at its
15	//! definition.
16	//!
17	//! # Which facets to initialize from, and why it matters more than the formula
18	//!
19	//! Phase 1.0 measured two things that make facet *selection* part of the
20	//! algorithm rather than an afterthought (numbers in TODO.md 1.0):
21	//!
22	//! 1. **The axis error is \`perpendicularity error / |n₁ × n₂|\`**, verified to
23	//!    0.1%. Adjacent facets differ in normal by the exporter's angular step, so
24	//!    \`|n₁ × n₂| ≈ sin(step)\` — 0.043 on a fine mesh, a ~23× amplification that
25	//!    gets *worse* as the mesh refines. So pair the angularly most distant
26	//!    facets available, never neighbours.
27	//! 2. **A facet's normal is perpendicular to the axis iff two of its vertices
28	//!    share a ruling** ([\`min_ruling_gap_rad\`]). 25.6% of corpus cylinder facets
29	//!    straddle three or more rulings, and they carry *all* of the
30	//!    perpendicularity error — aligned facets are exact to 0.0006° worst case
31	//!    over the whole corpus, straddling ones reach 1.0528°.
32	//!
33	//! Both are checkable here without ground truth, so [\`select_axis_pair\`] does
34	//! it in two passes: pick the most distant normal pair to get a provisional
35	//! axis, then re-pick among the facets that are ruling-aligned *with respect to
36	//! that axis*. The instrument that measured (2) and the code that acts on it
37	//! call the same function, so they cannot drift apart.

94	/// Below this, two unit normals are parallel to within double-precision noise

113	/// The second-smallest eigenvalue must exceed this fraction of the largest for

116	/// **A numerical floor and nothing more.** It was tempting to make this a rank

118	/// rank-deficient by construction on sphere data, where every line through the
119	/// centre satisfies it. Measured, that discrimination is not available at this
120	/// ratio: the degenerate sphere patch reads \`l1/l5\` = 2.06e-6 and the hardest

122	/// data-dependence in between. Choosing a cut there is the "detector needs just
123	/// one threshold" trap, so it is not chosen here.
124	///

126	/// (ρ, z) profile is a circle centred on the axis, so its fitted major radius

128	/// discrimination is the ladder's job and validation's, not this floor's — which
129	/// is what the plan meant by "ladder order and a conditioning floor must precede

137	/// The smallest angular gap, in radians, between any two of a facet's vertices
138	/// measured around the axis \`(axis_pos, axis_dir)\` — zero exactly when two
139	/// vertices share a ruling.
140	///
141	/// This decides whether a facet normal on a ruled surface is perpendicular to
142	/// the axis at all. Parametrize the cylinder as
143	/// \`p(θ, z) = a + r(cos θ · u + sin θ · v) + z · d\`. The facet's plane contains
144	/// \`d\` — equivalently \`n ⟂ d\` — iff the vertices, projected along \`d\` onto the
145	/// plane perpendicular to it, are collinear. They land on a circle of radius
146	/// \`r\`, and three points on a circle are collinear only when two of them
147	/// coincide. **So \`n ⟂ d\` exactly when two vertices share a ruling**, and a
148	/// triangle straddling three distinct rulings tilts its normal off perpendicular
149	/// however perfect the underlying cylinder is.
150	pub(crate) fn min_ruling_gap_rad(
151	    mesh: &ConnectedMesh,
152	    fi: usize,
153	    axis_pos: [f64; 3],
154	    axis_dir: [f64; 3],
155	) -> Option<f64> {
156	    let mut d = axis_dir;
157	    if normalize3(&mut d) == 0.0 {
158	        return None;
159	    }
160	    let (u, v) = perpendicular_basis(&d);
161	
162	    let face = &mesh.faces[fi];
163	    let n = face.vertex_count as usize;
164	    if n < 3 {
165	        return None;
166	    }
167	    let mut thetas = Vec::with_capacity(n);
168	    for k in 0..n {
169	        let vtx = &mesh.vertices[face.vertex_indices[k]];
170	        let w = [
171	            vtx.x - axis_pos[0],
172	            vtx.y - axis_pos[1],
173	            vtx.z - axis_pos[2],
174	        ];
175	        let axial = dot3(&w, &d);
176	        let radial = [
177	            w[0] - axial * d[0],
178	            w[1] - axial * d[1],
179	            w[2] - axial * d[2],
180	        ];
181	        thetas.push(dot3(&radial, &v).atan2(dot3(&radial, &u)));
182	    }
183	
184	    let mut min_gap = f64::MAX;
185	    for i in 0..n {
186	        for j in (i + 1)..n {
187	            let mut delta = (thetas[i] - thetas[j]).abs();
188	            if delta > std::f64::consts::PI {
189	                delta = std::f64::consts::TAU - delta;
190	            }
191	            min_gap = min_gap.min(delta);
192	        }
193	    }
194	    Some(min_gap)
195	}

197	/// \`|n_i × n_j|\` — how well-conditioned the pair is as an axis source, and
198	/// exactly the denominator in the amplification law.

268	    }

> For a sphere centered at the origin, the rotation generators c×p satisfy the null space condition exactly regardless of position, since (c×p)·p = 0 identically. However, using the centroid for the facet chord plane introduces O(h²) error because the centroid doesn't align with the circumcenter where the plane normal passes through the sphere's center. This suggests switching to the circumcenter for sphere-exactness, though that's a per-facet consideration.
> 
> I'm weighing whether to stick with the centroid and let the probe measure residuals, or explore alternatives like using facet-vertex pairs—though that breaks down since vertex normals aren't well-defined. Another angle: for a plane-tangent facet, the constraint v(p)·n = 0 should hold exactly at the true surface point with its true normal, so the error comes from using the facet plane's normal and points on the facet instead.
> 
> Actually, evaluating at each vertex of the facet using the facet's normal is cleaner—vertices sit exactly on the surface, so v(p_vertex) is exact, and the only error source is the normal mismatch. For an aligned cylinder quad, the facet normal is perpendicular to the axis exactly, and vertices are on the surface, but the circumferential direction at a vertex isn't perpendicular to the chord connecting vertices, so there's still a nonzero error term that scales with the geometry.
> 
> The centroid turns out to be the right evaluation point for a cylinder quad because its angle is the midpoint of the quad, which pairs perfectly with the chord-plane geometry—that's what makes it exact. For a cone quad, the facet plane passes through the apex exactly, so the potential is zero at any point on the plane including the centroid, and by symmetry the normal lies in the meridian plane at the centroid's angle, as does the centroid itself. So the circumcenter is exact for sphere facets, while the centroid works for cylinders and cones—they coincide for equilateral triangles but diverge otherwise. For a quad on a sphere, the four points are concyclic since they're coplanar and lie on the sphere, which means...
> 
> Actually, this is the key design decision that probe 1 should measure: how much error each evaluation point choice introduces across different surface types. I'll compute the row at both the centroid and the circumcenter (projected onto the facet plane, using the best-fit circle center for quads) and compare the results.
> 
> But I'm overcomplicating this. The real deliverable is determining at what support level the null-space dimension reads correctly. The evaluation-point question is secondary—I can measure it by computing the true null-space generators from the reference parameters and checking how well they satisfy the measured rows. That directly quantifies row exactness without guessing the right evaluation point.
> 
> So my probe will track per reference face and support size: the spectrum of relative eigenvalues, the predicted null dimension and type from the largest ratio gap, whether the prediction matches the true type, the straddle fraction of the support, and the residual of true generators against the measured rows—essentially asking whether the true answer lives in the measured null space.
